## **B.1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

**==> picture [32 x 12] intentionally omitted <==**

## _**Decision problem**_ 

This single technology appraisal evaluates the clinical and cost effectiveness of benralizumab as an add-on treatment for adult patients with relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) receiving oral corticosteroids (OCS) with or without stable immunosuppressive (IS) therapy. The anticipated marketing authorisation wording is: “******* ** ********* ** ** ****** ********* *** ***** ******** **** ********* ** ********** ************ ************** **** 

*************” 

The decision problem addressed in this submission, compared with the final scope issued by NICE, is summarised in Table 1.

|---|---|---|---|

|**Intervention**|Benralizumab|In line with final scope|Throughout the submission, benralizumab should be<br>considered as benralizumab + SoC, where SoC is<br>defined as OCS with or without stable IS. This aligns with<br>the use of benralizumab in MANDARA1|
|**Comparator(s)**|Established clinical management without<br>benralizumab, including:<br>•<br>OCS (do not currently have a<br>marketing authorisation in the UK for<br>this indication)<br>•<br>CYC (does not currently have a<br>marketing authorisation in the UK for<br>this indication)<br>•<br>Other IS agents (do not currently<br>have a marketing authorisation in the<br>UK for this indication)<br>•<br>RTX (does not currently have a<br>marketing authorisation in the UK for<br>this indication)|Established clinical<br>management, henceforth<br>referred to as “SoC”, in UK<br>clinical practice, including:<br>•<br>OCS<br>•<br>Other IS agents<br>(e.g. methotrexate,<br>azathioprine,<br>mycophenolate<br>mofetil)|The appropriate comparator for this submission is a<br>weighted average of the most used agents for the<br>management of EGPA in UK clinical practice. Analysis of<br>UK prescription data and clinical expert opinion indicate<br>that the most used agents to induce and maintain<br>remission for EGPA are OCS and IS (e.g. methotrexate,<br>azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil) and therefore,<br>these are considered to form SoC in the UK.2, 3The<br>treatment distribution was informed by CPRD data, which<br>was validated by clinical expert opinion as being<br>representative of UK clinical practice2-4<br>AstraZeneca does not believe that CYC and RTX are<br>appropriate comparators for this submission, considering<br>the different positioning of these agents in the EGPA<br>treatment pathway, compared to the anticipated<br>positioning of benralizumab. Specifically:<br>•<br>Clinical guidelines and clinical expert opinion<br>indicate that CYC and RTX are predominantly<br>restricted to the treatment of patients with severe<br>EGPA, defined as life- or organ-threatening<br>EGPA.3Patients with life- or organ-threatening<br>EGPA manifestations were excluded from<br>MANDARA and therefore are not addressed<br>within this submission|

## _**Health condition and position of the technology in the**_ 

## _**treatment pathway**_ 

## **Disease overview and burden** 

- EGPA is a rare, autoimmune, inflammatory condition, affecting approximately 2,600 people in the UK[15, 16] 

- EGPA is a hypereosinophilic disorder, characterised by elevated circulating and tissue eosinophils, which cause inflammation of small and medium-sized blood vessels, resulting in restricted blood flow and subsequent damage to multiple organs[17, 18] 

- EGPA manifests across multiple organ systems, with significant symptom burden.[18-20] Diagnosis is challenging, owing to symptom overlap with other diseases[21] 

- Severe, multi-system manifestations and organ damage have a considerable negative impact on patients’ health-related quality of life (HRQoL) due to substantial fatigue, functional impairment and limitations in daily activities including a reduced ability to work.[22, 23] Additionally, continuous cycles of adequate disease control alternating with symptom recurrence contribute to patients feeling low, anxious and frustrated about their condition.[22, 24] EGPA also negatively impacts carers’ mental health and ability to remain employed[25] 

- EGPA is characterised by four distinct health states: 

   - Remission: controlled disease, with no or mild symptoms[3, 26] 

   - Relapse: recurrence of EGPA symptoms or requirement for increased OCS dose[2, 21, 26-28] 

   - Non-refractory disease: not remission nor relapse, but stable or tapered OCS dose, that patients derive clinically meaningful benefit from 

   - Refractory disease: no remission in the prior 6 months, severe symptoms and a requirement for high OCS doses, with an amplified negative impact on mental health due to feelings of frustration, hopelessness and despair resulting from patients experiencing a lack of improvement over a prolonged period of time 

- EGPA is associated with a 5-year mortality of 17.6%, 2.3 times higher than observed in a matched control population[29] 

## **Clinical care pathway** 

- There are currently no reimbursed treatment options for EGPA in the UK.[30] Standard of care (SoC) in the UK comprises of high-dose OCS and IS (e.g. methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine) prescribed off-label to reduce inflammation[21, 26-28, 30] 

## **Unmet need** 

- OCS and IS are sub-optimal treatment options as there is substantial evidence associating OCS use with acute and chronic adverse events (AEs),[31-33] while IS are associated with toxicities, including hepatotoxicity.[21, 26-28, 32, 33] Additionally, OCS and IS fail to adequately control the disease[33-35] 

- Consequently, there is a high unmet need for novel targeted therapies which provide adequate and durable disease control and enable a reduction in OCS exposure 

## **Proposed positioning of benralizumab** 

- Benralizumab is anticipated to be an add-on to SoC for relapsing or refractory EGPA 

- Benralizumab would address the unmet need and allow patients to benefit from an innovative therapy which offers durable remission, and enables a reduction in OCS-dependence and the incidence of OCS-related AEs

## **B.1.3.1 Disease overview** 

## **Introduction to EGPA** 

## _**EGPA is a rare, autoimmune vasculitis caused by hypereosinophilia which leads to inflammation-induced damage to organs**_ 

EGPA, previously known as Churg-Strauss syndrome, is a rare, autoimmune vasculitis characterised by high levels of circulating and tissue eosinophils (hypereosinophilia) which drive necrotising inflammation of small and medium-sized blood vessels.[17] Eosinophils are specialised white blood cells that are involved in the host defence against infection. EGPA presents with a variety of clinical manifestations that can impact multiple organ systems simultaneously, resulting in cumulative, chronic organ damage.[18] Commonly affected organ systems include cardiac, gastrointestinal (GI), pulmonary, cutaneous and renal, with the most common manifestations including asthma, myocarditis (inflammation of the heart), mononeuritis multiplex (peripheral nerve disorders) and ear, nose and throat (ENT) infections.[18] 

## **Epidemiology** 

EGPA is a rare and poorly characterised disease with limited epidemiology evidence available. The most relevant UK-specific source identified in literature following a targeted search reported that EGPA affects approximately 45.6 per million people (children and adults) in the UK.[15] Based on this estimated prevalence, AstraZeneca anticipates that EGPA affects approximately 2,600 people in England in 2024 (assuming ONS mid-2023 estimate for the population of England of 57,690,323).[15, 16] The disease affects men and women equally, and is typically diagnosed in middle age, with a median age at diagnosis of 57.4 years.[15] EGPA rarely affects children (˂18 years) with a prevalence of 0.4 per million children, compared to 56.8 per million in adults (≥18 years).[15] 

## **Pathogenesis** 

EGPA is characterised by high levels of circulating and tissue eosinophils, which release cytokines and chemokines (small proteins that act as signalling molecules) causing necrotising inflammation of small or medium-sized blood vessels.[17, 36] Blood eosinophil counts (BECs) normally range from 50–500 cells/μL in healthy people; however, they are elevated in the blood and tissues of patients with EGPA (mean BEC of 1,385.5 cells/μL), and can increase to levels ten times greater than in people without EGPA.[11, 15] 

The proliferation and migration of eosinophils from the bone marrow into circulation is primarily regulated by IL-5, which binds to the receptor α subunit (interleukin-5Rα) expressed on eosinophils (Figure 2).[1, 11] Type 2 T helper cells (Th2) and type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) produce cytokines to promote eosinophilic growth and activation. Once in the circulatory system, eosinophils move into vessel walls and extensively infiltrate tissues, mediated by IL-5 and other cytokines and chemokines, leading to eosinophilic granuloma (white blood cell cluster) formation.[17] These granulomas cause ischaemic organ damage (organ damage due to restricted blood supply).[11, 37] Furthermore, the increased eosinophils and associated chronic inflammation can cause direct and indirect tissue damage.

## **Disease course** 

## _**There are four distinct health states: remission, non-refractory, refractory and relapse.**_ 

EGPA is a poorly characterised rare disease, given the limited innovation and research in this space to date, resulting in a scarcity of literature to help inform the evolution of the disease. Consequently, extensive work was undertaken by AstraZeneca to deepen the understanding of the disease in support of this submission. This included systematic literature reviews, an advisory board with patients and extensive consultation with clinical experts.[3, 38] A separate workstream was also undertaken which included consultation with patients with EGPA through eight in-depth interviews and with clinical experts through four in-depth interviews, as part of defining the health state descriptions for the purpose of conducting a UK-specific vignette study.[39] Any insights gathered from the advisory board and interviews with patients are henceforth referred to as “patient insights”. Further information on the work undertaken is provided in Section B.3.2.2. Collectively, EGPA is best described by four health states, as outlined below, with patients broadly experiencing a relapsing and remitting disease course based on the occurrence of clinical signs and symptoms and OCS dose required to control the disease (Table 3). 

**Remission** is defined as the disease being “under control”, requiring low doses of medication. Patients experience no symptoms or some mild symptoms, such as blocked sinuses, numbness and tingling and fatigue.[3, 26] 

**Relapse** is defined as the recurrence of EGPA signs and symptoms, or the requirement for increased doses of medication, after a period of remission.[26] Patients in relapse experience more severe symptoms than those in remission, including severe fatigue, loss of sensation in limbs, weight changes and skin problems.[2, 21, 26-28] Relapses contribute to irreversible and progressive organ damage, development of comorbidities, the need for increased dosages of OCS (associated with severe AEs and toxicity, as described in Section B.1.3.4), poor HRQoL (as described in ‘Impact on patient and carer quality of life’) and increased mortality compared with the other health states.[2, 21, 26-28]

Some patients are considered to be in neither remission nor relapse and are characterised by a spectrum of disease control that, according to clinical expert opinion, can broadly be categorised into two sub-states with different clinical profiles: non-refractory and refractory disease.[3] 

- On the “better” end of the spectrum, patients with **non-refractory** disease can achieve a stable or tapered OCS dose and experience clinically meaningful benefit compared with refractory disease, given that OCS dose reduction is a key treatment goal in EGPA 

- On the “worse” end of the spectrum, the **refractory** health state includes patients without remission in the prior six months and is characterised by severe symptoms, and a requirement for high doses of oral corticosteroids.[26-28] In addition, patients with refractory disease experience an amplified negative impact on mental health due to feelings of frustration, hopelessness and despair resulting from them experiencing a lack of improvement over a prolonged period of time (‘Impact on patient and carer quality of life’)[39]

## **Diagnosis** 

The multitude of symptoms and the considerable overlap between EGPA symptoms and those of other diseases create a challenge in the diagnosis of EGPA. Additionally, the rarity of the disease, the lack of specialist expertise, a lack of innovation and research in EGPA and no updates to management guidelines in recent years, all also contribute to difficulties in diagnosis.[21] Consequently, the mean time from onset of symptoms to EGPA diagnosis has been reported as 7.1–11.8 years.[38, 40] This delay in diagnosis can result in greater disease severity, progression and disease burden as patients present with a broader range of manifestations and associated symptoms contributing to organ damage, requiring additional OCS and IS in an attempt to induce remission.[20] Complex diagnoses lead to repeated hospital visits and worsening

symptoms over time. This can leave patients feeling anxious, depressed, confused and frustrated as they struggle with the uncertainty of their health.[22] Late diagnosis also increases the economic burden on the NHS as greater levels of specialist treatment and monitoring are required for progressed disease. 

## **Mortality** 

Mortality rates remain significantly higher in individuals with EGPA compared to matched control populations.[38, 41, 42] An analysis of real-world CPRD data in England reported that patients with EGPA had a 5-year mortality rate of 17.6% which is 2.3-times higher than the 7.5% observed in the matched control population.[43] In a prospective cohort study in the Netherlands, 22% of patients with EGPA in sustained remission died over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years (52 ± 25 months), compared to 6% over a mean follow-up of 4.7 years (56 ± 9 months) in a control group matched for age, sex, cardiovascular risk factors, and follow-up duration (p=0.022).[42] 

In addition, the UK-specific CPRD data have shown that the mortality risk varies dependent on the EGPA health state. Patients in relapse have the greatest mortality risk, with a standardised mortality ratio (SMR) of **** when compared to the general population in England.[2] Conversely, **** patients with the lowest mortality risk are those in remission, who experience a SMR of .[2] In support of the CPRD data, in a physician survey study covering 243 patients with EGPA, the reported 10-year mortality rate was 40% in patients with relapsed or refractory disease compared with 10% in the general EGPA cohort.[44] 

## **B.1.3.2 Disease burden** 

## **Symptom burden** 

_**EGPA causes a range of disease manifestations across multiple organ systems, causing organ damage and creating significant long-term health consequences for patients.**_ 

Patients with EGPA may first experience severe, adult-onset asthma, a high frequency of ENT symptoms, fatigue, pain, weight loss and fever. Following this, elevated levels of eosinophils infiltrate organ systems, particularly the lungs, heart, and GI system. Eosinophils also cause the inflammation of small and medium blood vessels which results in progressive organ damage.[45] It has been found that persistent damage to at least one organ at diagnosis was observed in 28.6% of patients in a retrospective Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) analysis of 283 patients with EGPA, emphasising the long-term effects of the disease.[2, 46] Considering the multi-system impact of EGPA, patients experience a broad range of immediate manifestations including chronic asthma, peripheral neuropathy and chronic sinusitis which contribute to the significant clinical and patient burden in EGPA. Overall, commonly reported symptoms are outlined in Figure 3 and below.

**Abbreviations:** ENT: ear-nose-throat; GI: gastrointestinal; OCS: oral corticosteroid **Source:** Adapted from Trivoli G, _et al_ . Rheumatology 2020;[45] Cottin V, _et al_ . European Respiratory Journal;[40] Doubelt I, _et al_ . ACR Open Rheumatology[47] 

Eosinophilic infiltration affects multiple organ systems, causing a range of severe, complex and debilitating manifestations affecting many aspects of daily living: 

- The majority (74–100%) of patients with EGPA have **asthma** at diagnosis,[38, 46, 48-51] with asthma pathology also driven by high levels of eosinophilic inflammation.[40] Based on literature, an average of 57.9% of patients with EGPA had severe asthma aligned with the definition of Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) Step 5[51-53] 

- **Cardiac manifestations** such as cardiomyopathy, pericarditis and myocarditis are also common in patients with EGPA.[11, 18] These cause immediate symptoms of shortness of breath, chest pain and irregular heartbeat, with further disease progression resulting in heart failure, heart attack and thrombosis 

- Neurological manifestations predominantly include mononeuritis multiplex, a peripheral **neuropathy** that affects up to 60% of patients with EGPA.[38, 40, 47, 49, 51, 54-57] In mononeuritis multiplex, damage occurs to multiple, individual peripheral nerves (nerves outside of the central nervous system). This leads to neuropathic pain and sensory and motor deficits, including weakness in limbs, loss of feeling, tingling or paralysis in areas of the body, resulting in difficulties with walking, standing, lifting and carrying objects[58, 59] 

- **GI manifestations** are also common, occurring in 3–42% of patients, and include abdominal pain (20–25%), haemorrhage (3–9%) and colitis (2–3%)[45, 47, 51, 54, 55, 57, 60, 61] 

- **ENT manifestations** , such as rhinitis, sinusitis and nasal polyps (soft growths in the lining of the nasal passage), present in up to 96% of patients with EGPA.[47, 49, 51, 54-56] Nasal polyps can cause complications due to blocked airflow and fluid drainage, often resulting in sinus infections and symptoms such as nasal congestion, reduced sense of smell or tase and difficulty breathing[62] 

- Similarly, **renal manifestations** can cause permanent kidney damage and potentially kidney failure, resulting in symptoms like tiredness, loss of appetite and nausea. Patients may also require dialysis or transplants, further increasing the disease burden[63, 64] 

Patients with EGPA experience disease manifestations at a higher incidence than those with other chronic diseases. A US MarketScan study of patients with EGPA (n=182) compared with patients with severe, uncontrolled asthma (n=640), demonstrated that patients with EGPA had

## **Impact on patient and carer quality of life** 

_**EGPA is characterised by heterogeneous, hypereosinophilic manifestations and organ damage which contribute to a considerable, negative impact on many aspects of quality of life. Patients experience multiple disruptions to daily living including severe fatigue, functional impairment, sleep disruption, emotional distress, anxiety and a reduced ability to work and engage in social activities. This is exacerbated by the frequent relapses and ineffective treatment options. EGPA also affects carers’ mental health and ability to work**_ 

As noted in Section B.1.3.1, EGPA is a poorly characterised rare disease, resulting in limited available literature detailing the impact of EGPA on HRQoL. As part of the extensive work undertaken by AstraZeneca to deepen the understanding of the disease, a literature review, an advisory board with patients, consultation with clinical experts and a UK-specific vignette study were conducted. The vignette study included consultation with patients with EGPA through eight in-depth interviews and with clinical experts through four in-depth interviews, in line with NICE’s guidance on structured elicitation methods (described further in Section B.3.4.4).[39, 66] 

Collectively, all the gathered insights indicated that the clinical manifestations of EGPA have a considerable, negative impact on patients’ HRQoL and daily activities. The heterogeneous, hypereosinophilic manifestations and organ damage associated with EGPA lead to a reduced ability to exercise (74%), impaired sleep quality and quantity (71%), decreased ability to work (63%), limited engagement in social activities (60%) and difficulty walking (54%).[19, 67] People also report difficulty breathing, substantial fatigue, functional impairment and neuropathy.[39] Symptoms such as coughing, wheezing and breathlessness can disrupt sleep, exacerbating existing fatigue, and can have “devastating consequences” due to the impact on “every aspect of people’s lives including employment, education, social life, and relationships”.[31] ENT manifestations and the resulting symptoms can lead to sleep impairment, anxiety and depression, while neurological manifestations impact the functional ability of patients, limiting their ability to carry out daily activities.[62] Collectively, EGPA symptoms also limit patients’ ability to engage in usual social interactions, leading to absenteeism and isolation. 

In an illness perception questionnaire (IPQ) designed to evaluate an individual’s beliefs and perceptions about their condition, patients with EGPA scored 10.5 out of a possible 22 symptoms in the IPQ identity dimension, representing strongly held beliefs about the number of symptoms attributed to the illness.[68] They also scored 4.3 and 3.9 out of 5.0, for timeline-acute/chronic and consequences dimensions, respectively. These scores indicate strong beliefs that the disease will last over a prolonged period of time and has negatively impacted the respondents’ ability to function.[68] 

The substantial fatigue experienced by patients with EGPA reduces their ability to remain employed and engage in typical daily activities.[69] In a questionnaire study of patients with EGPA, the multi-dimension fatigue inventory score, was 16.1 (range 4-20). This is substantially greater

<!-- page 24 -->

than the threshold for defining significant fatigue (≥13).[68] Additionally, patient insights gathered to support this submission further substantiated the significant impact the disease has on daily acitvites;[70] patients mentioned “I experienced fatigue and EGPA impacted my ability to exercise”, “Showering on a daily basis was exhausting”, “I couldn’t walk upstairs”. 

The literature review and vignette study also revealed that patients with EGPA experience poor mental health feeling low, scared, anxious and frustrated with their condition;[39] . Once diagnosed, patients may have a negative perception of their future.[20] The continuous cycles of remission and relapse, along with ongoing follow ups, contribute to a negative perception of the illness and can induce stress and anxiety as patients struggle to envision a disease-free future.[22, 24] Patients have expressed living in fear of potential relapse and worsening symptoms.[70] The impact of EGPA on mental health was prominent across the patient insights gathered where patients made statements such as “It is an anxiety-inducing condition”, “I was in a bad mental health space”, “I feel detached from others”.[70] 

As described above, the HRQoL of patients is dependent on EGPA health state (remission, nonrefractory, refractory and relapse) as each state is characterised by differing levels of symptom control and, therefore, wellbeing. Worsening symptoms and loss of disease control during relapses, irreversible organ damage and toxicity from the increased OCS/IS doses limit patients’ HRQoL and ability to conduct daily activities.[3, 21, 26-28] This will result in patients feeling more low, scared and anxious. Results from a study using the 22-item Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT22) also demonstrated significantly elevated scores in patients with active EGPA disease versus those in remission, and an increase in scores was associated with subsequent relapse.[71] Patients with refractory disease experience a greater negative impact on mental health than those in relapse; in addition to the impact of severe symptoms on HRQoL and daily living, they feel hopeless and frustrated,[39] as their disease has not achieved remission for a prolonged period of time. On the other hand, patients with non-refractory disease will have milder symptoms and, therefore, improved HRQoL compared to those in refractory and relapse states.[3] Patients in remission experience mild or no symptoms and therefore, better HRQoL. 

There is an indirect burden on carers who are responsible for patients with EGPA. EGPA impacts carers’ ability to remain employed as patients’ disease becomes progressively worse, with many carers experiencing difficulties with taking time off from work.[25, 72] Moreover, carers help patients cope mentally as they navigate their EGPA journey, from pre- to post-diagnosis, whilst also having to cope with the uncertainty of what is happening themselves. This can heavily impact carers’ mental health, as they face significant fear and the need for constant vigilance when caring for patients with EGPA, resulting in the requirement for support in their own right from healthcare professionals, particularly with the psychological impact of the disease.[25] In a qualitative study, 18 patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) and their informal carers participated in semi-structured interviews to explore patient experiences and the effects of caring. Of the 18 patients interviewed, 4 had EGPA. During these interviews, a carer for an EGPA patient expressed their worry that “one day we’ll go to bed and I’ll wake up and she won’t. It could be tomorrow.”[25] 

## **Economic burden** 

_**EGPA is associated with a substantial economic burden, due to both NHS healthcare resource use and the reduced work opportunities for patients with the disease**_

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 25 -->

EGPA is associated with high healthcare resource use (HCRU) and per-patient costs. A study of HCRU of patients with EGPA in England reported substantial HCRU in the first 12 months following an EGPA diagnosis:[15] 

- 97.1% of patients have had a GP visit, with a mean number of 16 visits per patient per year 

- Patients also required nurse and allied health professionals visits 

- The heterogenous manifestations of EGPA resulted in 33.7%, 31.8% and 25.2% of patients requiring visits to a respiratory, rheumatology and ENT specialists, respectively, adding pressure to NHS resources 

Additionally, up to 90.9% of patients have had an inpatient hospital stay, with a median length of stay of 5–11 days per visit.[73] A similar proportion of patients required outpatient hospital visits (up to 97.5%) and 77.6% of EGPA patients had an A&E visit.[73] The annual HRCU per patient was £14,261.10, highlighting the significant economic burden of EGPA to the NHS.[15, 73] 

The HCRU and per-patients costs are increased in those who experience disease relapse. Those require more frequent hospitalisation and thus incur greater costs compared with those in remission.[2] 

A work productivity and activity impairment (WPAI) questionnaire was conducted in patients with EGPA (US, UK, Germany, Italy, France and Spain) on the Adelphi Disease Specific Programme (DSP) dataset, with data analysed by AstraZeneca.[74] Overall, 32.1% of 177 patients reported that EGPA impacted their daily activities whilst 20.8% of 82 patients reported overall work impairment (a combination of lost work hours and lost productivity when able to work).[74] This impact on the working ability of patients with EGPA could result in loss of earnings, creating a financial burden for individuals. Patients also experience economic impacts, such as the expense to travel to healthcare facilities and the loss of time. Furthermore, a questionnaire study of 41 French patients with EGPA reported that 29.3% of patients received disability living allowance, disability pension or had disabled worker status.[75] 

## **B.1.3.3 Clinical care pathway** 

_**There are currently no reimbursed treatments for EGPA in the UK, with SoC consisting of high-dose OCS and IS.**_ 

The British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) published guidelines in 2014 for the management of adults with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV); EGPA is a type of AAV.[30] However, over the past decade since 2014, there have been no further advancements in terms of guidelines specifically for EGPA in the UK. Therefore, guidelines from other countries were reviewed, including the European evidenced-based guidelines and those by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) and the EGPA consensus task force.[21, 26-28] Importantly, those guidelines recommend mepolizumab, which is not available for use in EGPA in the UK. Nonetheless, those guidelines could serve as a basis for developing UK-specific recommendations since benralizumab would be expected to follow the same positioning in the treatment pathway as mepolizumab. 

## **Current treatment pathway** 

The goal of EGPA management is to control active inflammation and suppress the immune response, in order to induce sustained remission, prevent disease relapse whilst also minimising OCS use (and the related AEs and comorbidities).[26] However, in the UK, there are currently no

<!-- page 26 -->

treatments indicated for EGPA that are reimbursed by the NHS. Of note, no submission was made to NICE for mepolizumab (TA845).[76] 

UK clinical expert opinion was elicited and real-world treatment pattern data were collected to characterise the treatment pathway in England.[3, 4, 21, 26-28] Based on this, standard of care for EGPA consists of sub-optimal, off-label treatments, comprising of high-dose OCS with or without IS.[21, 26-28] 

- OCS are prescribed at high doses, off-label, as the mainstay treatment to induce remission and manage hypereosinophilia by reducing eosinophilic inflammation. Prednisolone is the most commonly prescribed OCS.[4, 22, 26-28] OCS were prescribed for 86.2% of people with EGPA in a retrospective CPRD study in England over a mean follow-up of 5.4 years post-diagnosis[4] 

- Although remission may be achieved in a proportion of patients with high-dose OCS alone, addition of a potent IS therapy is commonly required to induce and/or maintain remission.[26-28] The CPRD study identified that IS therapies were prescribed for 53.7% of people during the 5.4-year mean follow-up.[4] The most commonly prescribed IS therapies, according to CPRD analysis include, azathioprine, methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil.[3, 4, 27] This was validated by clinical experts as being reflective of UK clinical practice[3 ] 

As outlined in Section B.1.1, CYC and RTX are not part of UK SoC for the population of interest. These agents are restricted to the treatment of patients with severe EGPA, defined as life- or organ-threatening EGPA,[3] and would therefore have a different positioning in the EGPA treatment pathway, compared to the anticipated positioning of benralizumab. UK prescription data analysis confirmed that CYC was restricted to treating severe patients and RTX was only sparingly used in UK clinical practice, and does not form part of UK SoC, as validated by clinical experts.[3]

## **B.1.3.4 Unmet need** 

_**Current treatment options are limited and sub-optimal. OCS target high levels of eosinophils but are associated with severe AEs and comorbidities. IS suppress the immune system without specifically targeting hypereosinophilia in EGPA and are associated with toxicity. Additionally, these treatments do not adequately control the disease**_ 

OCS are prescribed off-label, as the mainstay treatment to induce remission and manage hypereosinophilia in EGPA. The CPRD analysis identified mean daily doses of OCS ranging from 12.4 to 23.1 mg/day over time in the 5 years following EGPA diagnosis.[4] These high doses of OCS, which are much higher than OCS doses used in severe asthma, are required to deplete the higher levels of eosinophils, which are up to ten times the normal range (Section B.1.3.1). 

OCS are effective anti-inflammatory agents, however, there is substantial evidence associating OCS use with acute and chronic AEs, including type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, pneumonia, cataracts, sleep apnoea and renal impairment, amongst other conditions.[32] Many patients with EGPA experience an accumulation of these comorbidities.[31-33] Patients highlighted that some immediate side effects of OCS treatment included mood swings, weight gain and night sweats, with weight gain affecting self-confidence and mental well-being.[77] 

Clinical experts have identified a link between OCS dose and the severity of the side effects which is supported by the literature.[33, 78] In a study of 138 patients with AAV, a cumulative OCS dose of ≥0.9 g was linked to an 80% likelihood of an increase in glucocorticoid toxicity.[79] Comparatively, the mean cumulative dosage has been reported to be as high as 6.3 g in patients with EGPA across a mean follow-up duration of 21.7 months,[80] suggesting the majority of patients are likely to experience OCS-related AEs. Considering the high exposure to OCS in EGPA, clinicians highlighted the urgent need to minimise OCS reliance, and consequently the important benefit associated with even tapering or stabilising the OCS dose (as observed in the non-refractory state).[3] 

Additionally, IS are used in EGPA management, however, they do not directly target eosinophils, instead suppressing the immune system. IS treatment is associated with a high risk of organ toxicity and side effects including cytopenia, hepatotoxicity, and major infections such as bacterial pneumonias herpes zoster recurrences, opportunistic infections and _Pneumocystis jiroveci_ pneumonia.[21, 26-28] The side effects of both OCS and IS have a considerable negative impact on quality of life, adding to the physical and mental burden for patients and requiring more frequent healthcare visits. 

Patients have also expressed their concern at the current treatment options available and the impacts on their health. Insights gathered from EGPA patients indicated that they “worried about the side effects of their treatments, particularly the steroids”, “the biggest challenge became the drugs and not the condition itself” and “they were keen to get off steroids”.[70] 

Furthermore, the combination of OCS and IS is ineffective at maintaining remission, as acknowledged by the British Thoracic Society (BTS).[81] As a result, relapse rates are high and the time to relapse is short. When treated with OCS alone or in combination with IS, 33–67% of patients experience remission, however, up to 82% of patients who achieve remission will relapse, within less than a year.[33-35] High relapse rates from OCS and IS have a two-fold implication. Firstly, relapsed disease is treated with increased doses of OCS and IS, which 

Company evidence submission for benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 28 -->

further exacerbates the risk of OCS-related AEs and IS-related toxicity. Secondly, the cycles of relapsing-remitting disease cause patients to feel low, scared, frustrated and anxious, exacerbating negative feelings about future outcomes. 

Insights gathered from patients and clinical experts highlighted the acute unmet need for novel therapies that can deplete eosinophils without causing toxicity, to allow a reduction in OCS use, reducing the risk of incidence of acute and chronic OCS-related AEs and IS-related toxicity. Therapies should also induce durable remission, slow disease progression and prevent further organ damage to reduce the burden of disease on patients and the NHS. Therefore, in addition to the natural history of EGPA, the economic analysis for this submission also modelled the impact of OCS use on patients’ HRQoL and NHS costs (Section B.3.2.2). 

Patients expressed preferences for targeted therapies which would have a greater impact on symptoms compared to SoC, stating that “having something that is new, has a greater positive impact on my condition and is less harmful would be amazing”.[70] 

## **B.1.3.5 Proposed positioning of benralizumab** 

Benralizumab is an effective treatment option with a favourable safety profile for patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA. Unlike current treatment options, benralizumab has a targeted mechanism of action, rapidly depleting eosinophils, and reducing inflammation (Table 2). 

Therefore, benralizumab can address the high unmet need as potentially the first treatment option that effectively induces and maintains remission, enabling to reduce the toxicity and adverse events associated with current SoC.(Section B.2.6).[1] 

The proposed positioning for benralizumab is as an add-on treatment for adult patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA who are receiving OCS with or without stable IS therapy, as validated by clinical experts.[3] (Figure 5).

## _**Equality considerations**_ 

A consideration was raised during draft scope consultation, regarding comorbid EGPA patients with severe eosinophilic asthma (SEA), already being eligible for treatment with benralizumab. This poses an equality consideration for the following reason: 

- Not all patients with EGPA have severe asthma (only 57.9% of patients according to GINA Step 5)[51-53] 

   - Patients with EGPA and comorbid severe asthma would only be able to access benralizumab if they meet the eligibility criteria for its recommendation within severe asthma, i.e. based on blood eosinophil count, prior exacerbation history and being inadequately controlled despite maintenance therapy with high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-agonists 

      - Even if patients are eligible for benralizumab in severe asthma after meeting these criteria, it is widely understood that access to severe asthma centres in England (where benralizumab is prescribed for severe asthma) is challenging. Despite the inclusion of SA biologics in the NHS England Rapid Uptake Products programme 2021/2022, the biologic uptake rate is still ~20% in this group of patients, based on AstraZeneca’s estimates[82] 

   - This inequality was also raised by NHS England in their draft scope response, highlighting the fact that only comorbid patients can access this evidence-based medicine, and only if they have access to a designated severe asthma centre 

Furthermore, if patients with EGPA and comorbid severe asthma access benralizumab, the dosing schedule will be in line with SEA dosing (30 mg Q4W for the first 3 doses, then Q8W thereafter), rather than the EGPA dose (30 mg Q4W). 

The less frequent asthma dose (30 mg Q8W) has not formally been tested in EGPA, and most real-world data for this dosing frequency are from patients with asthma and EGPA manifestations. A more frequent dose (30 mg Q4W) is considered necessary for EGPA because it is a more severe disease than asthma, and eosinophil levels are often higher.[21  ] UK clinicians expressed frustration at the inability to control patients’ symptoms at the severe asthma dose and have a strong desire to have access to the dose investigated and proved to be efficacious in MANDARA for EGPA (30 mg Q4W).[3] 

Therefore, AstraZeneca firmly believes that benralizumab needs to be made available for **all** eligible EGPA patients, at the dose that was investigated and proved to be efficacious.

## **B.2 Clinical effectiveness** 

- **The main clinical evidence base for benralizumab as an add-on treatment to SoC in adult patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA was informed from the MANDARA trial** • MANDARA was an international, Phase III, randomised, double-blind (DB), active-controlled, parallel group, multicentre, non-inferiority study comparing the efficacy and safety of benralizumab to mepolizumab, in patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA on corticosteroid therapy with or without stable immunosuppressive therapy 

**MANDARA demonstrated the efficacy and safety of benralizumab in adult patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA, receiving OCS with or without IS** 

- MANDARA met its primary endpoint with benralizumab treatment resulting in remission (BVAS = 0 and OCS dose ≤4 mg/day) of EGPA in 40/70 (58%[a] ) patients showing non-inferiority (NI) to mepolizumab (40/70 [57%[ a] ] patients)[1] 

- Treatment with benralizumab resulted in durable remission, low annualised relapse rates, reductions in daily dose of OCS, and complete OCS cessation in 40% of patients. Furthermore, treatment with benralizumab improved symptom control, and offered improvements in vasculitis activity, asthma control and pulmonary function[83] 

- • ******* ******* **** *** ******* ********** ********* ***** ************ *** ********** ** ******** ** ************ ********* ** ***** ** ********** *** ********* *** *** *******[**] 

- • The safety profile of benralizumab at the higher dose in EGPA was consistent with the known safety profile of benralizumab in severe asthma 

- **In the absence of head-to-head evidence of benralizumab versus UK SoC, an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) was conducted to generate relative efficacy estimates** • A Bucher ITC, which was anchored through the common comparator arm mepolizumab, compared data from MANDARA and MIRRA to evaluate the comparative efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC[1, 34] 

- • Benralizumab showed a statistically significant improvement in the proportion of patients in remission and a reduction in annualised relapse rate, compared with SoC

## **B.2.3.2 Baseline demographic and disease characteristics** 

A full comparison of baseline characteristics of patients enrolled in the DB treatment phase is shown in Table 6. Key patient characteristics were well balanced across the two treatment arms, with a similar mean age (52.0 and 52.7 years in the benralizumab and mepolizumab treatment arms, respectively) and proportion of patients in each age group (****% and ****% in the ≥18 to ≤65 years group).[1, 83] Considering the rarity of EGPA and the trial sample size of 140 participants, both the benralizumab and mepolizumab arms had a similar proportion of male patients (35.7% and 44.3% respectively) and were well balanced across all racial groups, with White patients making up the highest proportion in both groups (****% and ****%, respectively).[83] 

The profile of EGPA disease history was also similar between treatment arms, with both arms having similar proportions of patients with relapsing and refractory disease, similar mean time since diagnosis and similar vasculitis scores (BVAS and VDI).[1] Patients also had similar baseline eosinophil counts in the benralizumab and mepolizumab arms (306.0 cells/μL and 384.9 cells/μL, respectively).[1, 83] In terms of prior medication, a similar proportion of patients were using IS therapy at baseline in the benralizumab and mepolizumab arms (37.1% and 34.3%) and had a similar mean OCS dose (11.1 mg/day and 11.0 mg/day, respectively).[1] The mean BMI was also similar across both benralizumab and mepolizumab arms (**** kg/m[2] and **** kg/m[2] , respectively.[1, 83] BMI can impact the patients’ response to OCS, with a higher BMI associated with poor responses. 

As described in Section B.1.3.1, EGPA can occur at any age but is rare in children, with a median age of diagnosis of 57.4 years and it affects males and females equally.[15] Whilst the study population recruited slightly more females than males, there were no known differences related to age, race, ethnic group or geography. Overall, patient demographics from MANDARA were deemed representative of patients with EGPA in the UK, as validated by clinical experts.[3]

## **B.2.4.2 Statistical analysis** 

## **Primary analysis** 

The primary objective of the MANDARA trial was to assess the durability of response to treatment with benralizumab compared with mepolizumab in patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA who were receiving SoC therapy, assessed by the proportion of patients in remission at both Weeks 36 and 48 (EGPA remission was defined as BVAS = 0 and OCS ≤4 mg/day).[83] The primary analysis demonstrated the non-inferiority (NI) of benralizumab versus mepolizumab based on the primary endpoint of remission and the primary analysis data cut-off was the 10[th] of August 2023. Details of the statistical analysis for the primary efficacy endpoint are presented in Table 8, while details of statistical analysis for secondary endpoints can be found in the MANDARA protocol.[85] 

**Table 8: Statistical methods for the primary analysis in MANDARA** 

|**Hypothesis**<br>**objective**|•<br>The null hypothesis for the primary efficacy analysis was that the<br>proportion of patients achieving remission on benralizumab was<br>inferior to that of patients on mepolizumab by a NI margin of –25%<br>•<br>The alternative hypothesis was that benralizumab was non-inferior to<br>mepolizumab<br>•<br>The primary endpoint was considered to have been met if<br>benralizumab demonstrated non-inferiorityto mepolizumab|
|---|---|
|**Statistical**<br>**analysis**|•<br>The primary endpoint was evaluated using the marginal<br>standardisation method in logistic regression, with adjustment for<br>treatment group, baseline, OCS dose, baseline BVAS and region<br>(North America, Japan or the rest of the world)<br>•<br>From this model, the absolute difference in the percentage of patients<br>with remission (benralizumab minus mepolizumab) was estimated,<br>along with the associated two-sided 95% CI<br>•<br>To show non-inferiority, the lower 95% CI for the absolute difference<br>between benralizumab and mepolizumab needed to be above the<br>prespecified margin of –25 percentage points.<br>•<br>If the primary analysis showed non-inferiority, a formal test for the<br>superiority of benralizumab to mepolizumab at the two-sided 0.05<br>level (equivalent to a one-sided 0.025 level with a treatment effect<br>favouring benralizumab) was conducted with the use of the same<br>model|
|**Sample size,**<br>**power**<br>**calculation**|•<br>The sample size was determined from the assumption that<br>benralizumab and mepolizumab each have a remission rate of 32%.<br>Therefore, 140 patients would provide approximately 90% power to<br>demonstrate NI with a NI margin of –25% at the 2.5% one-sided<br>significance level|
|**Data**<br>**management,**<br>**patient**<br>**withdrawals**|•<br>To ensure correct data management, all patient data relating to the<br>study was recorded on printed or eCRF unless transmitted to<br>AstraZeneca or the designee electronically<br>•<br>The Investigator was responsible for verifying data entries and<br>permitting study-related monitoring, audits, IRB/IEC review and<br>regulatory agency inspections and providing direct access to source|

**NB:** This testing strategy for the primary endpoint required no multiplicity adjustment as it corresponded to a simple closed test procedure and involved only one dose level of the test treatment, benralizumab, relative to mepolizumab. There was no multiplicity protection for secondary or exploratory endpoints or subgroup analyses, and therefore, the results of these analyses are reported as point estimates and 95% confidence intervals, with all p values being nominal.[1] Furthermore, the widths of the of the confidence intervals have not been adjusted for multiplicity and should not be used to infer definitive treatment effects for secondary end points.[1]

## _**Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant trials**_ 

The main clinical evidence base for the efficacy and safety of benralizumab as an add-on treatment to SoC in adult patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA was informed from the MANDARA trial. The following sections present the efficacy results for the primary and secondary endpoints of the MANDARA trial. Further results from the MANDARA trial, including interim data from the OLE period, are presented in Appendix N. 

## **B.2.6.1 Primary outcome** 

## **Remission rate at Weeks 36 and 48** 

For the primary endpoint, benralizumab as an add-on treatment (henceforth referred to as “benralizumab”) resulted in main remission (BVAS = 0 and OCS ≤4 mg/day) in 57.7% of patients at both Weeks 36 and 48, compared with 56.5% with mepolizumab (as an add-on treatment), giving a treatment difference of 1.2% (95% CI: –14.1, 16.5; p=0.8773; Table 10).[a]

## **Time to first relapse** 

Benralizumab was associated with a similar time to first relapse compared with the mepolizumab group (HR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.53, 1.82; p=******) based on a Cox-proportional hazards model and log-rank test. Full results are presented in Table 12 and Figure 8. Major relapse occurred in zero patients in the benralizumab group and three patients (4.3%) in the mepolizumab group, meaning that a HR was not calculable.[1, 83]

## **Average daily dose of OCS** 

As discussed in Section B.1.3.4, the risk of OCS-related AEs in patients increases with higher OCS doses, with a cumulative glucocorticoid dose of ≥0.9 g associated with an increased likelihood of glucocorticoid toxicity in patients with AAV.[79] Therefore, reducing OCS dose is a key goal in the management of EGPA, as validated by clinical experts.[3] 

Benralizumab was associated with ≥50% reduction from baseline in the average daily dose of OCS during Week 48 to 52 in 84.7% patients; this is compared to 73.9% of patients receiving mepolizumab, resulting in a difference of 10.8% (95% CI: –2.3, 23.8; p=0.1047).[1] A 100% reduction from baseline in the average daily dose of OCS during Week 48 to 52 was observed in a greater proportion of patients in the benralizumab arm when compared to the mepolizumab arm (41.4% and 25.8%, respectively) resulting in a difference of 15.7% (95% CI: 0.7, 30.7; p=0.0406).[1] Additionally, ****% of patients in the benralizumab arm received no OCS, compared to ****% in the mepolizumab group. ## **Blood eosinophil count** 

As discussed in Section B.1.3.1, EGPA is characterised by increased circulating and tissue eosinophils which cause the inflammation of small or medium-sized blood vessels. Patients with EGPA have very high levels of circulating and tissue eosinophils (up to ten times higher than the normal range).[15] 

The results of the MANDARA trial indicate that treatment with benralizumab causes the rapid and near-complete depletion of blood eosinophils in patients with EGPA. A reduction in blood eosinophil count from baseline was observed in both treatment groups from Week 1, the first time point assessed, through Week 52, with greater reductions demonstrated in the benralizumab group compared to mepolizumab at all time points. Full results are presented in Table 15. 

The rapid and near-complete depletion of blood eosinophils MANDARA participants is expected to have resulted in the observed patient-relevant improvements, such as in lung function (spirometry), vasculitis activity (BVAS), OCS dose reduction and asthma control (ACQ-6).

## **Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (BVAS)** 

BVAS is a tool for the assessment of disease activity in systematic vasculitis, which records features that are attributable to vasculitis, after the exclusion of other causes, in different organbased systems. A scoring sheet is used to record the presence of each item and the total score of nine organ systems gives an indication of the disease activity of each patient and reflects the need for therapy. The higher the score, the more active the vasculitic disease at the time of evaluation, with a maximum possible score of 63 and a score of 0 representing remission. 

Benralizumab was associated with an adjusted BVAS response (BVAS score of 0 or 1) at Week 52 in ****% of patients, compared with ****% of those treated with mepolizumab (Table 16). The *** **** **** ****** difference in response rates was % (95% CI: , ; p= ).[83]

## _**Indirect treatment comparison**_ 

## **Context** 

The MANDARA trial provided a comparison of the efficacy of benralizumab versus mepolizumab, however, mepolizumab is not a relevant comparator for this evaluation as it is not a reimbursed treatment option in the UK. As per the decision problem, the relevant comparator is SoC in UK clinical practice, consisting of OCS with or without IS. Given the lack of head-to-head trial informing the relative efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC in patients with EGPA, an ITC was conducted to generate comparative efficacy estimates. 

## **B.2.9.1 Methods of the indirect treatment comparison** 

## **Feasibility assessment** 

As described in Section B.2.1, an SLR was conducted in June 2023 and updated in August 2024 to identify relevant clinical evidence on the efficacy and safety of treatments for EGPA. The original SLR identified 9 unique clinical studies. Of these 9 studies, 7 were randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and these were included in the feasibility assessment described below. Given RCTs are the gold standard for evaluating the effectiveness of treatments, the 2 non-RCTs were Company evidence submission for benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 55 -->

excluded from the feasibility assessment.[89, 90] The SLR update identified 3 further studies, 2 of which were non-RCTs, so only 1 further study was included in the feasibility assessment. 

A feasibility assessment (details in Appendix D) was then conducted with the 8 studies to evaluate data availability, heterogeneity between trials and network connectivity. The MIRRA trial (NCT02020889), which was one of the RCTs identified in the clinical SLR, compared the efficacy of mepolizumab versus SoC (consisting of OCS with or without IS, reflective of UK clinical practice).[34] Though multiple studies evaluated SoC (OCS with or without IS), MIRRA was the only trial which allowed for an anchored comparison with the MANDARA trial. The feasibility assessment, therefore, concluded that an anchored ITC between MANDARA and MIRRA would enable comparative efficacy estimates to be generated for benralizumab versus SoC, using mepolizumab as a common comparator arm. Given NICE’s preference for anchored ITCs, the other studies were excluded.[91] 

The MANDARA and MIRRA trials were comparable based on study design.[1, 34] A list of potential treatment effect-modifiers consisting of eligibility criteria and baseline characteristics reported across both the MANDARA and MIRRA trials were identified. The list also included covariates which have previously been considered treatment effect-modifying following a consultation of the literature.[34, 92-94] Clinical experts were consulted individually to provide input on what factors should be adjusted for in the comparisons. A pooled rank-ordered list of effect-modifiers was then generated based on the individual rankings from the clinical experts. Though differences in these ranked effect-modifiers were observed between study populations, these differences were not considered by clinicians to be meaningful. The similarity in the trial design, population and outcome measurements was confirmed by clinical experts.[3] Therefore, no adjustment for population characteristics was deemed necessary, and a Bucher ITC was considered the most appropriate approach. 

A comparison of trial design and patient baseline characteristics across the MANDARA and MIRRA trials is presented in Appendix D. 

## **Bucher ITC methodology** 

The Bucher ITC has a simple methodology which evaluates the differences between two treatments in two sets of clinical trials and preserves the randomisation of the originally assigned patient groups. 

As noted above, SoC in MIRRA, consisted of OCS with or without IS, reflective of UK clinical practice. Therefore, use of data from the SoC arm of MIRRA would produce an indirect comparison of benralizumab versus SoC that is generalisable to UK clinical practice. 

The comparative efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC was determined for nine outcomes in total. Two of those were used in the economic analysis and, therefore, further detail is provided on the methodology to generate these 2 outcomes below. Further detail about how these endpoints were defined and the remaining 7 outcomes are presented in Appendix D. 

- **Proportion of participants in remission** - For remission (defined as BVAS = 0 and OCS dose ≤4 mg/day), a binomial distribution with logit link function (i.e. logistic regression) was performed. An estimate of the odds ratio (OR) and its variance for each intervention versus its comparator was then derived 

Company evidence submission for benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 56 -->

- **Annualised relapse rate (ARR)** - relapse rates were annualised by applying a log offset of patient-level follow-up. A negative binomial distribution with log link function was used. An estimate of the rate ratio (RR) and its variance for each intervention versus its comparator was derived 

Inputs used in the Bucher ITC analysis are outlined below in Table 18.

**Abbreviations:** CI: confidence interval; OR: odds ratio; RR: rate ratio; SoC: standard of care 

To generate the relative efficacy estimates between benralizumab and SoC, the log RR or odds ratio (OR) for treatment effect of SoC versus mepolizumab (informed by the MIRRA trial) was subtracted from the log RR or OR for treatment effect of benralizumab versus mepolizumab (informed by the MANDARA trial). The variance of this value was the sum of the two variances, which was then converted to standard error (SE) by taking the square root. Finally, from the log RR/OR and the SE it was possible to calculate 95% confidence intervals to inform the statistical significance of the comparison. Bucher ITCs were conducted using R version 3.6.1 or higher, based on methods described by Bucher et al.[95]

## **B.2.9.3 Uncertainties in the indirect treatment comparisons** 

The Bucher ITC was deemed appropriate as no adjustment for treatment effect modifiers was required, as validated by clinical experts.[3] As detailed in Section B.2.9.1, the MANDARA and MIRRA trials were adequately comparable with regards to the study population, study design and outcome measurements.[1, 34] Furthermore, clinical experts highlighted that the level of benefit demonstrated in the ITC for benralizumab versus SoC was similar to that demonstrated for mepolizumab (also an anti-IL-5 antibody) versus SoC (as shown in the MIRRA trial), supporting the results.[3] 

Prior to analysis, clinical experts ranked a list potential treatment effect-modifiers. During the feasibility assessment, differences in these potential effect-modifiers were observed between the MANDARA and MIRRA study populations. NICE guidelines recommend conducting populationadjusted indirect comparisons when there is evidence suggesting that effect-modifiers are present and imbalanced between trial populations.[91] Though cross-trial differences in ranked effect modifiers were considered by clinicians to not be meaningful (and hence a Bucher ITC was considered the primary indirect comparison approach), an anchored MAIC was conducted (methodology presented in Appendix D) in support of this submission and to further validate the results from the Bucher ITC.[78, 91] The adjustments in the MAIC were made based on the pooled clinical expert rank-ordered list of treatment-effect modifiers. 

In conclusion, the results of the MAIC were similar to those of the Bucher ITC i.e. a similar level of benefit was shown for benralizumab vs SoC irrespective of the approach adopted to generate the relative efficacy estimates. A scenario analysis with the relative efficacy informed by the MAIC is presented in Section B.3.10.3.

## _**Adverse reactions**_ 

The safety and tolerability of benralizumab compared to mepolizumab in patients with EGPA was evaluated in the MANDARA trial and its open-label extension (OLE). Benralizumab at the higher EGPA dose was well tolerated and demonstrated a safety profile, consistent with that seen in previous asthma studies (SIROCCO [NCT01928771], CALIMA [NCT01914757], and BORA [NCT02258542]).[96-98] There were no additional adverse drug reactions (ADR) identified. Adverse events were coded using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MeDRA, version 26.0). 

The safety analysis for both the double-blind (DB) period and the DB + OLE periods was performed using the Safety Analysis Set comprised of all patients who received at least one dose of the investigational product (IP). In the MANADARA trial the IP refers to benralizumab or mepolizumab. All safety analyses for the OLE period were performed using the OLE Analysis Set, which included all patients who received at least one dose of IP during the OLE period. When considering data from the OLE period, the treatment group “mepolizumab/benralizumab” includes patients who were in the mepolizumab arm during the DB period and then received benralizumab during the OLE period.

## **AEs of interest** 

Based on the mechanism of action of benralizumab, AEs of interest included helminth infections and malignancy. No patients reported helminth infections during the DB or OLE period. There were three malignant neoplasm events (2 serious events of prostate cancer in the mepolizumab group and 1 non-serious event of marginal zone lymphoma in the benralizumab group) reported during the DB period. A total of 2 malignant neoplasm events (1 serious event of rectal cancer in the benralizumab group and 1 nonserious event of malignant melanoma in situ in the benralizumab group) were reported during the OLE period. None of the malignant neoplasm events reported were assessed as possibly related to the IP.[83]

## **B.2.10.3 Deaths, SAEs and discontinuations** 

## **Deaths** 

There were no AEs with an outcome of death reported during the DB period. There was one death during the OLE period in the mepolizumab/benralizumab group due to a pulmonary embolism. This event was considered by the Investigator to be related to the patient’s underlying conditions as the patients’ medical history included deep vein thrombosis, surgical history of internal fixation, and open reduction of fracture. None of the events leading to the patient’s death were considered by the Investigator to be related to the IP.[1] 

## **SAEs** 

There were no new safety concerns regarding the incidence of SAEs. During the DB period, 4 and 9 SAEs were reported in the benralizumab group and in the mepolizumab group, respectively. Out of 3 SAEs in the mepolizumab group, one was assessed by the Investigator as possibly related to IP, and 2 SAEs led to discontinuation of IP.[1, 83] All patients in the benralizumab group and most patients in the mepolizumab group recovered from SAEs reported during the DB period. ## **Other significant AEs** 

Other significant AEs, given the route of administration of benralizumab, include hypersensitivity events and injection site reactions. The overall proportions of patients with hypersensitivity AEs during the DB period were similar between the benralizumab group and the mepolizumab group, with ** and ** patients reporting hypersensitivity in these groups, respectively.[83] *** hypersensitivity AEs in the benralizumab group and ***** hypersensitivity AEs in the mepolizumab group were assessed by the Investigator as possibly related to IP.[83] There were no cases of anaphylactic reactions reported during the DB period. The overall proportions of patients with injection site reaction AEs during the DB period were low and similar between the benralizumab group and the mepolizumab group, with ** and ** patients reporting injection site reactions in these groups, respectively.[83] No injection site reaction AEs reported during the DB period were serious, most were transient in nature, and none resulted in discontinuation of IP. All injection site reaction AEs reported during the DB period were assessed by the Investigator as possibly related to IP and all were mild or moderate in intensity.

## _**Ongoing studies**_ 

The MANDARA OLE investigating benralizumab for relapsing or refractory EGPA is ongoing at the time of this submission. Patients who completed the DB period were eligible to enrol onto the ongoing OLE phase of the study and could then receive benralizumab for at least one year; of the 140 patients who entered the MANDARA trial,[1] *** entered the OLE. The OLE is investigating the same primary and secondary endpoints as the MANDARA trial, with a new data cut of results expected in 2025. Interim results for the OLE are presented in Appendix N. The trial is expected to complete in March 2026.

## _**Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence**_ 

## **B.2.12.1 Principal findings from the clinical evidence** 

## **Clinical effectiveness** 

The key clinical effectiveness evidence for benralizumab in EGPA was provided by the MANDARA study, a Phase III, randomised, DB, active-controlled, parallel group, non-inferiority study comparing the efficacy and safety of benralizumab to mepolizumab in adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA on corticosteroid therapy with or without stable immunosuppressive therapy. The results of this study showed that benralizumab was efficacious at inducing remission in 58% of EGPA patients at Weeks 36 and 48, meeting the primary endpoint of MANDARA. Treatment with benralizumab also resulted in durable remission, with remission lasting for at least 24 weeks 

Company evidence submission for benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 66 -->

in 57.1% of patients. Furthermore, the annualised relapse rate with benralizumab remained low (ARR of 0.5). In line with the induction of durable remission and avoidance of relapse, treatment with benralizumab had an OCS-sparing benefit, which is expected to prevent an increase in the incidence of OCS-related AEs and comorbidities. ******* ******* **** *** ******* **** ******** ** ******** ** ************ *** ********** ** ******** ** ************ ********* ** ***** ** ********** *** ********* *** *** *******[**] * 

As the goal of EGPA treatment is to induce sustained remission and reduce dependence on high doses of OCS, this clinical evidence showed benralizumab to be an efficacious treatment option. Treatment with benralizumab would reduce the range of EGPA manifestations and symptoms, slow disease progression and prevent further organ damage. 

## **Comparative efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC** 

The MANDARA trial provided a comparison of the efficacy of benralizumab versus mepolizumab, however mepolizumab is not a relevant comparator for this evaluation as it is not a reimbursed treatment option in the UK. As per the decision problem, the relevant comparator is SoC in UK clinical practice, consisting of OCS with or without IS. Given the lack of head-to-head trial informing the relative efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC in patients with EGPA, a Bucher ITC was conducted, using data for the benralizumab from the MANDARA trial and data for SoC arm (OCS with or without IS) from the MIRRA trial, anchored through the common comparator, mepolizumab.[1, 34] Based on this analysis, benralizumab was associated with a statistically significant improvement in remission rates and a reduction in annualised relapse rates, in comparison to SoC. 

## **Safety** 

Benralizumab at the higher EGPA dose in MANDARA was well-tolerated, with no new safety signals and an overall safety profile consistent with that observed for benralizumab in previous studies of severe asthma (SIROCCO [NCT01928771], CALIMA [NCT01914757] and ZONDA [NCT02075255]).[96-98] There were similar proportions of AEs between treatment arms in MANDARA and the majority of these were mild or moderate in severity. There was a low rate of treatment-related adverse events, and a lower proportion of SAEs reported in the benralizumab treatment arm compared to the mepolizumab arm. There were no AEs or SAEs with an outcome of death during the DB period and only 28.6% of patients in the benralizumab arm had an IPrelated AE, none of which resulted in the discontinuation of benralizumab. 

## **B.2.12.2 Strengths and limitations in context to UK clinical practice** 

EGPA is a rare and poorly characterised disease, and as is common in the rare disease space, there was limited literature informing the evolution of the condition. Extensive work was undertaken by AstraZeneca to deepen understanding of the disease and generate a robust evidence base for benralizumab, in support of this submission. Whilst being the only RCT to inform the clinical evidence base for benralizumab, MANDARA was a high-quality trial demonstrating both internal and external validity.

<!-- page 67 -->

## **Strengths** 

## _**Internal validity of MANDARA**_ 

As discussed in Sections B.2.3, B.2.4 and B.2.5, the MANDARA trial was methodologically robust, with the results considered to be at a low risk of bias due to the following: 

- Patients were randomised in a 1:1 ratio between treatment arms 

- The trial was DB and therefore, participants and outcome assessors were appropriately blinded to treatment allocation 

## _**External validity of MANDARA**_ 

Results from MANDARA can be generalised to the UK population for the following reasons: 

- MANDARA enrolled patients from the UK and five European countries (Belgium, France, Germany, Italy and the UK) anticipated to have similar demographics to the UK.[88] For example, 81.7% of England and Wales is White (2021 Census)[99] and ****% of the MANDARA population was White[83] 

- Clinical experts agreed that the baseline characteristics of patients from the MANDARA trial, and baseline treatment usage, were generalisable to patients in real-world practice in the UK, confirming the applicability of the trial results to the UK setting[3, 83] 

- MANDARA assessed the efficacy of benralizumab across a wide range of endpoints relevant to patients with EGPA and covering the spectrum of disease manifestations, including remission rates and durability of remission, relapse rates, OCS use, vasculitis activity and pulmonary function. 

- During MANDARA, concomitant OCS and IS were allowed, in line with SoC in the UK, emulating the use of benralizumab in clinical practice 

## **Limitations** 

MANDARA was a pivotal active-controlled phase III trial offering head-to-head evidence for benralizumab versus mepolizumab – a gold standard in evaluating the effectiveness of treatments.[1] However, given that mepolizumab is not a reimbursed treatment option in the UK, comparative efficacy estimates had to be generated for the relevant comparator for this submission; UK SoC comprising of OCS and IS. 

An ITC, in the form of a Bucher ITC, was conducted to obtain relative efficacy estimates to inform the economic analysis. Clinical experts highlighted that the level of benefit demonstrated in the ITC for benralizumab versus SoC was similar to that demonstrated for mepolizumab (also an anti-IL-5 antibody) versus SoC (as shown in the MIRRA trial), supporting the results.[3, 34] 

As noted in Section B.2.9.3, an anchored MAIC was also conducted in support of this submission, in line with NICE’s preference.[91] The results of the anchored MAIC were used to inform a scenario analysis in the cost effectiveness model. The scenario analysis results (Section B.3.10.3) indicated a minor change to the ICER, therefore further validating the results of the Bucher ITC.

## **B.3 Cost effectiveness** 

## **Overview of the economic analysis** 

- A _de novo_ economic analysis was conducted to assess the cost-effectiveness of benralizumab as an add-on to SoC treatment in adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA 

- Comparator: A weighted average of the agents used in UK SoC; OCS (prednisolone) and IS therapies (e.g. azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and methotrexate) 

- Model structure: A cohort-level, Markov state-transition model, which consisted of death and three alive health states which comprehensively captured the disease evolution: remission, stable disease and relapse.[3] Given data limitations, it was not possible to implement the refractory and non-refractory health states as individual health states. Therefore, these were modelled as sub-states within a ‘stable disease’ health state 

- Efficacy: MANDARA[1] (benralizumab efficacy) and Bucher ITC (benralizumab versus SoC relative efficacy) 

- Health-state utilities: EQ-5D derived from the Adelphi DSP study.[74] Disutilities associated with OCS-related AEs were also incorporated in the analysis 

- Cost categories: Drug acquisition costs, disease management costs and costs for treating OCS-related AEs 

## **Overall evidence strategy** 

- The rarity of EGPA and lack of research and innovation in this space thus far means that there was limited literature and no prior cost-effectiveness evaluations to inform model inputs 

- The evidence strategy adopted for this submission was in line with the NICE Real-World Evidence (RWE) framework, i.e. informing efficacy data from the RCT and other inputs using UK-relevant, EGPA-specific RWE[100] 

## **Key results** 

- The economic evaluation resulted in a deterministic ICER of £25,314/QALY gained 

- The probabilistic ICER was consistent with the deterministic ICER, with a corresponding cost per QALY of £26,310 

- The ICER was also robust to individual parameter uncertainty, with deterministic sensitivity analyses and scenario analyses having a minimal impact on the ICER 

## **Benefits not captured in QALY** 

- Benralizumab is expected to prevent further organ damage, alleviating the symptom burden and improving HRQoL for patients 

- Durable remission from treatment with benralizumab will allow patients to self-administer benralizumab at home, resulting in cost savings to the NHS and reducing disruption to patients’ work and saving the time and cost of travel to hospitals

## **B.3.2.1 Patient population** 

The population modelled in this cost-effectiveness analysis was adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA being treated with OCS, with or without IS. This was in line with the final scope from NICE for this evaluation and the population in the MANDARA trial.[1] Population demographics were derived from the CPRD cohort of patients with EGPA in England, to be most representative of UK clinical practice.[2] The baseline characteristics of individuals entering the cost-effectiveness model are summarised in Section B.3.3.1. 

## **B.3.2.2 Model structure** 

## **Defining health states in EGPA** 

EGPA is a poorly characterised rare disease and there are no prior appraisals or published economic models given limited innovation in this space. Furthermore, given the limited research into EGPA to date, literature to help inform the evolution of the disease is scarce. 

It was crucial for the economic analysis to capture the evolution of the disease and reflect the relevant health states as described in Section B.1.3.1. Consequently, extensive work was undertaken by AstraZeneca to deepen the understanding of the disease in support of this submission, as outlined in Table 30.

From the interviews with patients and clinical experts, it was evident that there are four distinct health states which are relevant: remission, non-refractory, refractory, relapse (Section B.1.3.1). Whilst remission and relapse have clear definitions, some patients experience disease that is not accurately described by either definition, and can broadly be characterised into two disease distinct sub-states with different, clinically meaningful profiles: non-refractory and refractory.[3] These patients were often grouped into a ‘stable disease’ state in clinical trials. However, understanding of eosinophilic-driven diseases has progressed significantly since the pivotal 

Company evidence submission for benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 72 -->

MIRRA and MANDARA trials first evaluated biologic therapies (mepolizumab and benralizumab) for EGPA.[1, 34] 

Currently, there is a clear focus on reducing patients’ OCS exposure given the well characterised detrimental long-term health consequences as well as the negative impact on quality of life. In EGPA, the relevance of OCS exposure is particularly high considering that approximately 64% of patients require two or more OCS courses per year.[15] This level of exposure is concerning, as evidence demonstrates that as few as 2–4 lifetime courses of OCS can lead to a significantly increased risk of adverse outcomes.[32, 79, 107] Additionally, a cumulative OCS dose of ≥0.9 g has been shown to be linked to an 80% likelihood of an increase in glucocorticoid toxicity.[79] Considering that the mean cumulative dosage has been reported to be as high as 6.3 g in patients with EGPA across a mean follow-up duration of 21.7 months,[80] the majority of patients are likely to experience OCS-related AEs. 

Given the high OCS doses required in EGPA, based on the hypereosinophilic nature of the condition, an OCS sub-model was incorporated in the Markov framework to capture the longterm health benefits and cost savings of OCS-sparing offered by benralizumab.[102] Further detail is provided in the OCS sub-model section. 

The definitions of the remission, refractory and relapse health states were aligned with the MANDARA trial.[1] The definition of the non-refractory health state was consistent with interpretation in UK clinical practice. All health state definitions were validated by clinical experts.[3] Further information about each health state in reference to the economic analysis (with the refractory and non-refractory reflected as sub-states within a ‘stable disease’ health state) is provided below in Table 31.
