## **Overview of the model structure** 

As is commonly the case in the rare disease space, no prior models were identified by the economic SLR that characterised the natural history of EGPA or assessed the cost-effectiveness of treatments in EGPA (as described in Section B.3.1). Therefore, a _de novo_ economic analysis was conducted to estimate the cost-effectiveness of benralizumab as an add-on treatment to SoC for adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA.[3] 

The cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted using a cohort-level, Markov state-transition model built in Microsoft Excel®. A Markov framework was deemed appropriate to capture the relapsing-remitting disease course of EGPA, based on its suitability to capture the risk of disease over time as well as episodic events.[3] Given the absence of prior NICE evaluations in patients with EGPA, an extensive review of NICE evaluations was undertaken into other related conditions to develop the optimal modelling approach. Evaluations in diseases such as vasculitis (TA308) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) (TA825), were identified which are very distinct conditions with distinct pathogenesis making them poor proxies to inform any model inputs.[77, 108] However, both diseases progress through remission/relapse states which were modelled using a Markov framework further supporting the approach adopted in this submission. 

The cost-effectiveness model featured three mutually exclusive, alive health states – which comprehensively captured the disease evolution; namely remission, stable disease, relapse – as well as a death state (Figure 9). Due to the limited sample size in MANDARA (N=70 patients in the benralizumab arm), transition probabilities to and from the non-refractory and refractory health states from other health states could not be derived from the trial data. Given these data limitations, the refractory and non-refractory health states were modelled as sub-states within the stable disease health state. Further detail on this approach is provided in Section B.3.3.3.

Patients entered the model in the stable disease health state (Section B.3.3.1), in accordance with the inclusion criteria of MANDARA (maintained on at least 7.5 mg of daily OCS, with or Company evidence submission for benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 75 -->

without stable immunosuppressive therapy). Within any given cycle, patients were eligible to transition between any alive health state, or to the absorbing death state. The transitions possible within the model are described in further detail in B.3.3.2. 

Health state occupancy was modelled at 4-week (28-day) intervals over the course of the lifetime horizon (maximum 60 years). Each health state was assigned a utility value, and costs associated with disease management; drug acquisition costs were also considered in the analysis. As discussed in Section B.1.3.4, OCS use can lead to an increased risk of a range of AEs and comorbidities. To capture the risks associated with OCS use, an OCS sub-model was incorporated in the Markov framework, which included disutilities and costs applied for each event, based on mean OCS dose per health state.[102] In each cycle, the costs and utilities were multiplied by the proportion of patients in each health state to calculate the weighted costs and QALYs per health state. The weighted costs and QALYs per cycle were summed up over the entire model time horizon for each treatment arm, and the incremental costs and QALYs were subsequently calculated. 

## **OCS sub-model** 

## _**Capturing long-term health and economic benefits of OCS sparing in EGPA**_ 

As explained in B.1.3.3, a key component of SoC in EGPA is OCS required to manage symptoms. Given the hypereosinophilic nature of EGPA, high chronic doses of OCS are typically needed to achieve an acceptable level of symptom control. CPRD analysis identified mean daily doses of OCS ranging from 12.4 to 23.1 mg/day over time in the 5 years following EGPA diagnosis.[4] 

Whilst OCS are effective anti-inflammatory agents, substantial evidence associates their use with increased risks for AEs, causing a high burden on the NHS, with OCS treatment shown to be one of the most common causes of hospitalisation due to AEs. Risks are increased even from shortterm use, with cumulative lifetime OCS exposure being the main driving factor responsible for increased risk of AEs.[102] 

Therefore, to accurately model EGPA, it was crucial to capture the range of AEs (comorbidities and acute events) and reflect the costs and HRQoL decrements associated with each of these events. Correspondingly, it was also important to capture the long-term benefits of OCS-sparing agents, such as benralizumab, and capture the cost savings and positive implications on HRQoL associated with reducing the incidence of chronic and acute OCS-related AEs. 

## _**Approach used in prior NICE appraisals**_ 

In the recent NICE technology appraisals for tezepelumab (TA880) and benralizumab (TA565), biologics recommended for the treatment of severe asthma and severe eosinophilic asthma, respectively, the effects of long-term OCS maintenance were considered to impact HRQoL and HCRU through the risk of developing OCS-related comorbidities.[103, 109] In these models, 10 AEs commonly associated with OCS exposure were included as acute AEs with incidence data based on patients’ average daily dose in that model cycle. However, during the tezepelumab evaluation, expert review noted that the full effects of OCS-sparing were unlikely to be fully captured within the model submitted in that evaluation. This underestimation was primarily due to the underlying assumption that all AEs were acute events incurring a one-off incidence cost and QALY loss, which underestimated the long-term costs and QALY losses from conditions such as T2DM, cardiovascular disease and osteoporosis. 

Company evidence submission for benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 76 -->

## _**Approach used in this submission**_ 

To address the limitation of the prior approach used to model OCS sparing, and better inform healthcare decision making, this submission utilised a recently published modelling approach designed to more comprehensively capture the heath economic outcomes related to reducing OCS use. The approach was referred to as the “OCS sub-model” and comprised of a Markov model structure to model the most common chronic comorbidities and acute events resulting from OCS use, and the associated costs and impact on HRQoL, in alignment with the model published by Gibson et al. 2024 (Figure 10).[102 ] 

Patients could enter the model in either the event-free health state or any of the chronic disease health states based on baseline population characteristics, presented in Section B.3.3.1, with patients developing increasingly multimorbid disease as they accumulated OCS dose over time. 

Three chronic comorbidities (in purple in Figure 10) were included in the sub-model: T2DM, established cardiovascular disease (eCVD) and osteoporosis. These were chosen as they were the key drivers of morbidity and mortality from OCS-related AEs impacting patient HRQoL and NHS costs.[102 ] The definition of eCVD included cardiovascular events for myocardial infarction and heart failure, and cerebrovascular disease including stroke. 

As well as developing chronic comorbidities, patients were at a risk of developing acute AEs (in blue in Figure 10). These were additional AEs that are commonly associated with OCS in the literature but are considered as “one-off” events captured in a simplified manner as acute events, driven by incidence. These included adrenal insufficiency, cataract, glaucoma, peptic ulcer, pneumonia, and renal impairment. Since these events were more acute in nature, they were modelled for the duration of one cycle length (28 days). 

No OCS-related mortality was captured in the OCS sub-model as all-cause mortality was captured in the EGPA model structure, which would already inherently capture the effects of chronic OCS use on the risk of death. As explained above, the OCS sub-model only captured the costs and impact on HRQoL associated with OCS exposure. Further details on this approach are provided in Section B.3.3.6. 

The overarching model structure, including the OCS sub-model was validated by clinical and health economic experts; all experts agreed the modelling approaches were appropriate balancing the need to reflect the evolution of the disease with simplicity considering the available data.[3, 78]

## **B.3.2.3 Intervention technology and comparators** 

## **Intervention: Benralizumab** 

The intervention considered in the cost effectiveness analysis was benralizumab as an add-on treatment to SoC. The model included the dose of benralizumab anticipated to be indicated for EGPA: 30 mg, Q4W by SC injection. As benralizumab is anticipated to be indicated as an add-on treatment for EGPA, “benralizumab” in this submission refers to treatment with benralizumab in addition to SoC. 

## **Comparators** 

As discussed in Section B.1.1, the appropriate comparator for this submission was a weighted average of the most used agents for the management of EGPA in UK clinical practice. Clinical guidelines and clinical expert opinion indicate that the most used agents to induce and maintain remission for EGPA are OCS and IS (e.g. methotrexate, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil) and therefore, these are considered to form SoC in the UK.[2, 3] The treatment distribution was informed by Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) data, which was validated by clinical expert opinion as being representative of UK clinical practice.[3, 4] 

The comparator treatments are summarised in Table 32.

## _**Clinical parameters and variables**_ 

## **Evidence strategy** 

- The rarity of EGPA and lack of research and innovation in this space thus far means that there was limited literature and no prior CE evaluations to inform model inputs 

- The main clinical evidence supporting the use of benralizumab as an add-on treatment in patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA is the pivotal, Phase III MANDARA trial which had a methodologically robust study design in line with the decision problem, making it an appropriate source of clinical data for the model.[1] However, mepolizumab is not reimbursed in the UK for EGPA and is not a comparator, as specified in the NICE final scope 

- • Therefore, an ITC was conducted, in the form of a Bucher ITC, to inform the relative efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC. These findings were summarised in Section B.2.9 

- The evidence strategy adopted for this submission was in line with the NICE RWE framework, i.e. informing efficacy data from the RCT and informing other inputs using UK-relevant, EGPAspecific RWE[100] 

- Extensive clinical validation was conducted to ensure inputs reflected UK clinical practice 

A summary of sources used to inform clinical parameters in the cost-effectiveness analysis is presented in Table 33.

## **B.3.3.2 Transition probabilities and response assessment** 

Patients entered the model in the stable disease health state, in line with the MANDARA inclusion criteria (stable dose of OCS of ≥7.5 mg/day for at least four weeks prior to randomisation and stable dose of IS for the four weeks prior to randomisation). Following model entry, transition probabilities determined how likely participants were to move between health states. Transition probabilities were treatment-specific, capturing the effect of benralizumab versus SoC in the achievement of durable remission.

## **Response assessment** 

At 52 weeks, patients in the benralizumab arm of the model were assessed for their treatment response. The definition of response was consistent with the primary endpoint of the MANDARA trial, i.e. BVAS=0 and an OCS dose ≤4 mg/day.[1] The probability of response was informed by MANDARA (Table 36). Responders continued to receive benralizumab treatment whilst nonresponders discontinued benralizumab treatment (Figure 14), and the movement through health states pre- and post-assessment is described in the section below. 

As mentioned in Table 33, the response assessment at 52 weeks was consistent with the length of the MANDARA trial,  the recommended use of benralizumab in severe asthma, and in line with the anticipated use of benralizumab in EGPA in UK clinical practice.[3] 

No response assessment was conducted for the SoC arm, in line with UK clinical practice.

## **Intervention: benralizumab** 

Prior to the response assessment, transition probabilities in the benralizumab arm of the model were derived from all patients in the benralizumab arm of MANDARA up until the time of response assessment (Table 37). Transition probabilities were derived using 28-day transition count data assuming last observation carried forward (i.e., patients were assumed to remain in a health state until an observation indicating they had moved elsewhere). Transition counts had a multinomial likelihood, which had a flat Dirichlet prior distribution using Gibbs sampling to obtain the posterior probability distribution of the health state transition matrix.[115] 

Following response assessment, patients who were identified as being responsive to benralizumab continued treatment; transition probabilities for responders were then informed only by the subgroup of responders in the benralizumab arm of MANDARA, following the methods specified above. It was assumed that responders’ transition probabilities remained constant throughout the remainder of the lifetime horizon of the model as benralizumab exhibits

## **B.3.3.3 Informing the proportion of patients in the refractory sub-state, by** 

## **treatment arm** 

As described in Section B.3.2.2, the refractory and non-refractory health states were modelled as sub-states within the stable disease health state. The refractory and non-refractory sub-states were captured in the model by allocating a proportion of patients in each sub-state, by treatment arm. The proportion of refractory patients was derived from CPRD data, and the approach is outlined below. The proportion of non-refractory patients was calculated as 100% minus the proportion of refractory patients as they were all-encompassing within the ‘umbrella’ term of stable disease. The refractory and non-refractory sub-states were associated with specific health-state utilities, akin to the other health states, remission and relapse. 

The following subsections describe the approach to inform the proportion of patients in the refractory sub-state by treatment arm. 

## _**SoC arm**_ 

- No data were available from the MANDARA trial to inform the SoC arm, as this was not the comparator in the trial[1] 

- Therefore, an analysis was undertaken by AstraZeneca using the CPRD dataset. The analysis determined that, of the cohort who receive UK SoC, ****% had refractory disease and that this proportion stayed constant over the 5 years of the study. A brief overview of this CPRD study is included below:[2] 

   - The study was a 5-year longitudinal retrospective observational cohort study conducted using the Clinical Research Practice Datalink (CPRD) Aurum primary care database with linkage to the Hospital Episode Statistics inpatient admitted

- Therefore, to remain consistent with the CPRD data, the economic analysis considered ****% of patients as having refractory disease within the stable disease health state, and this proportion was constant over the time horizon of the analysis, as validated by clinical experts.[3]

Following discontinuation of benralizumab, patients were modelled as per the effectiveness of SoC. This approach assumed that the efficacy of benralizumab was instantly lost upon discontinuation, consistent with the previous model evaluating benralizumab for severe asthma (TA565).[103] Once patients discontinued benralizumab, they were no longer eligible to reinitiate treatment at any subsequent timepoint. 

## **Discontinuation of OCS (OCS sub-model)** 

In line with prescription data analysis from CPRD, 86.2% of patients entered the model receiving concomitant OCS.[4] Treatment with benralizumab allowed patients to taper or discontinue OCS, in line with MANDARA. As described above, OCS dose reduction is a key treatment goal in EGPA, and the OCS sub-model allowed to capture the long-term health benefits and cost savings associated with the OCS-sparing benefit from benralizumab. 

The inputs related to the discontinuation of OCS are presented in Table 43. Although an endpoint of MANDARA was the percentage reduction in the mean daily dose of OCS during Weeks 48 to 52 compared to baseline, time-to-OCS discontinuation was not measured. Therefore, the rate of OCS discontinuation was instead estimated by analysing data on OCS dose, which was recorded during MANDARA. For this analysis, discontinuation was assumed to be defined as a patient with an OCS dose of zero for the last 28 days of trial participation (to include patients lost to follow up). The time attributed to discontinuation was taken as the start of the interval in the contiguous stretch leading up to the end of the patient’s trial participation in which the OCS dose was zero. The derived probability of OCS discontinuation from this approach ******* was consistent with the pre-defined percentage reduction endpoint of the trial, which was reported as 41.4% for patients receiving benralizumab.[83]

## **B.3.3.6 Adverse events** 

Benralizumab-related AEs were not included in the cost-effectiveness analysis given the low incidence of serious AEs observed in MANDARA,[1] and hence the minimal expected impact of AEs on patient HRQoL and NHS costs. This approach was aligned with the previous evaluation of benralizumab for severe eosinophilic asthma.[103] The safety profile of benralizumab at the higher EGPA dose in MANDARA was aligned with what is observed in severe asthma.[103] 

## **OCS-related AEs (OCS sub-model)[102]** 

As outlined in Section B.3.2.2, the impact of acute events and chronic comorbidities caused by OCS were modelled, capturing the impacts on cost and HRQoL. The risk of developing chronic disease (modelled using prevalence) and experiencing acute events (modelled using incidence) were characterised through Cox proportional hazard regression models adjusted for cumulative OCS dose, with higher doses increasing the risk of developing disease or experiencing an acute event. The model used the mean daily dose of OCS stratified by EGPA-related health state to reflect the increased need for higher doses of OCS in the relapse and stable disease health states (compared to remission). The mean daily dose for patients residing in EGPA-related health states is presented in Table 44. 

For each cycle patients resided in an EGPA-related health state, they accumulated 28 times the mean daily dose attributed to that health state, assuming the daily dose remained constant over the course of one cycle. A weighted mean dose for the entire cohort was then derived to inform the risk of developing chronic disease and acute events. Average daily doses of OCS by health state were derived from CPRD data, reflective of UK clinical practice.[2]

## **Chronic disease development** 

Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to determine the risk of developing chronic disease as a function of cumulative OCS dose.[102] To calculate the risk of comorbidity development based on OCS use, the regression model included: 

- Baseline event rates, assumed to be representative of the risk of comorbidity development for patients in the general population with no prior OCS dose (Table 45) 

- Coefficients representative of a one-gram increase in cumulative OCS dose, exponentiated to determine hazard ratios (HRs) which represent the increased risk of comorbidity development per gram of cumulative OCS dose (Table 46) 

A risk equation was applied, with the AE event risk defined as 1 minus the exponential to the power of the baseline risk, multiplied by an exponent of the additional risk per gram to the power of the cumulative dosage in grams and the value of OCS-sparing in avoiding events accumulated over time, dependent on the extent that the patient’s cumulative exposure to OCS was reduced. The value of OCS-sparing in avoiding events accumulated over time, dependent on the extent that the patient’s cumulative exposure to OCS was reduced.[102] 

The baseline event rates were sourced from Gibson et al.,[102] and were derived from the Cox proportional hazard models developed by the Observational and Pragmatic Research Institute (OPRI) which evaluated the chronic disease onset associated with OCS use based on the Optimum Patient Care Research Database (OPCRD) and the CPRD database.[32, 110] The OPRI study investigated the impact of OCS exposure on disease onset, burden and healthcare resource use over a minimum 2-year timescale in a broad, real-world, UK patient population which consisted of patients diagnosed with conditions where OCS may be prescribed. The morbidity rates from this study are therefore considered to be generalisable to EGPA patients in UK clinical practice. 

As patients resided in EGPA health states, the weighted average cumulative OCS dose was calculated across the cohort and the regression model was used to determine the mean risk of comorbidity development.

## **Chronic disease progression** 

Once OCS-related chronic disease had developed, subsequent chronic disease progression in the form of a multimorbidity was modelled to account for the increased risk of multimorbidity with continued OCS use observed in the broad population of OCS users.[118, 119] The inputs related to chronic disease progression are presented in Table 47. All inputs were HRs for the development of an additional morbidity relative to the morbidity already being experienced; for example, the mean HR for the development of T2DM in a patient who already has eCVD was 1.170.[118] The HRs were used to further adjust the Cox proportional hazard regression models. 

The relationship between T2DM and eCVD is well discussed in the literature, with T2DM being a significant risk factor for the development of eCVD, and eCVD being the most prevalent cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with T2DM,[120-122] the inputs for these health states were sourced from studies by the QResearch group and aligned with those used in the published study from Gibson et al.[102, 118, 119]

## **Acute events** 

As with chronic disease onset, Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to determine the risk of developing acute events as a function of cumulative OCS dose. The mean cumulative OCS dose was used to inform the regression model and determine the risk across the entire cohort. 

The inputs for the general population rate of experiencing acute events are presented in Table 48. As with the chronic disease, these event rates were derived from the Cox proportional hazard models developed by the OPRI group.[102] Acute events were modelled as acute events, and as a pragmatic approach, the effects lasted the length of the cycle. A one-off cost (Section B.3.5) and utility decrement (Section B.3.4) associated with each acute event were applied in the cycle of incidence, with no further effects on OCS-related disease progression thereafter.

## _**Measurement and valuation of health effects**_ 

As discussed in Section B.1.3.1, EGPA is characterised by severe, multi-system manifestations and organ damage, which contribute to a considerable negative impact on many aspects of patients’ quality of life. Patients experience multiple disruptions to daily living including severe fatigue, functional impairment, sleep disruption, emotional distress, anxiety and a reduced ability to work and engage in social activities. Additionally, current SoC (OCS and IS) have limited effectiveness with high relapse rates and short times to relapse. This leaves patients cycling through the EGPA health states, causing patients to feel low, scared, frustrated and anxious, exacerbating negative feelings about future outcomes. Furthermore, OCS are associated with severe, chronic and acute AEs, compounding the impact of EGPA on HRQoL. Therefore, utilities dependent on each health state and disutilities associated with OCS-related AEs were modelled to capture the potential impact of EGPA and OCS use on HRQoL. 

## **B.3.4.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials** 

The MANDARA trial collected HRQoL data using the SF-36 questionnaire. SF-36 is an instrument used for assessing general health and QoL, with questions on eight domains of health, including physical and social functioning.[123] The HRQoL analysis was based on data pooled from the mepolizumab and benralizumab arms, as this increased the sample size for the analysis, and the HRQoL data were stratified by disease status, independent of treatment arm. 

## **B.3.4.2 Mapping** 

The SF-36 data collected in MANDARA were mapped to EQ-5D-3L (henceforth referred to as just “EQ-5D”), to abide to the NICE reference case, which advocates for EQ-5D as the preferred method for valuing HRQoL. As there is no preferred mapping algorithm in the NICE reference case, two published methods were explored: Ara and Brazier, 2008 and Rowen et al., 2009.[124, ] 125 

The mapping algorithm developed by Rowen et al.[125] was used for the analysis, due to a larger sample size used to derive the mapping algorithm and the higher R[2] . Rowen et al. also concluded that when measuring goodness-of-fit statistics, their model performed better than the Ara and Brazier model. The Rowen model mapped SF-36 scores to EQ-5D scores, and utility values were generated using the UK value set derived by Dolan et al.[126] Once EQ-5D index scores were generated, health state utility values were generated based on a “crude” mean of index scores attributed to the time-updated health states observed in the MANDARA trial. In this 

Company evidence submission for benralizumab with for treating adults with relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 98 -->

instance “crude” refers to averaging across all observations, for which some patients had multiple observations. 

MANDARA started recruitment in 2019. The understanding of EGPA has subsequently evolved as explained in B.3.2.2, and it was important to reflect four relevant health states in the economic analysis. However, quality of life data in MANDARA were only collected for the remission, stable disease and relapse health states. To address this limitation, IPD have since been retrospectively analysed to generate the utility values for the non-refractory and refractory health states. Table 50 presents the results of SF-36 from MANDARA mapped to EQ-5D. 

However, the quality of life results from MANDARA were not consistent with the insights gathered from patient and clinical expert interviews for the two reasons outlined below.[3, 70] The potential reasons why this might be the case are presented in Table 51. 

1. Minimal utility difference between remission and relapse 

   - a. Clinical experts and patients consistently highlighted how HRQoL is significantly better in remission compared to relapse – based on the considerably alleviated symptom burden and lower doses of medication (OCS dose in particular) 

2. Refractory not being the health state with the lowest utility 

   - a. Clinical experts and patients mention the severe symptoms limiting their daily activities and social life combined with the psychological impact of not having achieved remission for 6 months and the despair, anxiety and frustration they experience in the refractory health state result in a significant negative impact on their wellbeing 

In summary, the mapped utility data from MANDARA did not accurately capture the patient experience of living with EGPA, as validated by clinical experts.[3] Therefore, the trial utility data were not used in the economic model, and alternative approaches were investigated further (Section B.3.4.4).

## **analysis** 

As described across Sections B.3.4.1 to B.3.4.3, there were limitations with HRQoL from MANDARA, and the SLR *** *** ******** *** ******** utility data. In light of this, extensive work was undertaken to address the limitations of the trial utility data and generate robust evidence to accurately represent QoL in an EGPA-specific population – which was challenging, given the rarity of the disease. There were two studies which were conducted to address this data limitation; the Adelphi Real World Disease Specific Programme (thereafter referred to as Adelphi DSP) and a UK-specific vignette study.[39, 74] 

Both RWE studies provided HRQoL data which were granular enough to inform HRQoL for all the four health states considered in this submission. Each study had its own merit: 

- Adelphi DSP: 177 patients (9 from the UK) completed the EQ-5D questionnaire in the study, which was a significant source of data, given the rarity of EGPA 

- UK-specific vignette study: UK-specific HRQoL data was collected, thus providing an opportunity to leverage data most reflective of UK EGPA patients 

An overview of each study is provided in Table 52. The health state descriptions derived from interviews, as part of conducting the vignette study are presented in Appendix O. The approach of obtaining alternative HRQoL values including vignettes, to help inform decision making, is consistent with the Committee recommendation in TA981.[130]

Although the utility value for the refractory health state was rated consistently by patients and the general population, the value was unusually low considering utility values observed for the other health states as well as other diseases. Considering the sensitivity of this parameter, a more conservative set of assumptions was chosen, based on Adelphi DSP. 

Adelphi DSP was deemed the most appropriate source to inform HRQoL in the base case for the below reasons: 

- It provided utility for all four health states, in the form of EQ-5D, NICE’s preferred measure of HRQoL 

- 177 patients completed the EQ-5D questionnaire, which is a significant source of data, given the rarity of EGPA – this was the biggest sample size to inform HRQoL [compared to MANDARA (N=140) and patient valuation of the vignette study (N=21)] 

- The utility values were mapped using a UK tariff – thereby making the results suitable for UK decision making

- Standard deviations around the mean utility scores were low 

- Adelphi DSP was the EAG and Committee’s preferred assumption in TA958 and was considered the most appropriate source to inform QoL for decision making[132] 

- The values were validated by clinical experts as being reflective of the HRQoL of UK EGPA patients[3]

## **B.3.4.5 Adverse reactions** 

As explained in Section B.3.3.6, benralizumab-related AEs were not included in the costeffectiveness analysis given the low incidence of serious AEs observed in MANDARA,[1] and hence the minimal expected impact of AEs on patient HRQoL and NHS costs. The safety profile of benralizumab at the higher EGPA dose in MANDARA was aligned with what is observed in severe asthma.[103] 

The analysis captured the impact of OCS-related comorbidities and acute events on HRQoL, through the application of utility decrements. For each cycle that patients resided in a chronic disease health state, they accrued the relevant utility decrement which was applied additively to the health state utilities for EGPA. As acute events occurred only in the cycle of incidence, a oneoff utility decrement was applied in the same cycle. Chronic disease utility decrements were input into the cost-effectiveness model as annualised utility decrements and were scaled to 28-day decrements to match the cycle length of the model. Where patients experience multiple comorbid AEs, a multiplicative approach was taken to combining the associated disutilities. 

The utility decrements applied in the model are presented in Table 55. In the absence of HRQoL data from MANDARA stratified by OCS-related morbidity or acute event, all utility decrements were sourced from a catalogue of EQ-5D index scores based on UK preference weights, derived from a general population sample of 79,522 patients, ensuring incorporation of the preferences of the UK general public.[133]

## **B.3.4.7 Age-based utility decrement** 

Age-adjusted utility values were implemented in the model to account for the expected decrease in HRQoL over time associated with aging. The utility estimates for each model cycle were adjusted based on the difference between patients’ mean age during the current cycle and the mean age at baseline (see Section B.3.3.1 for starting age). The age-adjusted utilities were implemented using mean EQ-5D-3L values by age, estimated from the latest available wave of the Health Survey for England (HSE) that included the EQ-5D-3L.[134] A proportional age

adjustment factor for each year was calculated based on the mean utility at the measured age (e.g., the starting age from the CPRD cohort is **** years) and the corresponding age-adjusted utility in every year. The age adjustment was applied to the mean utility in a multiplicative fashion in each cycle of the model.

## **Drug acquisition costs** 

## _**Intervention: benralizumab**_ 

Patients in receipt of benralizumab in the economic model incurred costs of benralizumab and costs associated with the background use of SoC. ## _**Comparator: SoC**_ 

As discussed in Section B.1.3.3, SoC for patients with EGPA consists of OCS and IS. Therefore, the comparator arm costs consist of a weighted average of OCS (prednisolone) and IS agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and methotrexate). OCS treatment can be discontinued, however, IS therapy is generally not discontinued, and this was reflected in the way these treatments were modelled. The cost per cycle of SoC treatment was dependent on the percentage of EGPA patients receiving OCS, which varied each model cycle as patients discontinued the treatment, and a fixed cost of IS, which was taken as a weighted average of the costs of the three most common therapies.

The acquisition costs associated with SoC are presented in Table 58. Prednisolone was chosen to represent all OCS used in EGPA, as discussed in Section B.3.2.3, which has its price per pack converted to a cost per mg, to apply to the daily dose of OCS used in the model. It was assumed that the daily dose for each health state was held constant for the duration of a model time horizon. The IS weighted average was comprised of azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and methotrexate. There was not an option to discontinue IS treatment in the model, so IS costs are fixed over time. The distribution for each OCS and IS therapy was informed by CPRD and is presented in Table 58. Costs were derived from the electronic market information tool (eMIT), which provides information about prices for generic drugs and pharmaceutical products in the UK.[104] 

## **Drug administration costs** 

Benralizumab is a self-administered pre-filled pen, therefore no administration-related costs were modelled. Similarly, OCS and relevant IS are administered orally, incurring no administration costs. 

## **B.3.5.2 Health-state unit costs and resource use** 

As detailed in Section B.1.3.1, EGPA is associated with a high-cost burden to the NHS due to the multiple organ systems affected, the lengthy period of time taken to an official diagnosis (reported as 7.1–11.8 years.[38, 40] ) and, therefore, the multidisciplinary approach taken to treatment. This includes visits to HCPs of varied disciplines, as well as hospital visits for disease management and monitoring. Therefore, in the cost-effectiveness model, for each cycle that patients resided in a health state, they incurred the relevant disease management and monitoring costs. Health state costs were input as annual costs and were scaled to 28-day costs to match the cycle length of the model and were inflated to net present values using inflation factors collated from historical versions of PSSRU.[106] 

The frequency of healthcare resource use were derived from CPRD (Table 59), in which a retrospective analysis of HCRU in EGPA based on patient records and stratified by health states was conducted.[2] The study considered patients in the CPRD database with their first EGPA diagnosis code between 1 January 2006 and 28 February 2019, with at least 12 months of prediagnosis registration. 

Unit costs were sourced from NHS reference costs 2021–2022[105] and PSSRU 2023[106] and are presented in Table 60. The frequency of resource use per year was multiplied by the respective unit costs to derive health-state specific HCRU costs per year for the model.

## **B.3.5.3 Adverse reaction unit costs and resource use** 

As explained in Section B.3.3.6, AEs for benralizumab were not modelled. The model captured the costs of morbidities and acute events associated with chronic OCS use. As acute events occurred only in the cycle of incidence, a one-off event cost was applied in the same cycle. Chronic disease health state costs were input as annual costs and were scaled to 28-day costs to match the cycle length of the model. The costs utilised in the model for chronic OCS-related comorbidities are presented in Table 61 and aligns with the approach of Gibson et al. 2024.[102]

## _**Severity**_ 

Hypereosinophilia in patients with EGPA leads to a wide variety of serious disease manifestations, such as asthma, cardiac issues, GI conditions and ENT manifestations, resulting in long-term organ damage and causing significant morbidity and mortality.[18-20] EGPA symptoms, such as neuropathy, pain, fatigue and weight loss and the associated accumulated organ damage negatively impact patient HRQoL in the long-term, leading to mental health impacts, reduced physical activity and impaired ability to work.[22, 23] 

Despite the established severity of EGPA, this submission would not be eligible for the NICE severity modifier based on a QALY shortfall analysis (Table 62).

## _**Base-case results**_ 

## **B.3.9.1 Base-case incremental cost-effectiveness analysis results** 

Table 65: presents the _deterministic_ base case results of the economic evaluation of benralizumab (at PAS price) as an add-on treatment to SoC, versus SoC. Over a lifetime horizon, benralizumab was associated with QALY gains of ***** QALYs per person and incremental costs of £****** per person, yielding an ICER of £25,314 per QALY gained. Benralizumab can therefore be considered a cost-effective treatment option and provides a positive NHB to the NHS at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £30,000/QALY, supporting the use of benralizumab for treating EGPA to improve population health. 

Table 66 presents the _probabilistic_ base case results of the economic evaluation of benralizumab, as an add-on treatment to SoC, versus SoC. Benralizumab was associated with a probabilistic ICER of £26,310 per QALY gained, falling within 4% of the deterministic ICER, indicating that cost-effectiveness results were largely insensitive to joint parameter uncertainty. 

The clinical outcomes and disaggregated base case cost-effectiveness results (by cost category, including health states) and QALYs (by health state) are presented in Appendix J.

## _**Exploring uncertainty**_ 

Parameter uncertainty in the model was assessed via both probabilistic and deterministic sensitivity analyses; the results of which are presented in Sections B.3.10.1 and B.3.10.2, respectively. In addition, key assumptions and alternative sources of input parameters in the model were explored in several probabilistic scenario analyses, the results of which are presented in Section B.3.10.3. Overall, it is considered that all relevant uncertainties included in the analyses have been adequately accounted for and the base case results were found to be robust to uncertainty in the key model inputs and assumptions. 

## **B.3.10.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

A probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was conducted to assess the simultaneous effect of uncertainty in the different model parameters and to demonstrate whether the model results are robust to those variations. A Monte-Carlo simulation with 1,000 iterations was performed where model inputs were randomly sampled from the specified probability distributions. The values of the inputs were determined by random variation with statistical distributions as outlined in Table 63. 

An ICER convergence plot, probabilistic cost-effectiveness plane and cost-effectiveness acceptability curve plot versus SoC are shown in Figure 16, Figure 17 and Figure 18, respectively. The ICER convergence plot demonstrates that 1,000 iterations were sufficient to achieve stability in the ICER. The probabilistic cost-effectiveness plane shows that the probabilistic iteration results are close to each other, and that the deterministic and probabilistic ICERs are similar. The probability that benralizumab was cost-effective versus SoC was predicted as 70.1% at a threshold of £30,000 per QALY (Figure 17), and the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve shows that this probability is >50% above a threshold of ~£26,000 per QALY (Figure 18).

## **B.3.10.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

In order to assess the robustness of the base case cost-effectiveness results and identify drivers of the ICER, DSA was conducted, in which individual inputs (Table 63, Section B.3.8.1) were varied whilst keeping all other model inputs constant. The parameters were varied by their 95% confidence intervals if the standard error was known; all other parameters were varied by +/20%. 

The impact of varying individual inputs on the ICER associated with benralizumab compared to SoC is shown in the form of a tornado diagram (Figure 19). 

The inputs with the greatest impact on cost-effectiveness estimates was the refractory health state utility and the odds of achieving remission, derived from the Bucher ITC. Variation of the

## **B.3.10.3 Scenario analysis** 

Several probabilistic scenario analyses were conducted to assess the impact of the uncertainty associated with key inputs and assumptions in the economic model, as detailed in Table 62. Results of these scenario analyses are presented in Table 67. 

Overall, the results of the scenario analysis were consistent with the results of the probabilistic base case analysis, demonstrating the results to be robust to uncertainties in the model inputs and assumptions. The ICER and NHB were most sensitive to the use of the general population and patient valuations from the vignette study, which resulted in an increase in QALYs. In all scenario analyses, benralizumab remained cost-effective compared to SoC at a willingness-topay threshold of £30,000/QALY.

## _**Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation**_ 

Benralizumab is anticipated to be associated with several benefits not captured in the QALY calculation, hence enhancing its value to the NHS: 

- In the UK, there are currently no reimbursed treatment options indicated for EGPA. Of note, no submission was made to NICE for mepolizumab, an anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody (mAb), meaning there are currently no effective biologic treatments available for all patients with EGPA. Therefore, national commissioning of benralizumab as a treatment for EGPA would result in improved access to effective treatment for all patients with EGPA, in line with the England Rare Diseases Action Plan 2024[140] 

- Further benefits which align with the England Rare Diseases Action Plan 2024 include increased awareness of EGPA for medical practitioners following a NICE recommendation.[140] With time, this could help streamline the care of EGPA patients and improve efficiency by reducing the time to diagnosis and thus improving coordination of care and reduce the use of HCP visits, with EGPA patients likely to see the correct medical practitioner more quickly 

- EGPA causes progressive organ damage, creating significant long-term health consequences for patients. Consequently, patients with EGPA are at a high risk of heart disease, cardiomyopathy, respiratory failure and heart failure, with cardiac involvement associated with higher EOS counts. By depleting eosinophils and inducing sustained remission, benralizumab is expected to prevent further organ damage and reduce the risk of cardiac and respiratory involvement, slowing disease progression. This would increase the HRQoL of patients, as the symptom burden is decreased. This will also result in cost savings for the NHS, as patients will not need to be treated for progressive organ damage. This is evidenced by the stability in the vascular damage index (VDI) in the benralizumab arm during MANDARA.[47, 83] However, in the absence of long-term evidence at the time of the cost-effectiveness analysis, a reduction in disease progression and long-term organ damage with benralizumab versus SoC was not modelled which can be considered a conservative approach 

- Benralizumab induces sustained remission compared with SoC which is expected to allow patients with EGPA to self-administer benralizumab at home. This will result in cost savings to the NHS as well as benefits to patients, which have not been modelled in this costeffectiveness analysis: 

   - The increased convenience of homecare is expected to ease some of the financial burden of living with EGPA for patients, such as saving the time and cost of travel and reducing disruption to employment

## _**Validation**_ 

## **B.3.13.1 Internal validation** 

Internal validation was carried out to assess whether outputs from the model (relapse and remission) were consistent with the data sources used to inform model development (see Appendix J). 

## **B.3.13.2 External validation** 

To validate the economic model used in this submission, extensive feedback was gathered from clinical experts and health economic experts in the UK which was leveraged to finalise the model inputs.[3, 78] Both clinical experts and health economic experts validated the model structure, model inputs and assumptions as being representative of patients with EGPA and of UK clinical practice, as detailed throughout this submission.[3, 78] 

## **B.3.13.3 Validation of Excel model** 

Model verification was carried out to assess the extent to which mathematical calculations were performed correctly and their consistency with the model’s specifications, to ensure that there were no unintentional computational errors. Activities undertaken included: 

- Extreme values analysis, to confirm that the model continues to yield appropriate results. 

- Review of model equations and parameters against their source, to ensure that there are no transcription errors. 

- Review of input derivation and implementation, to ensure that these have been derived and implemented correctly. 

The model was subject to a rigorous review by health economists not involved in model development to ensure the model functioned as intended and generate accurate results which were consistent with input data and robust to extreme analyses. Furthermore, an extreme-value sensitivity analysis was conducted on all applicable model inputs. While conducting the analysis, the validator noted the direction and magnitude of change for each extreme value tested and confirmed that this aligned with the expected result (e.g., if all drug cost inputs are set to 0, the model should output total drug costs of 0 as well). The model validation process uncovered minimal discrepancies and no impactful model calculation errors. Feedback from the validation was addressed in the model.

## _**Summary**_ 

This submission seeks reimbursement for benralizumab as an add-on treatment to SoC, for adult patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA – in line with its full marketing authorisation. 

## **Disease background & unmet need** 

EGPA is a rare, autoimmune condition, affecting a small population of approximately 2,600 people in the UK.[15, 16] EGPA is a hypereosinophilic disorder, characterised by elevated circulating and tissue eosinophils, causing inflammation of small and medium-sized blood vessels, resulting in restricted blood flow and subsequent damage to multiple organs.[17, 18] Company evidence submission for benralizumab with for treating adults with relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ID6266) 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 127 -->

Severe, multi-system manifestations and organ damage have a considerable negative impact on patients’ HRQoL.[18-20] The rarity of the disease, the lack of specialist expertise and symptom overlap with other conditions make diagnosis so challenging that it can take up to 12 years.[38, 40] 

Currently, there are no approved treatments in the UK, with high-dose OCS and IS being used as SoC in clinical practice.[21, 26-28, 30] However, these therapies are sub-optimal. Firstly, both OCS and IS have limited effectiveness as demonstrated by high relapse rates and short times to relapse.[33-35] Secondly, OCS is associated with multiple AEs while IS are toxic. 

## **Clinical evidence** 

The pivotal, Phase III MANDARA trial met its primary endpoint, and demonstrated that treatment with benralizumab was efficacious with regards to durability of remission, low annual relapse rates and reductions or cessation of OCS use.[1] 

MANDARA was a pivotal active-controlled phase III trial offering head-to-head evidence for benralizumab versus mepolizumab – a gold standard in evaluating the effectiveness of treatments.[1] However, given that mepolizumab is not a reimbursed treatment option in the UK, comparative efficacy estimates had to be generated for the relevant comparator for this submission; UK SoC comprising of OCS and IS. In the ITC, benralizumab demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in the proportion of patients in remission and a reduction in annualised relapse rate, compared with SoC. 

## **Cost effectiveness evidence** 

EGPA is a poorly characterised, given limited innovation and research in this space to date. Therefore, there is a scarcity of literature and no prior economic models to help inform the evolution of the disease. In light of this, AstraZeneca has undertaken extensive work to generate robust evidence to help inform decision making for the population of interest in this evaluation. The evidence strategy adopted for this submission was in line with the NICE RWE framework i.e. informing efficacy data from the RCT and informing other inputs using UK-relevant, EGPAspecific RWE. In addition, extensive discussions were conducted with clinical and health economic experts to validate the inputs and assumptions used. Finally, scenario analyses have been conducted to test the impact of these inputs and assumptions.[3, 78] 

The economic evaluation undertaken demonstrated that benralizumab is associated with a deterministic ICER of £25,314 per QALY gained. Benralizumab can therefore be considered a cost-effective treatment option at a threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained. The key drivers of the ICER included quality of life, relative efficacy and health care resource use. Overall, the results of the sensitivity and scenario analyses were consistent with the results of the probabilistic base case analysis, demonstrating the results to be robust to uncertainties in the model inputs and assumptions. 

National commissioning of benralizumab would offer benefits not captured in the QALY by preventing future organ damage and thus, improving patients’ long-term health. In addition, it would offer convenient management of the disease through self-administration minimizing impact of treatment on daily life. Finally, introducing a new treatment option should help to increase awareness of the condition and overall contribute to improved future management, aligned with the ambition set out in the England Rare Diseases Action Plan 2024.[140]

## **Conclusion** 

Providing access to benralizumab would be a paradigm shift in the management of EGPA in the UK, offering patients an efficacious alternative to the current sub-optimal SoC options. Clinical evidence and the economic case demonstrate that benralizumab would address a significant unmet need in this small, underserved patient population and constitute a cost-effective use of NHS resources.

## **Summary of Information for Patients (SIP):** 

## **The pharmaceutical company perspective** 

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from NICE for their treatment to be sold to the NHS for use in England. It is a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation. It is not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to double-check for marketing and promotional content before it is sent to you. 

The **Summary of Information for Patients** template has been adapted for use at NICE from the Health Technology Assessment International – Patient & Citizens Involvement Group (HTAi PCIG). Information about the development is available in an open-access IJTAHC journal article. 

## **SECTION 1: Submission summary** 

**1a) Name of the medicine** (generic and brand name): 

**Generic name** : Benralizumab 

**Brand name** : Fasenra[®] 

**1b) Population this treatment will be used by:** Please outline the main patient population that is being appraised by NICE: 

Benralizumab will be used for adults (aged 18 years or older) who are diagnosed with **relapsing** or **refractory** eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), receiving **oral corticosteroids (OCS)** with or without stable **immunosuppressive therapy (IS).** 

**Please note:** Further explanations for the words and phrases highlighted in **black bold text** are provided in the glossary ( **Section 4b** ). Cross-references to other sections or documents are highlighted in **orange** .

The **marketing authorisation** (licence) for benralizumab is currently pending. More information on this can be found in **Document B, Section B.1.2** . 

Broadly, the marketing authorisation is anticipated to be in line with the population of this submission, which is adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA.

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 



<!-- page 141 -->

## **The main focus of this submission is for benralizumab treating EGPA** 

## **What is EGPA?** 

EGPA, previously known as Churg-Strauss Syndrome, is a rare condition caused by a high number of **eosinophils** (a type of white blood cell).[1] Normally, eosinophils help the **immune system** to fight infections. In EGPA, eosinophil levels are higher than normal. This leads to inflammation in **blood vessels** .[1] This inflammation restricts blood flow to tissues and organs throughout the body, causing a range of symptoms. If not treated correctly, the symptoms of EGPA can worsen over time and cause damage to organs ( **Figure 1** ).[1] 

**Figure 1: How EGPA develops** 

**==> picture [441 x 185] intentionally omitted <==**

## **How many people have EGPA?** 

Given that EGPA is a rare disease, there are limited publications available, but a recent UK-specific study estimated that 46 out of every one million individuals have EGPA in the UK. Therefore, there are approximately 2,600 people in England with EGPA.[2, 3] 

## **What are the symptoms of EGPA?** 

Patients with EGPA can have a variety of symptoms, some of these are shown in **Figure 2** . These symptoms are very diverse and can affect many different parts of the body.[1, 4-8] As EGPA gets more severe, it can lead to heart failure, digestive issues, and weakness in limbs, loss of feeling, tingling or paralysis in areas of the body, resulting in difficulties with walking, standing, lifting and carrying objects.[9-12] 



<!-- page 142 -->

**Figure 2: Common EGPA symptoms** 

**==> picture [440 x 88] intentionally omitted <==**

## **How does EGPA progress?** 

EGPA develops in stages. Firstly, patients with EGPA may develop asthma, fatigue, pain, weight loss and fever. Following this, eosinophils attack organs, causing inflammation and organ damage.[13] 

EGPA is best described by four **disease states** . 

- **Remission** is when the disease is under control. Patients experience no symptoms or mild symptoms. Patients only need relatively small doses of medication to control inflammation.[14] This is the “best” disease state for patients. 

- **Relapse** is the re-appearance of EGPA symptoms that need to be managed by higher doses of medication.[14] Patients in relapse experience more severe symptoms than those in remission.[14-17] 

However, some patients have disease that does not quite fit into the definitions of remission or relapse. Instead, they have what is described as either **non-refractory** or refractory EGPA, which represents a disease spectrum. 

- On the “better end” of the spectrum, there are patients with non-refractory disease. These patients’ disease has not quite achieved remission. Their symptoms are less severe than those in relapse and are reasonably well managed with stable doses of medication.[18] 

- On the “worse end” of the spectrum, there are patients with refractory disease. These patients have not achieved remission in 6 months despite receiving high doses of medication and experiencing moderate to severe symptoms. Therefore, this is the “worst” of all disease states for patients.[14, 16-18] 

The non-refractory and refractory disease states are sometimes grouped into a single ‘ **stable disease** ’ state. 

## **Impact of EGPA on quality of life** 

EGPA significantly affects the **quality of life** of patients. This is because the disease causes a range of debilitating symptoms and organ damage. EGPA symptoms and their impact on quality of life include: 

- Ear, nose and throat issues can disrupt sleep, and research shows that some people with these symptoms may go on to develop anxiety and depression.[19] 

- Nerve problems, such as numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, can make it hard for people to do everyday tasks.[11, 12] 



<!-- page 143 -->

- Coughing, wheezing and difficulty breathing can cause tiredness and affect multiple aspects of life, including work, education, social life and relationships.[20] These symptoms might also cause people to avoid social activities, making them feel isolated.[20] 

- Severe fatigue is also common in patients with EGPA.[21, 22] This can reduce patients’ ability to remain employed and live a “normal” life.[23] 

Patients have expressed the significant toll the disease takes on their mental health due to the severe symptoms of EGPA. EGPA can occur in cycles of remission and relapse; patients experience stress and anxiety as they go through cycles of their disease being controlled followed by periods where the disease is not controlled,[24, 25] with frustration about how the illness impacts their lives.[26] 

According to patients and clinicians, the impact of EGPA on patients’ lives can depend on their disease state ( **Figure 3** ).[14, 27] 

**Figure 3: EGPA disease states** 

**Best quality of life Remission** : patients in remission have mild symptoms or no symptoms.[14, 27] **Non-refractory** : patients with non-refractory disease have mild to moderate symptoms.[18] **Relapse** : patients in relapse have a poor quality of life due to severe symptoms.[14-17] 

**Refractory** : patients with refractory disease have moderate to severe symptoms.[18] Patients with **Worst quality of life** refractory disease experience an amplified negative impact on mental health due to feelings of frustration, hopelessness and despair resulting from them experiencing a lack of improvement over a prolonged period of time.[22] 

EGPA can also have a financial impact on individuals, as the disease can affect a person’s ability to work, which can result in a loss of income. Patients may also face other financial challenges, including the cost of travelling to medical appointments. 

## **Mortality** 

EGPA can reduce a patient’s life expectancy.[28, 29] Research shows that patients with EGPA are 2.3 times more likely to die in any time period, compared with the general public.[30] The risk of death can also vary by EGPA disease state: patients in relapse tend to have a shorter life expectancy than those in remission.[31] 



<!-- page 144 -->

## **Impact on families and carers of people with EGPA** 

Carers of patients with EGPA also experience an impact on their lives, for example: 

- There is a financial impact because carers may need to take frequent time off from work to accompany patients to medical appointments and to care for patients.[32, 33] 

- There is a social impact because caring for someone with EGPA leaves carers with less time to work and socialise with others. This can lead to feelings of isolation and loneliness.[32] 

- Also, there is a psychological impact with carers experiencing negative impacts on their mental health as they worry about the future of their loved one.[32] Social isolation can also have a psychological impact on carers.[32] 

Abbreviations: EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; UK: United Kingdom 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

## **How is EGPA diagnosed?** 

EGPA can be difficult to diagnose. This is because of its rarity and its broad range of symptoms, which can be similar to symptoms from other diseases.[15] Patients often see multiple different medical practitioners for different symptoms before finally being diagnosed.[15] This means patients have to wait up to 12 years between experiencing symptoms and getting a diagnosis.[4] 

When patients present with symptoms, they will undergo a series of tests, including:[34] 

- Blood tests – to check the levels of eosinophils in the blood 

- Chest X-ray – to check for lung damage 

- Lung function – to check for asthma 

- **Biopsy** – to check for tissue damage 

- **Bronchoscopic lavage** – to check the levels of eosinophils in the lungs 

- Heart test – to check for heart damage 

These tests help doctors reach a definitive diagnosis. 

Abbreviations: EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis 

## **2c) Current treatment options** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

• What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines. It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. Please also consider: 



<!-- page 145 -->

- if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 

- are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

## **How is EGPA currently treated in the UK?** 

## **Standard of care (oral corticosteroids + immunosuppressants)** 

The goal of EGPA treatment is to reduce eosinophil levels to help suppress the immune system and control inflammation. This would allow patients with EGPA to experience remission.[14] 

There are currently no treatments approved for EGPA available on the National Health Service (NHS). The current **standard of care** for EGPA is oral corticosteroids (OCS) with or without immunosuppressants (IS). For the rest of this document, standard of care refers to OCS with or without IS. OCS are sometimes simply referred to as “steroids”. **Figure 4** shows which patients this submission is relevant to. 

**Figure 4: Treatments available for EGPA, relevant to this submission** 

**==> picture [438 x 171] intentionally omitted <==**

OCS can reduce inflammation and may help some patients achieve remission.[14-17] It has been found that OCS were prescribed in the vast majority of patients with EGPA in England.[35] Sometimes, OCS need to be combined with IS to help patients achieve remission.[14] IS do not target eosinophils but are powerful at suppressing the immune system. The most commonly prescribed IS are called azathioprine, methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil.[16, 35] 

However, the current standard of care options are limited and sub-optimal. Patients often need to take high doses of OCS to reduce the high levels of eosinophils associated with EGPA.[35] However, high daily OCS doses can cause important **side effects** for patients.[1] OCS can cause weight gain, heart conditions, depression, diabetes and **osteoporosis** .[1, ] 36, 37 IS are also associated with a high risk of organ toxicity and side effects, including **cytopenia** , **hepatotoxicity** , and major infections.[14-17, 36, 37] 



<!-- page 146 -->

In addition, OCS and IS treatments are associated with high relapse rates and are not effective in maintaining remission. Up to 82% of patients, receiving OCS with or without IS, who achieve remission will experience relapse and its associated symptoms within less than one year on average.[37-39] High relapse rates from OCS and IS have a two-fold implication. Firstly, relapsed disease is treated with increased doses of OCS and IS, which further increases the risk of OCS-related and IS-related side effects.[1, 36, 37 ] Secondly, the cycles of their disease being controlled followed by periods where the disease is not controlled cause patients to feel low, scared, frustrated and anxious, amplifying negative feelings about future outcomes.[22] 

There is an unmet need for a well **tolerated** treatment which can help patients achieve and maintain remission. This will allow patients to reduce OCS doses, hence avoiding the significant side effects associated with its use. 

## **Cyclophosphamide** 

Cyclophosphamide is mainly used in patients with life-threatening or organ-threatening EGPA (referred to as ‘severe EGPA’).[14-17] Cyclophosphamide is toxic to organs and can cause infertility,[40, 41] hence why doctors prefer to limit its use to patients with severe EGPA. This submission does not cover patients with life-threatening or organ-threatening – EGPA, as shown in **Figure 4** therefore, cyclophosphamide is a not relevant alternative to benralizumab. 

## **Rituximab** 

Rituximab is sometimes used in patients with life-threatening or organ-threatening EGPA, who are not included in this submission.[14, 16, 17] Additionally, doctors have confirmed that rituximab is not routinely used in the UK.[18] Therefore, rituximab is not a relevant alternative to benralizumab. 

Abbreviations: EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; IS: immunosuppressants; NHS: National Health Service; OCS: oral corticosteroids; UK: United Kingdom

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

Context: 

• Patient-based evidence (PBE) is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about patient needs and disease experiences. Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

## **EGPA from the patient perspective** 

As discussed in **Section 2a** , EGPA can have a negative impact on patients’ quality of life. The symptoms of EGPA can make it difficult to carry out daily activities, socialise, exercise and work.[20] Each disease state impacts quality of life for patients to a different extent as shown in **Figure 3** . Patients with refractory disease tend to have the worst quality of life while patients in remission tend to have the best quality of life. Also, patients with EGPA cycle through different disease states which impact their mental wellbeing, resulting in stress and anxiety. 

AstraZeneca conducted in-depth interviews with patients and doctors to gain a better understanding of what it is like to live with EGPA. Based on patient interviews, there were some particular challenges they were facing: 

## **Fatigue** 

Patients expressed that fatigue impacted their ability to exercise and perform routine tasks:[42] 

“I experienced fatigue and EGPA impacted my ability to exercise” “Showering on a daily basis was exhausting” “I couldn’t walk upstairs” 

## **Impact on mental health** 

Patients also expressed the impact of EGPA on their mental health.[42] Patients discussed feeling isolated, living in fear of potential relapse and worsening symptoms.[42] These negative feelings have a large impact on the mental and physical health of patients with EGPA. These feelings are more intense in patients with refractory EGPA, whose disease is not being controlled. Some patients noted:[42] 

“It is an anxiety inducing condition” “I was in a bad mental health space” “I feel detached from others” 



<!-- page 148 -->

## **Impact on social life** 

A study identified the impact of EGPA on social life, with a patient expressing:[43] 

“I’ve withdrawn from people and seldom go out (…), preferring to talk by text, email and chat. I can’t concentrate on work. I feel distant from my husband. I’ve found it very difficult to talk to friends, they don’t quite understand” 

## **Coping with treatment** 

Furthermore, patients have shown concern over the long-term use of OCS and the side effects they cause:[42, 43] 

“I have been reduced it (sic) steroid tablets but am concerned about all the side effects from the medications. I have started to get joint [pain] and particularly in the knees and elbow. I am taking several medications to combat steroid side effects.” “[I] worry about the side effects of my treatments, particularly the steroids” “[the] biggest challenge becomes the drugs and not the condition itself” “I’m keen to get off steroids” 

Patients have expressed a need for a successful treatment which reduces EGPA symptoms in the same way as OCS but without their harmful side effects:[42] 

“Having something that is new, has a greater positive impact on my condition and is less harmful would be amazing” 

Abbreviations: EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; OCS: oral corticosteroids; PBE: patient based evidence

## **About benralizumab and how it works** 

As mentioned above, EGPA is caused by a high number of eosinophils. The way benralizumab works is shown in **Figure 5** . Benralizumab is a **monoclonal antibody** that specifically attaches to eosinophils. Once attached, it attracts another type of white blood cells which kill the eosinophils.[44-46] This reduces the levels of eosinophils in the body, which is the goal of EGPA treatment. As a result, inflammation is reduced.[9] 

**Figure 5: How benralizumab works**

Benralizumab is expected to be used alongside standard of care (OCS with or without IS) for patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA.[18] 

Benralizumab is currently approved in the UK for the treatment of severe asthma.[47]

## **How is benralizumab taken for EGPA?** 

Benralizumab is taken as an injection (FASENRA Pen®).[49] Benralizumab is injected under the skin ( **subcutaneously** ). This can be administered by a healthcare provider. Over time, once patients reach remission, benralizumab can be administered by patients themselves or caregivers at home, after receiving training.[49] 

## **How much medicine do patients take and when?** 

It is expected that patients with EGPA will take 30 milligrams (mg), a single injection of the FASENRA Pen[®] , of benralizumab every 4 weeks.[48] 

Abbreviations: EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; mg: milligram

## **Studies of benralizumab in EGPA** 

The primary **clinical trial** assessing benralizumab for the treatment of EGPA is the MANDARA trial.[50] A summary of the key information for MANDARA is provided in **Table 1.** 

The MANDARA trial was a **Phase 3 trial** . This means the trial assessed how well benralizumab worked to treat EGPA (its **efficacy** ) and how safe the medicine was, compared to another treatment called mepolizumab. Mepolizumab is another monoclonal antibody that can be used to treat EGPA, but it is not available in the UK.[51]

|**Number of patients included**|140|



**Figure 6** shows how the trial was carried out. The trial consisted of two main periods. Patients were randomly assigned to take either benralizumab or mepolizumab for one year (this is called the **double-blind** period where participants and researchers do not know what treatment each participant is receiving). After that year, patients could continue taking benralizumab for another year (this is called the **open-label** period where both the participants and researchers know which treatment is being given to each participant).[50]

## **Comparison of benralizumab to standard of care** 

The MANDARA trial did not compare benralizumab to UK standard of care (OCS with or without IS). To compare benralizumab versus standard of care, an **indirect treatment comparison** (ITC) was required. An ITC is a way to compare the effects of different treatments that were not included in the same study. MANDARA compared benralizumab to mepolizumab. Another trial called MIRRA compared mepolizumab to standard of care. Therefore, mathematically combining the results of the MANDARA and MIRRA trials produced a comparison of benralizumab to standard of care. 

Results of the ITC showed that benralizumab was better than standard of care in helping patients achieve remission and avoid relapse. 

Abbreviations: EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; ITC: indirect treatment comparison; OCS: oral corticosteroids

## **Impact of benralizumab on quality of life** 

Throughout MANDARA, patients were asked to answer questions about their quality of life **,** using various questionnaires. Patients receiving benralizumab showed similar improvements in quality of life between the start and end of the trial compared with people receiving mepolizumab.[50] Two other real world studies (known as the **Adelphi diseasespecific programme [DSP]** and a UK-specific **vignette study** ) confirmed that remission and non-refractory disease are associated with a better quality of life than refractory disease or relapse.[22, 53] Therefore benralizumab treatment, which helps patients achieve remission, could be expected to improve their quality of life.

## **Side effects of benralizumab** 

Every medicine has the potential to result in side effects **,** and the same medicine can produce different reactions in different people. In MANDARA, benralizumab was well tolerated.[50]

The trial was conducted between 2019 and 2023, during which time the COVID-19 pandemic took place. This likely contributed to the high number of COVID-19 events.
