## **3i) Value and economic considerations** 

Introduction for patients: 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

Healthcare administrators need to get the best value from their limited budgets. To do this, they want to know whether a new medicine provides ‘good value for money’ compared to existing medicines. They will look at the costs of the new medicine and how the health of patients is likely to improve if they take it. The pharmaceutical company that develops the medicines provides this information to healthcare administrators using a **health economic model** . The pharmaceutical company uses the health economic model to perform an analysis, which compares the costs and benefits of the new treatment (benralizumab) with standard of care (OCS with or without IS). This analysis is conducted in the relevant patient population (adults diagnosed with relapsing or refractory EGPA, receiving OCS with or without stable IS). This analysis helps determine if benralizumab used to treat EGPA would be a good use of NHS resources. 



<!-- page 157 -->

## **How the model reflects EGPA** 

The economic model was designed to reflect the natural evolution of EGPA and clinical practice in the UK. The model focused on the comparison on benralizumab versus standard of care (OCS with or without IS) in patients with EGPA. 

The model included the following disease states: remission, stable disease, relapse and death. These disease states were selected to mirror the experience of patients with EGPA over their lifetime. 

In the model, all patients began in a ‘stable disease’ state (comprised of refractory and non-refractory patients). The stable disease state mirrored patients who entered the MANDARA trial (as described in **Section 3d** ). Each month, patients could move between 

disease states or stay in their current disease state. This reflected whether they entered remission, experienced a relapse or remained in stable disease. The movement of patients from relapse and stable disease to the remission state indicated a successful outcome in the model. 

Disease states were associated with different healthcare resource use costs and quality of life. 

## **Modelling the effectiveness of benralizumab** 

The results of the MANDARA trial and the indirect treatment comparison informed how patients moved between the disease states in the economic model. The rates of remission and relapse from the MANDARA trial informed the chances that patients receiving benralizumab would remain in their disease state or move to a different disease state. Results from the ITC, discussed in **Section 3e** , informed the same movements for patients receiving standard of care. 

The ITC results showed that patients receiving benralizumab were more likely to enter remission and less likely to experience a relapse, compared with standard of care. This was reflected in the model with patients in the benralizumab arm being more likely to remain in the remission state and less likely to enter the relapse state, compared to standard of care. 

Prescription data from real world patients with EGPA in England informed the OCS doses received. Patients in remission received the lowest OCS dose and patients in relapse received the highest. As benralizumab was associated with greater remission rates (and lower relapse rates) than standard of care, benralizumab was indirectly associated with lower OCS doses in the model. The negative impact and costs of the side effects associated with OCS treatment on health were also considered in the model. Therefore, the costs and negative impact on quality of life associated with OCS-related side effects were overall lower for patients receiving benralizumab compared with standard of care. 

## **Modelling how much benralizumab improves clinical outcomes** 

To accurately reflect possible disease progression, patients could die at any point in the model, due to EGPA or any other cause. The effect of benralizumab on survival was not directly modelled. Instead, each disease state was associated with a different risk of death. The remission state was associated with the lowest risk of death while the relapse state was associated with the highest risk of death. Benralizumab was associated with a higher chance of remaining in the remission state and less chance of relapse, compared 



<!-- page 158 -->

to standard of care. Therefore, the risk of death was overall lower for patients receiving benralizumab compared with standard of care. 

## **Modelling how much benralizumab improves quality of life** 

The quality of life data used in the model were from an Adelphi disease-specific programme study. In the Adelphi DSP, patients with EGPA completed questionaries about their experience with the disease and their quality of life. The response to the questionnaires was then used to assign a numerical value on quality of life, which was different for each EGPA disease state. 

The results showed that patients with refractory disease tend to have the worst quality of life while patients in remission tend to have the best quality of life.[53] This reflected the fact that the symptom burden, mental and emotional impact of EGPA would likely be reduced when a patient experienced remission. 

Therefore, an improvement in quality of life was modelled when a patient experienced remission. As treatment with benralizumab is associated with a higher chance of experiencing remission, patients experience an overall better quality of life. 

## **Modelling how the costs of treatment differ with benralizumab** 

Benralizumab was more expensive than standard of care (OCS with or without IS) when costs over a patient’s lifetime were considered. However, benralizumab offered increased survival and quality of life for patients with EGPA. 

Various NHS costs were included in the model. These costs included: 

- The cost of benralizumab 

- The cost of OCS and IS 

- The cost of monitoring patients with EGPA (e.g. GP or hospital visits) 

- The cost of treating side effects of OCS treatment, such as diabetes, heart conditions and osteoporosis 

Benralizumab may result in cost savings for the NHS compared to OCS and IS for patients with EGPA. This is because patients receiving benralizumab were more likely to be in remission compared to patients receiving standard of care. Costs in the remission state were less compared to other disease states for these reasons: 

- Reduced requirement for medical visits (e.g. GP consultations or hospitalisation) 

- Lower OCS dose required so reduced costs associated with treating and managing OCS side effects 

## **Uncertainty** 

Due to the rarity of EGPA and hence limited literature, new UK-specific real-world evidence was generated to inform this submission. These data were validated by EGPA clinical experts.[18] 

As is the case for any economic model, there were various assumptions that were made in the analysis. Information on these assumptions can be found in **Document B, Section B.3.8.2** . All assumptions were sense-checked by EGPA clinical experts. A variation of model inputs was tested, and the results of these tests are explained in **Document B,** 



<!-- page 159 -->

**Section B.3.10.** Overall, the cost-effectiveness results did not change significantly when alternative inputs were used, which means that the results were robust. 

## **Benefits of benralizumab not captured in the economic analysis** 

Treatment with benralizumab may have many different positive impacts for patients with EGPA and for the NHS. By preventing relapses and allowing durable remission,[39] benralizumab may save important resources in hospitals, such as the time of nurses, pharmacists and doctors. The model aimed to capture as many of these benefits as possible, but there were other benefits that could not be fully captured. For example: 

- The approval of benralizumab is expected to increase awareness of EGPA among healthcare professionals. With time, this could help reduce the time to diagnosis and improve the quality of care for patients with EGPA 

- As benralizumab can be self-administered at home, patients can benefit from reduced costs from less frequent travel to healthcare facilities and not having to take time off work 

- Benralizumab is expected to prevent further organ damage and reduce disease progression. This was not modelled because of limited long-term evidence 

## **Conclusions** 

This section provides an overview of the modelling performed by AstraZeneca. However, AstraZeneca’s estimation of cost-effectiveness is not the only result considered by NICE. NICE may prefer some assumptions which are different from the assumptions that the company used in their model. 

Given this, AstraZeneca has not presented any specific cost-effectiveness results in this summary, but it should be noted that the final cost-effectiveness results for this submission will be discussed in the Committee meeting and will be available on the NICE website once a final decision is made.

## **Benralizumab is a new and innovative treatment, and would represent an important advancement in the treatment of EGPA** 

EGPA is a rare, inflammatory condition.[1] It causes a range of symptoms and can lead to organ damage.[1] EGPA also has a substantial negative impact on the quality of life of patients.[22-24] There are currently no treatments for EGPA available on the NHS. The current standard of care for EGPA are OCS and IS, however these do not control the disease adequately and are associated with severe side effects.[1, 14-17, 36-38] 

Benralizumab would represent the first treatment approved for EGPA in the UK. Benralizumab has a unique and targeted mechanism of action, focusing on reducing eosinophil levels.[39] This would represent an advancement in the treatment of EGPA. 

Benralizumab treatment would offer patients durable remission, while allowing them to reduce or stop OCS use,[39] which may help to reduce new OCS-related side effects. Benralizumab would also provide patients with the opportunity to experience reduced symptoms and it may prevent further organ damage.[39] This could reduce the negative impact that EGPA has on patients’ lives. 

Abbreviations: EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; IS: immunosuppressants; NHS: National Health Service; OCS: oral corticosteroids; UK: United Kingdom 

## **3k) Equalities** 

Are there any potential equality issues that should be taken into account when considering this condition and this treatment? Please explain if you think any groups of people with this condition are particularly disadvantaged. 

Equality legislation includes people of a particular age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation or people with any other shared characteristics 

More information on how NICE deals with equalities issues can be found in the NICE equality scheme Find more general information about the Equality Act and equalities issues here 

Some patients with EGPA have severe eosinophilic asthma. Patients with severe eosinophilic asthma are eligible for treatment with benralizumab. This poses an equality consideration for the following reasons: 

- Not all patients with EGPA have severe eosinophilic asthma[5, 55, 56] 

- Patients with EGPA and severe eosinophilic asthma would only receive benralizumab if they met the eligibility criteria for its recommendation within severe eosinophilic asthma 

- Access to severe asthma centres in England (where benralizumab is prescribed for severe asthma) is challenging 

- If patients with EGPA and severe eosinophilic asthma access benralizumab, the dosing schedule prescribed will be for severe eosinophilic asthma, which is less frequent than the dosing schedule for EGPA. This less frequent asthma dosing has not formally been tested in EGPA. More frequent dosing is considered necessary for EGPA because it is a more severe disease than asthma, and eosinophil levels are often higher. 



<!-- page 161 -->

Therefore, AstraZeneca firmly believes that benralizumab should be made available for **all** eligible patients with EGPA, at the dose that was investigated and proved to be effective.

## **Section A: Clarification on effectiveness data** 

## **A1. Literature searches** 

Please cite any search filters used in the clinical effectiveness searches, reported in 

## Appendix D of the company submission (CS).[1] 

The search terms to identify randomised clinical trials (RCTs) were based on the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy for identifying randomised trials.[2] Observational studies were identified using a filter developed by the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN).[3] 

Broad disease area search terms were designed by an information specialist to include a range of terms that may be used to accurately describe eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), whilst ensuring sensitivity and specificity of the search strategy and minimising the risk of missing relevant publications. The disease area search terms were similar to those used in a published systematic review of EGPA.[4] Search terms relating to relevant concepts were identified through discussion within the research team, scanning background literature and browsing database thesauri. Searches were scoped in Ovid Embase (the most comprehensive database).

## **between the refractory and relapse states.** 

## **Re-cap of key context** 

## _**Disease states in EGPA**_ 

EGPA is best described by four disease states outlined below (see Figure 1): 

- **Remission** (A) is when the disease is under control. Patients experience no symptoms or mild symptoms. Patients only need relatively small doses of oral corticosteroid (OCS) to control inflammation. This is the “best” disease state for patients. 

- **Relapse** (B) is an episode of significantly worsening symptoms requiring an escalation in treatment (increase in OCS dose) or hospitalisation. Patients in relapse experience more severe symptoms than those in remission. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 173 -->

- **Non-refractory** (C) is when patients’ disease has not achieved remission, but their symptoms are less severe than those in relapse and are reasonably well managed with stable doses of OCS; their condition remains mostly unchanged and may even improve slowly. 

- **Refractory** (D) is when patients have not achieved remission in six months despite receiving high doses of OCS and experiencing moderate to severe symptoms. This is the “worst” of all disease states for patients, because although symptom burden can be lower than in a relapse, this state lasts for a minimum of six months and, therefore, the negative impact on mental health and overall quality of life (QoL) is larger. 

## _**Defining disease states in EGPA**_ 

EGPA is a poorly characterised rare disease, given the limited innovation and research in this space to date, resulting in a scarcity of literature to help inform the evolution of the disease. Consequently, extensive work was undertaken by AstraZeneca to deepen the understanding of the disease in support of this submission. This included systematic literature reviews, an advisory board with patients and extensive consultation with clinical experts.[7-10] A separate workstream was also undertaken which included consultation with patients with EGPA through eight in-depth interviews and with clinical experts through four in-depth interviews, as part of defining the health state descriptions for the purpose of conducting a UK-specific vignette study.[11] 

All the gathered insights helped understand that, collectively, EGPA is best described by the four disease states outlined above, with patients broadly experiencing a relapsing and remitting disease course characterised by the occurrence of clinical signs and symptoms and different OCS doses required to control the disease. The definitions were validated during interviews with clinical experts.[9] A visual depiction of the disease states is outlined in Figure 1.

**How can refractory disease (referred to by NICE as “not under control”) be considered “stable”?** 

In EGPA, the term “not under control” in the refractory state reflects that a patient has not achieved remission (defined as Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score [BVAS] = 0 and OCS dose ≤4 mg/day). This state is classified as “stable” as the patient has persistent disease activity and is, therefore, experiencing symptoms, but the clinical status of the patient has not significantly deteriorated to the point of requiring significant interventions (e.g. hospitalisation).

**Difference between refractory disease (referred to by NICE as “not under control”) and a relapse (referred to by NICE as “flare up”)** 

In summary, the distinction between these two states is outlined below: 

- Refractory disease indicates a failure to achieve remission at any time in the prior six months, but with no significant exacerbation or worsening of symptoms. Importantly, this state lasts for a minimum of six months and therefore the negative impact on overall QoL is larger. 

- Relapse reflects an episode of significantly worsening symptoms requiring an escalation of treatment or hospitalisation. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 176 -->

## **b) In the CS Doc B (table 6) 25.7% of patients in the benralizumab arm had both refractory and relapsing disease at baseline.[5] Please explain how patients can be in both disease states.** 

An inclusion criterion of MANDARA was for patients to have a history of refractory OR relapsing disease. Per the MANDARA inclusion criteria, 

- Refractory disease was defined as failure to attain remission (defined as BVAS=0 and oral corticosteroid [OCS] dose ≤7.5 mg/day of prednisolone or equivalent), following standard induction regimen for at least 3 months and within 6 months prior to screening, or recurrence of symptoms upon OCS tapering at any dose of ≥7.5 mg/day prednisolone or equivalent 

- Relapsing disease was defined as at least 1 confirmed EGPA relapse within last 2 years and >12 weeks prior to screening. 

In line with these definitions, it was possible for patients to have both refractory and relapsing disease at baseline (Figure 2). 

There is an important distinction between relapsing disease and a relapse. Patients were not included in MANDARA if they were experiencing a relapse at baseline. The health state being referred to in the economic model is a “relapse”. The definition of a relapse in the economic model is provided above in Figure 1.

## **Classification of patients** 

In order to derive mutually exclusive health states for the economic model, the classification of patients in the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) analysis was performed in a twostage approach. Details are provided below and illustrated in Figure 3. 

## _**Step 1**_ 

- The primary clinical outcome (including a classification of disease state) was described in the incident cohort at the index date and during the follow-up period at every 6-month timepoint for 2 years (6, 12, 18, 24 months), with a 6-month look-back period at each timepoint, and then annually for years 3–5 (36, 48 and 60 months) with a 12-month look-back period at each timepoint. 

- At each measurement, patients were categorised into one of three mutually exclusive disease states (remission, relapse, or stable disease) considering the previous observation period and assigned that disease state to the whole follow up period until the next timepoint. 

The definitions used for each disease state is presented in Table 1.

## **Classification of patients** 

In order to derive transition probabilities for the economic model from MANDARA (comprehensive overview of the approach outlined in Appendix 1), a 2-stage process was adopted; firstly, patients were categorised in the 3 mutually exclusive states: remission, relapse and stable disease, followed by further stratification of the stable disease state into non-refractory and refractory states. Definitions are provided in Table 3 and Table 4. 

**Table 3: MANDARA disease state definitions used to derive transitions for the economic model** 

|**Disease state**|**Definition in MANDARA**|
|---|---|
|Remission|•<br>BVAS=0; AND<br>•<br>OCS dose ≤4 mg/day|
|Relapse|•<br>Active vasculitis (BVAS >0); OR<br>•<br>Active asthma symptoms and/or signs with a corresponding worsening in<br>ACQ-6 score; OR<br>•<br>Active nasal and/or sinus disease, with a corresponding worsening in at least<br>one of the sino-nasal symptom questions;<br>warranting any of the following:<br>•<br>An increased dose of OCS therapy to >4 mg/day; OR<br>•<br>An increased dose or addition of IS therapy; OR<br>•<br>Hospitalisation related to EGPA worsening|
|Stable disease|Not in Remission and not in Relapse|



**Abbreviations:** ACQ-6: asthma control questionnaire 6; BVAS: Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score; EGPA: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis 

**Table 4: MANDARA stratified stable disease state definitions** 

|**Disease state**|**Definition in MANDARA**|
|---|---|
|Refractory|Failure to achieve Remission (defined as BVAS=0 and OCS dose ≤4 mg/day) for the<br>preceding 6 months|
|Non-refractory|In stable disease (i.e. not in Remission and not in Relapse) and not Refractory<br>•<br>Stable OCS dose; OR<br>•<br>Tapered OCS dose related to EGPA|



**Footnote:** Please note this stratification is performed within the stable disease state. Given data limitations, it was not possible to implement the refractory and non-refractory health states as individual health states. Therefore, these were modelled as sub-states within a ‘stable disease’ health state. The costeffectiveness model included mutually exclusive alive disease states of remission, stable disease, and relapse.

## **A8. OCS dosage** 

**Priority question: Please detail how (a) ‘maintenance doses’ of OCS and b)** 

**‘courses’ of OCS vary by disease state (remission, relapsed, refractory, nonrefractory) in the MANDARA trial. Please disaggregate this information by the disease states and patient characteristics (such as asthma severity).** 

## **‘Maintenance doses’ of OCS vs ‘courses’ of OCS** 

Overall OCS doses from MANDARA have been analysed by disease state as an aggregate based on prescription data. The data lack granularity to disaggregate the OCS dose into ‘maintenance doses’ and ‘courses’ of OCS, as the prescriptions did not distinguish whether the OCS doses are for ‘maintenance’ or acute treatment. However, the ‘courses’ of OCS were included in the aggregate OCS dose by disease state. Consistent with that, relapse was associated with a higher daily OCS dose because those patients are expected to be prescribed additional OCS courses when treatment escalation is required. 

The OCS-sparing treatment goal applies to total exposure, i.e. maintenance OCS and OCS ‘courses’. Additionally, OCS-related AEs occur based on cumulative dose (regardless of whether the OCS was used as a maintenance or a ‘course’). It is, therefore, appropriate to consider a reduction in the overall OCS use.

## **A9. Patients with severe disease excluded from MANDARA** 

The NICE scope details the population as ‘adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA, receiving OCS with or without stable IS therapy’.[19] In the MANDARA trial, the inclusion criteria excludes patients which have previously had rituximab within 6 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 188 -->

months prior to screening, oral cyclophosphamide within 2 weeks prior to baseline, intravenous cyclophosphamide within 3 weeks prior to baseline and recent or ongoing organ-threatening or life-threatening EGPA.[20] Please explain the rationale for excluding patients with recent severe disease (especially when the disease course may be very heterogenous). 

MANDARA was designed to be a head-to-head, non-inferiority study to mepolizumab. At the time of planning, mepolizumab was anticipated to be the standard of care for when benralizumab would be entering clinical practice and evaluated by HTA bodies. 

Consequently, the study population of MANDARA was aligned as closely as possible to MIRRA. As per the inclusion criteria of the MIRRA study, patients with organ threatening or lifethreatening EGPA (i.e. severe EGPA) within 3 months prior to screening and through randomisation were also excluded from the MANDARA study. 

## **A10. Immunogenicity** 

During the clinical expert interviews (Data on File 3),[9] it was agreed that the **** *** **** **** **** treatment effect of benralizumab . The EAG noted that 9% of the MANDARA safety population presented with anti-drug antibodies in response to benralizumab, one of which was neutralising.[13] Is there an increased risk of immunogenicity, and potential for a reduction in efficacy in patients in the long-term (i.e., >1 year) receiving the higher dose (Q4W) of benralizumab than those receiving the lower dose (Q8W), and if so, has this been taken into account (particularly for patients that have been exposed to biologics before)? The EAG are aware this data may not yet be available for this population, but please provide any supporting information from the severe asthma population. 

## **Risk of immunogenicity/potential for reduction in efficacy, based on dose frequency** 

Data exploring the potential risk of immunogenicity with the higher dose (every 4 weeks [Q4W]) of benralizumab in an EGPA population is not available. However, data in a severe asthma population are available; the results and conclusions from the BORA study[21] (NCT02258542; phase 3 extension study evaluating the safety and efficacy of benralizumab in patients with severe eosinophilic asthma) are outlined below: 

- ADA responses were generally similar between patients in the every 8 weeks (Q8W) and the every 4 weeks (Q4W) group.[22] 

- Benralizumab serum concentrations in ADA-positive patients remained stable during BORA, and ADA-positive patients exhibited near complete depletion of EOS over time. 

In summary, based on BORA, there was no evidence that different dose regimens (Q8W vs Q4W) impacted ADA incidence or that ADA-positive status had an effect on safety, efficacy, or exposure of benralizumab over time. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 189 -->

In addition, based on a recent systematic literature review (SLR) and meta-analysis of asthma biologics exploring the incidence of ADAs and their impact on reported clinical outcomes showed that the incidence of neutralising antibodies was higher in the Q8W arm (8.17%) vs every Q4W (5.81%).[23] The SLR also highlighted that only 2.9% of individuals in the included studies developed ADAs over the study follow-up period and that longer dosing intervals were associated with higher ADA development.[23] 

## **Risk of immunogenicity/potential for reduction in efficacy, based on prior exposure to biologics** 

During the MANDARA OLE, ADA levels were assessed in patients randomised to receive mepolizumab in the DB period with the hypothesis of understanding the ADA rate in patients who switched treatment from mepolizumab to benralizumab. No meaningful differences in ADA rates was observed in this population indicating that prior exposure to a previous biologic treatment does not result in elevated immunogenicity risk and greater incidence and prevalence of ADAs.[24] 

Based on all the evidence outlined above, the risk of immunogenicity or subsequent potential for reduction in efficacy of benralizumab does not increase with a higher frequency dose or prior exposure to biologics. Consequently, this was not reflected in the economic model.

During the OLE, patients switching from mepolizumab to benralizumab took their first dose of benralizumab at Week 52. The subsequent steep reduction in blood EOS count as well as reduction in OCS usage at Week 56 is owing to the switching of interventions and their different mechanisms of action and resulting EOS depletion. Further detail is provided below. 

## **Impact of benralizumab, compared to mepolizumab, on blood EOS count and OCS usage** 

## _**Blood EOS count**_ 

Benralizumab uniquely binds to IL-5rα, blocking all pathways to eosinophil activation resulting in rapid and near complete depletion of sputum and blood eosinophils.[27] Mepolizumab, however, selectively targets the activity of the IL-5 cytokine, without affecting the remaining cytokine network involved in eosinophil activation; as such, mepolizumab induces a reduction in sputum 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 191 -->

and blood eosinophils to a lesser extent than benralizumab. This is further supported by the MEX study which shows that treatment with mepolizumab in severe refractory eosinophilic asthma resulted in continued exacerbations, suggesting it was less effective at EOS depletion.[28] Importantly, benralizumab achieves this near-depletion of blood EOS as rapidly as within a week, as demonstrated by the % change difference in eosinophils detailed in Table 13 and illustrated in Figure 6.

## **Section B: Clarification on cost-effectiveness data** 

## **B1. Model transitions to the relapse state** 

**Priority question: Figure 12, page 77 of the CS Doc B,[5] indicates that in the economic model for benralizumab it is possible for patients to transition to the relapse state from the remission state or the stable state. Figure 13, page 78 of the CS Doc B,[5] indicates that in the economic model for SoC there are 2 arrows going from relapse to stable and no arrows going the other way.** 

**a) For SoC, please confirm if there is an error in the diagram regarding the arrow directions, and which evidence source informs transitions from stable to relapse and from relapse to stable.** 

Yes, there is an error in the diagram. An updated version has been provided in Figure 7. 

**Figure 7: Model structure parameterisation by treatment arm – SoC arm (update of Figure 13 from company submission Document B)** 

**==> picture [455 x 239] intentionally omitted <==**

**Abbreviations:** CPRD: Clinical Practice Research Datalink; ITC: indirect treatment comparison; SMR: standardised mortality ratio; SoC: standard of care 

A comprehensive overview of the approach adopted to inform transition probabilities in the economic model, by treatment arm, is provided in Appendix 1. This question focuses on specific transitions in the SoC arm – so the relevant information is provided below. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 199 -->

The transition from stable disease to relapse in the SoC arm was informed by a stepwise approach, outlined below: 

- The transition probability from stable disease to relapse was first derived for the benralizumab arm from MANDARA. 

- As outlined in response to question B.4 (a), with no evidence to inform transition probabilities for SoC, the benralizumab arm informed the baseline risk transition probabilities and the outcomes of the ITC were applied to the benralizumab arm to generate the transition probabilities for the SoC arm. 

- To inform the specific transition from stable disease to relapse in the SoC arm, the rate ratio (RR) of the annualised relapse rate from the ITC was applied to the transition probability from the benralizumab arm. 

The ITC informed transitions to remission (odds of remission endpoint) and transitions to relapse (annualised relapse rate endpoint) – however, no data were available to inform transitions to stable disease. In light of this, the transition from relapse to stable disease was assumed equivalent to that in the benralizumab arm. 

## **b) Please clarify the possible changes in the disease that may explain a transition from the stable state to the relapse state.** 

Patients residing in the stable disease health state will transition to the relapse state due to any of the reasons listed as part of the definition of relapse (see Figure 1): 

- An increase in BVAS to a score >0 due to active vasculitis 

- Active asthma symptoms and/or signs with a corresponding worsening in ACQ-6 score 

- Active nasal and/or sinus disease, with a corresponding worsening in at least one of the sinonasal symptom questions; 

warranting any of the following: 

- An increased dose of OCS therapy to >4 mg/day; OR 

- An increased dose or addition of IS therapy; OR 

- Hospitalisation related to EGPA worsening. 

## **c) In the annualised relapse rate ITC analysis, did the number of relapses** 

## **include both cases of patients previously in the stable state and in the remission state?** 

Yes, the number of relapses included both patients previously in the stable state as well as patients in the remission state.

## **B4. Constant baseline risk probabilities during lifetime?** 

**Priority question: The SoC remission/stable/relapse transition probabilities were derived from the benralizumab transition probabilities and, in most cases, using the Bucher ITC estimates. Since the benralizumab transition probabilities are assumed to be constant over time after 52 weeks, the implication is that the SoC transition probabilities are constant over time as well. Clarification A10 concerns the issue of no waning of effectiveness of benralizumab. This question concerns the baseline risk transition probabilities. The baseline risk transition probabilities in this submission are those of benralizumab.** 

## **a) Are the baseline risk transition probabilities in this submission those of benralizumab because there is no evidence to inform transition probabilities for SoC?** 

Yes, with no evidence to inform transition probabilities for SoC, the benralizumab arm informed the baseline risk transition probabilities and the outcomes of the ITC were applied to the benralizumab arm to generate the transition probabilities for the SoC arm. Further context is provided below. 

The MANDARA trial provided a comparison of the efficacy of benralizumab vs mepolizumab, however, mepolizumab is not a relevant comparator for this evaluation as it is not a reimbursed treatment option in the UK. As per the decision problem, the relevant comparator is SoC in UK clinical practice, consisting of OCS with or without IS. Given the lack of head-to-head trial informing the relative efficacy of benralizumab vs SoC in patients with EGPA, an ITC was conducted to generate comparative efficacy estimates. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 205 -->

SoC in MIRRA, consisted of OCS with or without IS, which was reflective of UK clinical practice. Therefore, use of data from the SoC arm of MIRRA produced an indirect comparison of benralizumab vs SoC that was generalisable to UK clinical practice. 

A comprehensive overview of the approach adopted to inform transition probabilities in the economic model, by treatment arm, is provided in Appendix 1. 

## **b) On page 87 of the CS Doc B it refers to the percentage of patients in refractory being constant over 5 years.[5] Was this the sole justification for constant SoC transition probabilities over time, or were there other justifications?** 

The CPRD study provided evidence that the proportion of patients with refractory disease did not change over 5 years. Therefore, the assumption of the proportion of patients with refractory disease being constant over 5 years is based on these empirical data, representative of UK patients. This assumption was validated during interviews with clinical experts.[9] 

Importantly, the proportion of refractory patients being constant over time is not linked to transition probabilities for SoC. A comprehensive overview of the approach adopted to inform transition probabilities in the economic model, by treatment arm, is provided in Appendix 1.

## **B8. CPRD analysis** 

- a) Please provide a summary of the statistical methods used to evaluate whether 

or not the percentages of treatment use and whether the percentage refractory varied over time. 

No formal longitudinal analysis was conducted as part of the CPRD study. The results were descriptive analyses, with the distribution of health states described at index, and then at regular intervals during follow-up (e.g. every 6 months for 2 years, annually for years 3–5). 

Based on Occam's razor, in the absence of evidence that the proportion of patients with refractory disease varies over time, it is appropriate to conclude that it does not. 

b) Please explain how the 486 people with EGPA included in the CPRD analysis were identified in order to ensure it was representative of the population in England. 

The 486 patients included were all identified incident cases in the study period 1/1/2006 to 28/2/2019 from CPRD Aurum, which is representative of the English population.[9, 37] Given the study included all available incident cases within a representative database, it can be concluded that the sample of patients with EGPA is representative of the population of patients with EGPA in England. 

The full inclusion criteria are provided below: 

## **All EGPA patients** 

## _**Inclusion criteria**_ 

- At least one EGPA diagnosis code identified through GP visits (CPRD Aurum) or inpatient admissions (HES APC) during 1 January 2006 to 28 February 2019. Patients with an EGPA diagnosis record before this period are included as long as they have at least one EGPA diagnosis record during 1 January 2006 to 28 February 2019. 

- An acceptable patient’s data-quality flag. 

- Eligible for linkage to the Hospital Episode Statistics inpatient, outpatient and accidents and emergencies records and the ONS death data from the UK. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 212 -->

- Contributing at least one day in the CPRD database after index date. 

## _**Exclusion criteria**_ 

Patients with any of the following diagnosis first occurring after most recent EGPA diagnosis record will be excluded: 

- Wegener's granulomatosis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA); or 

- Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA); or 

- Polyarteritis nodosa; or 

- Takayasu arteritis; or 

- Giant cell arteritis. 

## **Incident EGPA patients** 

The incident EGPA cohort is a subset of the All EGPA patient population with the following additional exclusion criteria applied: 

- At least 12 months look-back period before and inclusive of the index date. 

- Patients with an EGPA diagnosis record prior to 1 January 2006 in CPRD Aurum or HES APC databases are excluded from the incident cohort. To avoid overestimation of incident diagnoses, individuals must have at least 12 months of available data prior to the index date to be included in the calculation of incidence rates. 

Details of the EGPA code are provided as Data on File.[38] 

## c) Please describe how the mg/day dose estimates for the SoC treatments were calculated. 

The approach adopted is described below: 

Drug therapy variables were created from records with valid information. Medication was only recorded in primary care (CPRD Aurum), not in the hospital database (HES), so all drug information was captured solely from CPRD Aurum, specifically in the table Drug Issues. Medications were identified using code lists from the relevant CPRD Aurum prodcode mapped to the Dictionary of Medicines and Devices (dm+d) codes. Prescription records in CPRD Aurum which have a quantity of zero or negative and duration of zero recorded were excluded from any analysis. Missing or invalid values in other variables describing the prescription such as dosage, quantity unit identifier, or cost, were allowed. 

A prescription of EGPA medication was defined using relevant product codes in the patient therapy record. The following definitions were applied: 

- Treatment discontinuation: the most prescribed duration of each substance in the incident cohort was 28 days. Treatment discontinuation was defined as 60 days with no prescriptions of each substance. 

- Prescription estimated duration: First, the time between one prescription and the next was calculated. For time between prescriptions below the treatment discontinuation gap for each substance the time between prescriptions was assumed to be the real duration. For those 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 213 -->

prescriptions with a time gap between prescriptions greater than the treatment discontinuation gap: 

      - if the duration was available, it was used for the determination. 

      - if the duration of the prescription was missing or equal to zero, the median duration, for similar prescriptions with the same strength and quantity, was estimated and imputed. 

      - in case of insufficient data to estimate the median (all duration equals to zero or only one prescription for a specific strength and quantity) a fixed value of 28 days was imputed (most frequently duration prescribed). 

- Dosage: The daily dose was calculated as the product of quantity and substance strength, divided by the prescription estimated duration. In case of two prescriptions in the same day, the substance strength was added, and average quantity and prescription estimated duration was used for the calculation. 

- Medication exposure episode: exposure episode was defined as the time from index date to treatment discontinuation date. 

   - d) Please explain what, if any, steps were taken in the CPRD resource use analysis for remission/stable/relapse states to avoid capturing resource use associated with OCS adverse events which have been costed separately. 

The health-state specific resource use, informed by the CPRD analysis, were “all-cause resource use related to an EGPA diagnosis”. This was deemed the most appropriate and robust data source to inform HCRU in the company submission (CS), because the reported frequency was too low for robust analyses, and resource use for outpatient visits, emergency department (ED) visits and critical care visits were unavailable in the alternative data input “EGPA-related HCRU” (as shown in Table 27). Nonetheless, a sensitivity analysis was run using the EGPA-related HCRU, with a minimal impact on the cost-effectiveness results; the deterministic ICER increased to £28,146 (previously £25,314).

## **B9. EGPA manifestations** 

- a) Please list the 2-4 EGPA manifestations other than asthma/respiratory/ENT 

that are the most severe for patients. 

Considering the multi-system impact of EGPA, patients experience a broad range of immediate manifestations; commonly reported symptoms are outlined in Figure 16 below. 

**Figure 16: The organ systems impacted by EGPA** 

**==> picture [440 x 151] intentionally omitted <==**

**Abbreviations:** ENT: ear-nose-throat; GI: gastrointestinal; OCS: oral corticosteroid **Source:** Adapted from Trivoli G, _et al_ . Rheumatology 2020;[39] Cottin V, _et al_ . European Respiratory Journal;[40] Doubelt I, _et al_ . ACR Open Rheumatology[41] 

“Severe” manifestations can be interpreted as either impacting the daily life of EGPA patients e.g. neuropathy manifestations leading to mobility challenges or increasing their mortality longterm e.g. cardiac manifestations. Some manifestations other than asthma/respiratory and ENT are listed below: 

- Cardiac (cardiac myopathy, pericarditis, myocarditis)[7] 

- Renal (active glomerulonephritis, hypertension, proteinuria, haematuria, progressive glomerulonephritis, and kidney failure)[42] 

- Gastro-intestinal (GI) involvement (severe GI tract involvement, GI bleeding, abdominal pain and colitis)[39] 

- Neuropathy[43, 44] 

   - b) Are the manifestations in (a) related to established stages of disease for 

EGPA? 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 215 -->

EGPA is described as having three phases: the prodromal (allergic), eosinophilic, and vasculitic phases.[45] 

- The prodromal phase is characterised by adult-onset eosinophilic asthma. 

- In the eosinophilic phase, clinical symptoms are due to eosinophilic organ infiltrates that typically affect the lungs, GI tract, and heart. 

- The vasculitic phase is mediated by eosinophilic infiltration, eosinophilic vasculitis, and extravascular eosinophilic granulomas, which can cause damage to the nervous system, skin, and kidneys, although every organ may be affected. 

Recent understanding is that these phases may overlap, may not appear sequentially, or may not occur in every patient.[39] Even within each phase, clinical presentation and quality of life will vary substantially dependent upon the level of disease control. The most severe manifestations of EGPA, listed in the response to question B.9 (a), are related to the second “eosinophilic” phase and final “vasculitic” phase of EGPA. Cardiac and GI manifestations occur in the eosinophilic phase. Renal manifestations and neuropathy commonly occur in the vasculitic phase. 

## c) Do the manifestations in (a) have an effect on the HRQoL of patients 

## independently of the chronic and acute adverse events associated with OCS treatment? 

Yes, all the manifestations impact a patient’s quality of life independently from the QoL shortcomings associated with OCS treatment. 

OCS treatments are associated with acute and chronic AEs, including type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, pneumonia, cataracts, and sleep apnoea, amongst other conditions. These adverse events differ from the symptoms associated with EGPA manifestations which impact a patient’s HRQoL. 

As discussed in the submission section B.1.3.2, the manifestations of EGPA create long term health consequences that reduce a patients HRQoL.[46] The response to question B.9 (d) details the HRQoL impact of the manifestations stated in B.9 (a). The HRQoL impact of the manifestations of EGPA were captured in the cost effectiveness model within the health state utilities, separate to the HRQoL impacts of OCS-related AEs. 

## d) Please provide HRQoL evidence for the manifestations. 

Patients with cardiac manifestations can experience symptoms including shortness of breath, chest pain and irregular heartbeat, with further disease progression resulting in heart failure, heart attack and thrombosis. This can lead to impairment in social functioning, mental health, perceptions of general health, sleep, and vitality as well as leading to anxiety and depression.[47] Further HRQoL issues as a result of cardiac manifestations are inability to exercise, fear of recurrent issues, interruption of daily activities, absenteeism and impaired ability to do housework.[48] 

Patients with renal manifestations can experience symptoms like fatigue, tiredness, loss of appetite and nausea. This can impact the ability of people with EGPA to socialise, with the fatigue preventing patients holding down a steady job.[49] Patients with kidney failure, a severe 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 216 -->

renal manifestation, may require dialysis which can be time consuming and inconvenient because they are required to regularly travel to a hospital to receive the treatment.[50, 51] 

Patients with GI manifestations experience nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea which can lead to psychosocial impacts such as impaired quality of life, comorbid psychiatric disorders, chronic life stress and impaired coping. GI manifestations affect daily performance and productivity in a patient’s working life and can lead to a greater extent of short periods of sick leave.[52] 

Patients with neuropathy may have weakness in limbs, loss of feeling, tingling or paralysis in areas of the body. This can result in difficulties with walking, standing, lifting and carrying objects, impacting an individual’s ability to carry out daily activities and work.[53, 54] 

## e) Please provide evidence on the time to development of the manifestations listed in (a) from EGPA diagnosis. 

There is limited literature to inform this response; therefore, clinical experts have been consulted.[16] The development of manifestations is not time dependent. A patient could have been diagnosed with EGPA very recently and present with cardiac, renal, or GI manifestations. Conversely, a patient could have had EGPA for a significant period but never experienced these manifestations. 

## **B10. IS treatment adverse events** 

## a) What, if any, severe adverse events are associated with IS treatment? 

IS treatment is associated with a high risk of organ toxicity and side effects including, but not limited to, cytopenia, hepatotoxicity, and major infections such as bacterial pneumonias herpes zoster recurrences, opportunistic infections and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia.[55-58] 

## b) Is there overlap in the SAEs associated with IS treatment and OCS treatment? 

OCS and IS have different mechanisms of action, so there is no overlap in the serious adverse events associated with OCS and IS treatment. 

- OCS are anti-inflammatory treatments and directly target EOS. They are associated with acute and chronic AEs, including T2DM, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, pneumonia, cataracts and sleep apnoea.[46] 

• IS suppress the immune system without specifically targeting hypereosinophilia in EGPA.[55-58] Adverse events associated with OCS are broader and do not occur as a consequence of immune system suppression, whereas adverse events associated with IS treatment are caused by immune system suppression only. AEs caused by IS use are outlined in response B.10 (a). 

## c) How significant is the impact on HRQoL of the IS treatment adverse events? 

IS contribute to the HRQoL burden experienced by patients with EGPA. The side effects of IS have a negative impact on quality of life, adding to the physical and mental burden for patients and requiring more frequent healthcare visits. Patients who develop cytopenia following IS 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 217 -->

treatment may experience symptoms of fatigue, weakness, dizziness and poor concentration.[59] This can reduce their HRQoL and impair their ability to work. 

## d) Please provide any evidence on the time to development of SAEs associated with IS treatment. 

There is limited literature to inform this response; therefore, clinical experts have been consulted.[16] AEs such as infections and hepatotoxicity generally appear quickly after IS treatment (e.g. 3 months) whereas cytopenia is a late complication which can appear after longterm IS treatment (e.g. 3 years). 

## **B11. Modelling responders for benralizumab after 1 year** 

- a) In the economic model, it appears that patients who initially respond at 52 

   - weeks, defined by the remission state at 52 weeks, who subsequently 

   - transition to a stable or relapse state continue to receive benralizumab. 

Please explain the rationale for this assumption. 

AstraZeneca thank the EAG for bringing this to our attention. The model has now been updated, such that all patients who respond at 52 weeks (defined as BVAS=0 and OCS dose ≤4mg/day) continue to receive benralizumab, and all patients in the stable or relapse states discontinue benralizumab and receive standard of care (SoC). This revision had a minimal impact on the results; the deterministic ICER increased to £26,092 (previously £25,314). A revised version of this model has also been submitted alongside responses. 

- b) In the economic model, no matter the state of patients at 52 weeks, roughly **% of patients receiving benralizumab are assumed to be responders and therefore in week 56 the percentages of patients in each of the 

   - remission/stable/relapse states are calculated as the sum product of the 

   - transition probabilities and the state percentages multiplied by **%. Please comment on why the predicted percentage of patients in the model at 52 weeks did not match the **%. 

It was assumed that the clinical response assessment would take place at the end of Week 52; therefore, patients would move to the responder health state at the next modelled cycle, i.e. Week 56. This is why approximately **% of patients receiving benralizumab appear to be responders at Week 56 instead in the company submission model. In real life, time is continuous, and patients would therefore discontinue the next day post-assessment; however, for the purpose of the economic model, the cycle length is a discrete period of time (4 weeks). Therefore, patients discontinue at the start of Week 56. Of note, this approach has limited impact on the results as the half-cycle correction would further adjust for this – see Figure 17.

## **B13. Risk of OCS-related adverse events** 

The risk of OCS-related adverse events is modelled as a non-linear relationship to the cumulative OCS dose. The method used assumes that the OCS dose is 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 219 -->

cumulative. Please explain the clinical basis for the risk of adverse events being related to cumulative OCS dose over all years, rather than, say, the last few years; e.g. why is it not possible that if someone is in remission for a few years, their risk of OCS adverse events does not fall? 

Evidence from literature suggests that that the risk of OCS-related AEs is correlated with cumulative OCS exposure over all years. 

Further detail is provided below: 

- Data linking the incidence of AEs and cumulative OCS exposure are well cited within the literature with recent evidence demonstrating that as little as 0.5–1.0 g (equivalent to 2–4 lifetime courses) of cumulative exposure to OCS is associated with adverse outcomes.[46, 60] 

- Each year of exposure to any OCS prescription results in a higher subsequent likelihood of AEs. Each prior year (at any point before the current year) of exposure to 1 to 3 prescriptions resulted in 1.07 times the odds of having a new AE in the current year whilst exposure to ≥4 prescriptions in any prior year resulted in an odds ratio of 1.20.[61] 

- Even intermittent OCS use is associated with adverse outcomes; the events increase with increasing dose. Compared with non-OCS patients, the risk of experiencing any adverse outcomes was elevated for one-off OCS and increased with increasing frequent pattern of intermittent OCS prescribing.[60] 

- Whist there are a paucity of data on the timing between OCS exposure and risk of AEs, it should be considered that the damage from most of the OCS-related chronic events and AEs as part of the OCS sub-model are irreversible, i.e. the co-morbid condition will not disappear or resolve itself upon a reduction/cessation of OCS (e.g. cataracts, cardiovascular disease, renal impairment etc.) 

- In addition, there may be long-term cellular changes that occur with long-term OCS use. Genome wide association studies in COPD have identified that OCS use is associated with epigenetic modifications, namely methylation of CpG dinucleotides.[62] It was found that CpG sites annotated to processes associated with clinically relevant side effects of OCS, such as hyperglycaemia/insulin resistance, weight gain, and osteoporosis were plausibly associated. This suggests that OCS have permanent effects on the genome, causing epigenetic modifications which could increase in frequency with cumulative OCS exposure, hence contributing to the risk of adverse events and the inability for these events to be stopped or reversed following discontinuation of OCS.

## **Appendix 1** 

This appendix presents a comprehensive overview of the approach adopted to inform transition probabilities in the economic model, by treatment arm. 

Throughout this document, specific information pertaining to the below has been provided in response to some questions. The relevant questions are noted within the below explanations. 

## **Benralizumab arm** 

## _**Prior to the response assessment (Week 0 to Week 52)**_ 

- Transition probabilities in the benralizumab arm of the model were derived from all patients in the benralizumab arm of MANDARA up until the time of response assessment (Week 52). 

## _**Following the response assessment (Week 52 onwards)**_ 

- Patients who were identified as being responsive to benralizumab (defined as BVAS=0 and an OCS dose ≤4 mg/day) at Week 52 continued treatment; transition probabilities for responders were then informed only by the subgroup of responders in the benralizumab arm of MANDARA. 

- It was assumed that responders’ transition probabilities remained constant throughout the remainder of the lifetime horizon of the model. This assumption was consistent with the assumption of no treatment waning effect in the evaluation of benralizumab for severe eosinophilic asthma (TA565).[18] 

The dataset from MANDARA and model syntax used to estimate transition probabilities in the benralizumab arm are provided in response to question B5. 

## **SoC arm (Week 0 onwards)** 

- In the absence of head-to-head clinical trials assessing the efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC in patients with EGPA, an ITC was conducted. 

- The outcomes of the ITC were applied to the transition probabilities derived from all patients in the benralizumab arm of MANDARA to generate the transition probabilities for the SoC arm, as outlined in the response to question B.4 (a). The approach adopted and assumptions underpinning specific transition probabilities in the SoC arm (from stable disease to relapse and from relapse to stable disease) are outlined in the response to question B.1 (a). 

- No response assessment was conducted for the SoC arm, in line with UK clinical practice. All patients who discontinued benralizumab at Week 52 received SoC and were subject to SoC transition probabilities. 

- In the absence of evidence to suggest that transition probabilities change over time, transition probabilities for the SoC arm remained constant over the time horizon. 

Figure 18 and Figure 7 [presented in the response to question B.1 (a)] illustrate key data inputs used to parameterise the model structure for the benralizumab arm and the SoC arm.

## **Living with the condition** 

|**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|EGPA vasculitis is the rarest of the ANCA associated vasculitides and patients not only have asthma but also<br>sinus and nose symptoms and may have a number of other symptoms including: rashes, nerve damage<br>including pins and needles or numbness, bowel trouble and blood loss, anaemia, heart problems, muscle and<br>joint pain and fatigue.<br>A young adult patient told us:_EGPA is hard to live with, not just in terms of asthma but in the effect of quality of_<br>_life when you are flaring and fatigue is something I find incapacitating, as well as the associated troubles like_<br>_multiple chest infections._<br>Nerve and joint pain plus the respiratory issues caused by the asthma are factors that reduce mobility, and the<br>risk of chest infections that increase with treatment increase isolation as patients shield to avoid getting<br>infections.<br>As EGPA is chronic, patients have to live with their illness and the damage caused by it prior treating it as well as<br>damage caused by the treatment for ever. As flare ups and relapses are not uncommon, the burden of the illness<br>is high.<br>From a carer:_Our life has changed since the diagnosis. The side effects of the treatment were not easy to deal_<br>_with – cyclo and steroids are horrific. My husband was given a new treatment as he had three severe_<br>_exacerbations of asthma in a year, but although it was better he couldn’t taper his steroids. Now waiting for him_<br>_to have more than 4 exacerbations to be eligible for other treatment. What a life to live for him and for us._<br>_Wishing him to become more ill to get treatment to get better so our life together will get better. I am ashamed to_<br>_admit it, but yes this is our reality._|
|---|---|

## **Current treatment of the condition in the NHS** 

|**7. What do patients or**<br>**carers think of current**<br>**treatments and care**<br>**available on the NHS?**|Corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate are the most common treatments our members have<br>reported getting for their EGPA, then some get mepolizumab or benralizumab through asthma clinics.<br>Patients believe that the available treatment is not always as effective as targeted therapy and have commented<br>on the change in their lives with change of medication. Most concerns are about the long-term side effects from<br>the treatment, but many have reported side effects of steroids. They have also reported that even though they<br>get immunosuppressant as steroid sparing medication, they don’t manage to get on very low dosage or<br>successfully stop steroids.<br>_‘’_ _I was manic most of the time and found it difficult to focus. Work became very challenging and home life was_<br>_tough on my wife having to deal with my mania, grouchiness caused by lack of sleep and I was ravenous all the_<br>_time. ‘’_|
|---|---|
|**8. Is there an unmet need**<br>**for patients with this**<br>**condition?**|Yes, there is. EGPA is rare but it can be severe, and the impact of the illness is high on the patient’s life.<br>Targeted therapy is needed and early intervention before severe damage is done is a must to improve outcomes<br>and get patients in remission fast.|

## **Advantages of the technology** 

|**9. What do patients or**<br>**carers think are the**<br>**advantages of the**<br>**technology?**|In general the  EGPA patients who are on benralizumab through asthma clinics have only positive comments<br>about it. It controls their EGPA and their asthma, they have less chest infections and they can taper their steroids<br>successfully. They refer to it as life changing. Better quality of life, less hospital appointments, they can live a more<br>normal life going to work etc.<br>_Nothing is more powerful than patients talking from their heart so here are some quotes:_<br>_‘’Benralizumab has been life changing for me, having multiple asthma attacks previously and needing high dose_<br>_steroids for over a year to control the inflammation, I am now off steroids completely and my severe asthma due to_<br>_egpa is really well managed with Benralizumab. It has meant I don't require stronger treatment such as_<br>_cyclophosphamide.’’_<br>‘_’Benralizumab has meant less chest infections, less asthma attacks and less mobility as I can go out and not be_<br>_as worried about the cold air or petrol fumes/pollution affecting normal breathing.’’_<br>_‘’_ _I feel really grateful that benralizumab is now an option for egpa patients, especially as my first flare started at 24_<br>_in what they think was the second stage of egpa and my first egpa asthma attack aged 25, a drug like_<br>_cyclophosphamide would have much more long term detrimental effects, in comparison.’’_<br>_‘’Since Benralizumab my day to day is pretty normal..I still tire but am able to function at work and at home. In fact_<br>_I almost forget about my condition at times but obviously reminded by the daily drugs.’’_<br>_‘’Benra has been life changing for me. I can’t say better than that. I am able to lead a normal life. Work and home_<br>_life is better. My asthma is under control. I doubt that I would be able to work if I had to rely on pred.’’_|
|---|---|

## **Other issues** 

|**13. Are there any other**<br>**issues that you would like**<br>**the committee to consider?**|EGPA is rare, EGPA can be severe, EGPA is chronic.<br>At the moment to be treated with benralizumab you have to be lucky to be looked after by a hospital that can<br>prescribe it through their respiratory clinic. It is a postcode lottery that creates an inequality of care to these<br>patients. Not all EGPA patients are looked after in asthma clinics, and some get there after being treated<br>unsuccessfully for their EGPA.<br>_‘’_ _I then started at the asthma clinic..’’_(6 months after diagnosis and not responding in two<br>immunosuppressants plus steroids – now on benralizumab)<br>_‘’ I moved to Liverpool just before my flare, which was very lucky, as I found after it's one of the few specialist_<br>_centres to prescribe benralizumab in the country. My own local hospital, for instance, does not use it as far as I_<br>_am aware. I was just very lucky to be living at the right place at the right time, for the right treatment.’’_|
|---|---|

## **What is the expected place of the technology in current practice?** 

|**9. How is the condition**<br>**currently treated in the**<br>**NHS?**|Patients may present to ENT, chest medicine, rheumatology, clinical immunology, neurology, cardiology. The<br>diagnosis is usually delayed because of the different ways in which the condition can present. After the inevitable<br>delay in diagnosis, there is a wide heterogeneity in the ways that different units treat this condition. Some<br>clinicians only use corticosteroids, while some use less powerful immunosuppressive agents like methotrexate or<br>mycophenolate mofetil.<br>The international recommendations are to treat with intravenous cyclophosphamide and yet this may be a<br>problem because not all units may have access to infusion suites. For patients with relapsing disease, (almost<br>every single patient will relapse eventually), the choice is with Rituximab. The evidence base is not great for this<br>drug, and neither is the confidence in the academic community. Especially, for ANCA negative EGPA, this is not<br>thought to be a great option. This means overuse and abuse of corticosteroids, with the inevitable side effects of<br>corticosteroid therapy.<br>Remission maintenance is typically with Methotrexate or Azathioprine. Relapse on one of these maintenance<br>agents would require increases in steroid dosing as well as considering repeat rounds of remission induction.<br>Currently IL5 inhibition is not available in the UK specifically for EGPA (NICE TA845), but it is sometimes<br>accessed for patients who also meet the criteria for severe eosinophilic asthma (NICE TA671), where a choice<br>from Mepolizumab, Benralizumab or Reslizumab is available.|
|---|---|

BSR and BHPR<br>guideline for the management of adults with ANCA-associated vasculitis. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2014<br>Dec;53(12):2306-9.<br>2. Hellmich B, Sanchez-Alamo B, Schirmer JH, Berti A, Blockmans D, Cid MC, Holle JU, Hollinger N,<br>Karadag O, Kronbichler A, Little MA, Luqmani RA, Mahr A, Merkel PA, Mohammad AJ, Monti S,<br>Mukhtyar CB, Musial J, Price-Kuehne F, Segelmark M, Teng YKO, Terrier B, Tomasson G, Vaglio A,<br>Vassilopoulos D, Verhoeven P, Jayne D. ## **Sources of evidence** 

|**Sources of evidence**||
|---|---|
|**18. Do the clinical trials**<br>**on the technology reflect**<br>**current UK clinical**<br>**practice?**|The only study of note is the MANDARA trial(Wechsler et al. NEJM 2024;390:911-21), a head-to-head study of<br>Benralizumab and Mepolizumab. This was a non-inferiority study. The primary endpoint was remission at 36 and<br>48 weeks (defined as a BVAS of 0 on glucocorticoids ≤ 4mg per day). Benralizumab was found to be non-inferior,<br>but not superior to Mepolizumab. The improvements seen were modest. This appears to have been a problem<br>with study design, rather than drug effectiveness. Entry criteria allowed for patients to already have a remission<br>BVAS score of 0, which applied to 49% and 47 % of the Benralizumab and Mepolizumab groups respectively at<br>baseline. This improved to 59% and 56% respectively at 48 weeks. The minimum dose of steroids for entry to the<br>study was 7.5 mg per day, regardless of the reason for administration. It is therefore possible that patients were<br>taking steroids for reasons other than EGPA, which would skew the data. This also meant the mean steroid dose<br>was only reduced by 8.04 mg by the end of the study (11.02 +/- 5.25 mg at baseline, versus 2.98 +/- 3.76 mg at<br>week 48).<br>In real clinical practice, patients being considered for this drug will have active disease (BVAS >0) and are likely to<br>be on steroid doses more than 7.5 mg per day to acutely control relapse.|
|**18a. If not, how could the**<br>**results be extrapolated to**<br>**the UK setting?**|The potential gains for appropriately selected patients are likely to be greater than seen in the MANDARA study<br>due to the problems with study design, as mentioned above (Item 18).|
|**18b. What, in your view,**<br>**are the most important**<br>**outcomes, and were they**<br>**measured in the trials?**|Yes – even for patients entering the trial already in remission (BVAS = 0), maintaining this whilst achieving<br>clinically meaningful steroid dose reduction is important to prevent long term cumulative glucocorticoid toxicity.|

|**6. What is the main aim**<br>**of treatment? (For**<br>**example, to stop**<br>**progression, to improve**<br>**mobility, to cure the**<br>**condition, or prevent**<br>**progression or**<br>**disability.)**|To induce and maintain disease remission, with the aim of<br>•<br>Reducing symptom burden<br>•<br>Improving quality of life<br>•<br>Preventing accrual of disease-related chronic organ damage (in particular, cardiomyopathy, airway<br>remodelling, chronic kidney disease, neuropathy)<br>•<br>Whilst minimising treatment-related side effects and damage|

|**7. What do you consider**<br>**a clinically significant**<br>**treatment response?**<br>**(For example, a**<br>**reduction in tumour size**<br>**by x cm, or a reduction**<br>**in disease activity by a**<br>**certain amount.)**|More time spent in remission and prevention of disease flares.<br>Reduced glucocorticoid usage and related toxicity.<br>Reduced emergency and unplanned care.|
|**8. In your view, is there**<br>**an unmet need for**<br>**patients and healthcare**<br>**professionals in this**<br>**condition?**|Yes.<br>There are no licensed therapies for EGPA available in the UK (except for patients who quality for biologic<br>therapy via severe asthma pathways). There is scant evidence for the efficacy of alternative (unlicensed)<br>therapies that are commonly used in conjunction with glucocorticoids in UK practice, such as conventional<br>synthetic DMARDS (mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), azathioprine and methotrexate) and rituximab.**Proven,**<br>**effective therapies are needed.**<br>We recognise that glucocorticoid dependency is very common in EGPA, and that this is associated with<br>significant toxicity including mood and sleep disturbance, cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders including<br>diabetes, osteoporosis, cataract formation etc.**Alternative treatments that can reduce glucocorticoid use**<br>**and toxicity are a priority in this patient group.**<br>Unrelated to therapy, unmet needs include diagnostic delay, and access to expert and unified multidisciplinary<br>care.|

## **What is the expected place of the technology in current practice?** 

|**9. How is the condition**<br>**currently treated in the**<br>**NHS?**|In the UK, EGPA (once diagnosed) is exclusively managed in secondary care; often but not always in specialist<br>respiratory or vasculitis (rheumatology/renal) services.<br>First-line treatment is with glucocorticoids. In patients with relapsing or steroid-dependent disease, conventional<br>DMARDS (e.g. MMF, azathioprine, methotrexate) are often used in attempt to lower glucocorticoid burden and to<br>reduce relapse risk, though there are very limited controlled data for their efficacy to support this approach. In<br>patients with severe disease manifestations, remission-induction treatment with cyclophosphamide and/or<br>rituximab (using protocols established in RCT for other forms of systemic vasculitis) are often used, though<br>patients with EGPA were not specifically included in many of these studies. None of these therapies are licenced<br>in EGPA.<br>More recently, patients with severe asthma as a manifestation of EGPA may receive anti-IL5 therapy (e.g<br>mepolizumab, benralizumab) or other biologics (e.g. tezepelumab) via existing commissioned routes in specialist<br>severe asthma services.|
|---|---|
|**9a. Are any clinical**<br>**guidelines used in the**<br>**treatment of the condition,**<br>**and if so, which?**|Evidenced-based consensus recommendations for treatment of EGPA include:<br>American College of Rheumatology:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34235894/<br>European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36927642/<br>European EGPA Study Group:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37161084/<br>The British Society of Rheumatology will soon publish an updated management guideline (to be endorsed by the<br>UK Kidney Association) for patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis including EGPA (expected Q1 2025)<br>**Importantly, all these guidelines recommend anti-IL5 therapies in the treatment of EGPA.**|
|**9b. Is the pathway of care**<br>**well defined? Does it vary**<br>**or are there differences of**<br>**opinion between**<br>**professionals across the**<br>**NHS? (Please state if your**<br>**experience is from outside**<br>**England.)**|The pathway of care is poorly defined in many regions.<br>Diagnostic delay is common – owing to disease rarity, heterogenous presentation, spectrum of differential<br>diagnoses and failure to recognise.<br>Patients may initially present to primary care or acutely to emergency services. They may then be referred to a<br>variety of secondary services (including respiratory medicine, rheumatology, nephrology, neurology, ENT<br>surgery) depending on clinical phenotype and local expertise / service set up.<br>Long-term follow up may continue with any of these specialities and is commonly lead by rheumatologists and<br>renal physicians with experience in managing other forms of vasculitis (such as GPA & MPA). We know that<br>access to specialist centres and MDT care is associated with better outcomes (e.g<br>https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38782514/) but that such services are not well developed in all regions, and that|

||many patients are managed in general renal/rheumatology services. The upcoming BSR/UKKA management<br>recommendations for AAV including EGPA highlight the importance of specialist MDT care and will recommend<br>that all patients have access to this.|
|---|---|
|**9c. What impact would the**<br>**technology have on the**<br>**current pathway of care?**|We propose that access to benralizumab for EGPA should be under guidance the of established MDTs for<br>vasculitis and related diseases, usually within renal and rheumatology departments. These existing MDTs<br>include multi-speciality clinical expertise, with pharmacy and specialist nursing support, and have experience in<br>the management of patients with other forms of vasculitis requiring commissioned therapies (e.g. avacopan in<br>AAV, tocilizumab in GCA). The introduction of benralizumab is therefore likely to improve the care pathway, as<br>patients will have MDT referral for both diagnostic review and consideration of treatment eligibility, thus<br>improving equity of access for patients and patient outcomes.<br>We anticipate that approval of a new class of treatment may raise awareness of disease and possibly reduce<br>diagnostic delays.|
|**10. Will the technology be**<br>**used (or is it already used)**<br>**in the same way as current**<br>**care in NHS clinical**<br>**practice?**|Patients with severe asthma as a manifestation of EGPA may already receive benralizumab via existing<br>commissioned routes in specialist asthma services. Patients with asthma who do not meet severity criteria for<br>biologic therapy, even if severe non-asthma manifestations of EGPA are present (e.g., cardiomyopathy,<br>neuropathy, kidney disease etc) do not currently have access to this evidence-based treatment.<br>Beyond severe asthma pathways, the therapy is not in currently in use for treatment of EGPA in the NHS.|
|**10a. How does healthcare**<br>**resource use differ**<br>**between the technology**<br>**and current care?**|Care for EPGA will remain in secondary care, and the introduction of this therapy is likely to increase patient<br>access to dedicated MDT review.<br>Therapy can be self-administered at home, so unlikely to increase demand for day-case care.<br>No specific blood monitoring is required for benralizumab; indeed, in comparison with conventional DMARDS<br>and cyclophosphamide the requirement for monitoring blood tests is likely to be reduced.<br>Likely to reduce emergency and unplanned care due to reduction in flare rate and glucocorticoid complications.|
|**10b. In what clinical setting**<br>**should the technology be**<br>**used? (For example,**<br>**primary or secondary care,**<br>**specialist clinics.)**|Secondary care (with specialist MDT oversight) and specialist clinics, including multi-disciplinary vasculitis<br>clinics.|
|**10c. What investment is**<br>**needed to introduce the**<br>**technology? (For example,**|No additional facilities or equipment needed.<br>Therapy can be delivered and self-administered at home using existing pharmacy pathways.|
