|**11. Do you expect the**<br>**technology to provide**<br>**clinically meaningful**<br>**benefits compared with**<br>**current care?**|Yes – RCT and observational studies demonstrate significant glucocorticoid sparing potential, and high rates of<br>(often glucocorticoid free) clinical remission – areas of unmet need and clinical priority as highlighted above.|
|**11a. Do you expect the**<br>**technology to increase**<br>**length of life more than**<br>**current care?**|Yes.<br>The FFS (five factor score) is predictive of mortality in EGPA and includes renal insufficiency (serum creatinine<br>>1.58 mg/dl), proteinuria >1 g per day, cardiomyopathy, gastrointestinal involvement, and central nervous<br>system (CNS) involvement. Patients with these disease features (in the absence severe asthma manifestations)<br>do not currently have access to anti-IL5 therapy in the UK.<br>Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death (>30%) in EGPA long-term, likely due to both disease and<br>treatment-related complications. Glucocorticoids contribute to this risk - evidence in other autoimmune rheumatic<br>disorders show a dose-dependent increased risk of MI, stroke, and death, even at doses ≤5 mg/day. Thus, the<br>ability to reduce / withdraw glucocorticoids with benralizumab treatment (in proportions reported in the<br>MANDARA study) is very likely to reduce long-term cardiovascular risk and associated mortality (although not<br>captured during the short-term trial follow up).|
|**11b. Do you expect the**<br>**technology to increase**<br>**health-related quality of life**<br>**more than current care?**|Yes.<br>Unrelated to asthma manifestations, patients with EGPA experience high symptom burden due to multisystem<br>nature of disease – chronic rhinosinusitis, debilitating neuropathy, and symptoms related to cardiac failure are<br>particularly challenging. This is compounded by the burden of symptoms accrued as a result of glucocorticoid<br>toxicity – diabetes, osteoporosis and fracture risk, mood disturbance, cataracts, weight gain etc.  Access to a<br>proven therapy that increases periods of disease-free remission and glucocorticoid reduction will have a<br>significant and long-term impact on quality of life.|

|**13. Will the technology be**<br>**easier or more difficult to**<br>**use for patients or**<br>**healthcare professionals**<br>**than current care? Are**<br>**there any practical**<br>**implications for its use (for**<br>**example, any concomitant**<br>**treatments needed,**<br>**additional clinical**<br>**requirements, factors**<br>**affecting patient**<br>**acceptability or ease of use**<br>**or additional tests or**<br>**monitoring needed.)**|Therapy is administered by a subcutaneous auto-injector, acceptable to nearly all patients.<br>No additional blood monitoring is required during benralizumab treatment.<br>Observational data suggests treatment with benralizumab permits withdrawal of oral immunosuppressants in a<br>significant proportion (>25%) of patients. This will reduce both treatment-related adverse events and the<br>requirement for regular blood test monitoring (as is required with conventional DMARDs, cyclophosphamide etc)|
|**14. Will any rules (informal**<br>**or formal) be used to start**<br>**or stop treatment with the**<br>**technology? Do these**<br>**include any additional**<br>**testing?**|We propose that Benralizumab for EGPA patients should be assessed, discussed and managed by established<br>specialist renal/rheumatology/vasculitis MDTs, that already have expertise in the multi-system nature of EGPA<br>and the infrastructure and experience in biologics in other forms of vasculitis.<br>We propose at least annual review by the MDT to review treatment efficacy (relating to disease activity, flare rate,<br>glucocorticoid tapering, withdrawal of other immunosuppressive agents) and to determine duration of ongoing<br>treatment. Potential indications to stop treatment may include failure to reduce flares, failure to taper<br>glucocorticoids or other treatments.<br>We would support a requirement to collect real-world outcome data of patients treated with the technology for<br>EGPA, relating to both efficacy and safety both in the short term, and longer term, beyond one year.|

|**Sources of evidence**||

|**18. Do the clinical trials**<br>**on the technology reflect**<br>**current UK clinical**<br>**practice?**|In the MANDARA study, the comparator treatment to Benralizumab was Mepolizumab; Mepolizumab is not<br>commissioned for EGPA in the UK but was demonstrated to be effective in the MIRRA study.|
|**18a. If not, how could the**<br>**results be extrapolated to**<br>**the UK setting?**|Placebo-treated patients in the MIRRA study more likely to represent the current UK population treated with<br>standard care in EGPA.|
|**18b. What, in your view,**<br>**are the most important**<br>**outcomes, and were they**<br>**measured in the trials?**|Sustained disease remission, glucocorticoid-minimisation, and quality of life – addressed in RCT and<br>observational data.<br>Survival – not primarily addressed in relatively short-term trial follow up.|
|**18c. If surrogate outcome**<br>**measures were used, do**<br>**they adequately predict**<br>**long-term clinical**<br>**outcomes?**|Evidence in other, comparable, autoimmune rheumatic diseases shows that glucocorticoid dose and duration<br>associates with development of cardiovascular disease and with mortality. Whilst specific data are lacking (largely<br>due to disease rarity), we would expect this to hold in EGPA, and that reduction in glucocorticoid use would<br>associate with reduced cardiovascular risk and improved survival in this patient group.|
|**18d. Are there any**<br>**adverse effects that were**<br>**not apparent in clinical**<br>**trials but have come to**<br>**light subsequently?**|None that we are aware of.|
|**19. Are you aware of any**<br>**relevant evidence that**<br>**might not be found by a**<br>**systematic review of the**<br>**trial evidence?**|No|
|**20. How do data on real-**<br>**world experience**<br>**compare with the trial**<br>**data?**|Published observational and ‘real-word’ data replicate RCT findings – with greater time spent in remission,<br>reductions in glucocorticoid dose, increased glucocorticoid withdrawal, and ability to withdraw other<br>immunosuppressive agents.|

## **Key messages** 

|**22. In up to 5 bullet**<br>**points, please summarise**<br>**the key messages of your**<br>**submission.**|•<br>EGPA is a rare disease, and patients face significant unmet needs, including diagnostic delays,<br>glucocorticoid-dependence (with resultant toxicities) and a lack of other proven or licensed therapies, making<br>effective alternatives like benralizumab highly desirable.<br>•<br>Benralizumab demonstrates significant benefits in randomized trials and real-world studies, including<br>increased remission rates, reduced relapse risk, and glucocorticoid-sparing effects, which are priorities for<br>improving patient outcomes.<br>•<br>Benralizumab represents a groundbreaking, targeted treatment for EGPA, offering a safer and more effective<br>alternative to conventional, less-proven, therapies like cyclophosphamide and synthetic DMARDs.<br>•<br>The therapy's subcutaneous administration allows for at-home use, minimal additional resource<br>requirements, and its introduction has the potential to reduce emergency and unplanned care, while<br>promoting referral to specialist MDTs for improved disease management.<br>•<br>Endorsed by international guidelines (e.g., EULAR, ACR, upcoming British Society of Rheumatology/UK<br>Kidney Association recommendations), access to benralizumab would address critical gaps in EGPA<br>management and aligns with best practices in vasculitis care worldwide.|
|---|---|

||**8. In your view, is there**<br>**an unmet need for**<br>**patients and healthcare**<br>**professionals in this**<br>**condition?**|The ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAVs) encompass three conditions: Eosinophilic granumatosis with<br>polyangiitis (EGPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Until recently,<br>trials for the AAVs have focused on patients with GPA and MPA and treatment regimens for EGPA have been<br>extrapolated from this evidence. For the first time, there is now evidence that targeted therapy with anti-IL5<br>medication is effective and very well tolerated in EGPA; with minimal side effects and no requirement for<br>intensive blood monitoring.<br>This technological appraisal- Benralizumab for treating relapsing or refractory eosinophilic granulomatosis with<br>polyangiitis- was discussed at the UKIVAS steering group meeting (comprising rheumatologists, nephrologists,<br>nurse specialists and patient charity representative) in Birmingham on 26th November 2024, held at our annual<br>educational meeting. This UKIVAS steering group gives full support to this TA.<br>There is a clear unmet need in terms of treatment for patients with EGPA who can have a range of disease<br>manifestations (lung, cardiac, neuro, skin, haematological and renal involvement). At present, the mainstay of<br>treatment is with high dose glucocorticoids, non-specific disease modifying (DMARD) medications such as<br>methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate for “non-severe” disease, or cyclophosphamide (a chemotherapy<br>agent) for severe manifestations. Non-specific DMARDs and cyclophosphamide have significant adverse effects<br>including liver and blood count abnormalities, increased risk of infection and can impact on fertility and risk of<br>malignancy. The cost (in terms of money and patient and healthcare time for blood monitoring and infusion<br>delivery) is higher for DMARDs and cyclophosphamide than Benralizumab, which is self-administered by<br>subcutaneous injection. The impact of disease activity, dealing with flares and subsequent increases in steroid<br>dosages can also significantly impact on patients’ health-related quality of life.<br>Glucocorticoids are effective short term in EGPA but can lead to a range of adverse effects and specifically<br>worsen health related quality of life. Patients experience relapse frequently on steroid reduction in EGPA, with<br>more than 80% of patients in real world data sets having at least one relapse and 20% experiencing severe<br>(organ or life threatening) relapse. Bell et al Cureus 2023.<br>Patients with EGPA here describe their experience with glucocorticoids during acute flares of EGPA:<br>“when my steroids are high… I’m taking, well for me say about 30 mg a day, I get a kind of a depression almost.<br>And it’s almost like - Well why should I bother getting up? (53-year-old female, EGPA, UK)”|
|---|---|---|

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

“My worst worry is about that prednisone, because right now it is not too bad, I am not too old, but I am pretty sure I am not able to use 25 mg of prednisone for the rest of my life, because something else is going to go (47year-old male, EGPA, Canada)”. 

Trial data for Benralizumab show a reduction in relapse rates to approximately a third, with a 50% reduction in cumulative glucocorticoid dosages and 40% steroid withdrawal over 36 weeks. Despite inclusion of people with a range of disease manifestations of EGPA within successful clinical trials– including patients with asthma, neuropathy, sinonasal disease, cardiomyopathy, glomerulonephritis, and skin purpura- currently within the NHS, only patients with one type of EGPA presentation, that of acute severe asthma, qualify for treatment with benralizumab via asthma pathways. 

There is also currently no facility for specialist rheumatology or nephrology MDTs to provide appropriate treatment with IL5 medications for any aspect of EGPA, despite the multi-organ nature of EGPA being managed by these teams. Such patients need to be referred onto severe asthma services to access IL-5 treatment. This situation is an anomaly in comparison with biologic therapy for all other forms of systemic vasculitis (e.g. Avacopan or Rituximab for ANCA associated vasculitis or Tocilizumab for giant cell arteritis) whereby specialist MDT teams within Rheumatology and Nephrology routinely manage these conditions. 

This means that patients with EGPA are likely to be suffering potentially avoidable delays in appropriate treatment in the case of asthma manifestations, and potentially less effective treatment in the case of people without severe asthma manifestations, who do not qualify under the severe asthma inclusion criteria. 

In clinical practice this leads to multiple flares of EGPA disease activity, requiring high dose steroid rescue courses and accumulated burden from glucocorticoid adverse effects.

## **What is the expected place of the technology in current practice?** 

|**9. How is the condition**<br>**currently treated in the**<br>**NHS?**|Within the UK, EGPA is currently treated `by different specialities depending on disease manifestation.<br>Rheumatology departments and MDTs commonly diagnose and treat multisystem autoimmune disease including<br>EGPA vasculitis. Vasculitis MDTs led by renal physicians (such as in Cambridge) can also manage and treat all<br>forms of vasculitis, so would also manage EGPA. Other specialists will be involved depending on disease<br>manifestation and severity including ENT, cardiology, dermatology, neurology, and respiratory, ideally within the<br>context of a multidisciplinary team. In some cases, patients may be diagnosed via acute severe asthma<br>pathways and then referred to rheumatology/renal services for treatment of their wider EGPA vasculitis.<br>First line treatment is with glucocorticoids and DMARDS such as methotrexate, mycophenolate or azathioprine.<br>In severe manifestations (cardiac, glomerulonephritis or neurological manifestations), cyclophosphamide or<br>Rituximab are used for remission induction. These treatments are not licenced for EGPA and their use is mainly<br>extrapolated from other types of ANCA associated vasculitis trials and recommendations.<br>More recently, patients with severe asthma as a manifestation of EGPA may receive anti-IL5 therapy (e.g<br>mepolizumab, benralizumab) or other biologics (e.g. Tezepelumab) via existing commissioned routes in<br>specialist severe asthma services. We do note though that the recommended dosage of Benralizumab under the<br>TA565 for use of severe eosinophilic asthma, is 30 mg every 4 weeks for the first 3 doses then every 8 weeks;<br>whilst the trial data for Beralizumab in EGPA refers to 30mg every 4 weeks continuously. The panel may<br>therefore want to consider the choice of dosage appropriate for EGPA.|

Patients can present with a range of different symptoms and there can be significant delay in diagnosis<br>in primary and secondary care, partly due to difficulties in differentiating EGPA from common conditions such as<br>asthma and other differential diagnoses such as hypereosinophilic syndrome, infection or malignancies.<br>In line with other multisystem inflammatory conditions, patients are commonly referred to and managed by<br>rheumatology teams in the longer term, but may also be under renal, respiratory, cardiology, neurology,<br>dermatology, haematology and ENT teams as required.<br>Specialist Rheumatology and Renal MDTs are now required for discussion and management of biologics in the<br>case of other types of ANCA associated vasculitis, connective tissues diseases and large vessel vasculitides,<br>and this is where complex EGPA patients are also often discussed and managed within local networks. Patients<br>with refractory or relapsing EGPA and asthma symptoms are then referred to acute severe asthma services<br>hosted within respiratory departments to assess for anti-IL5 therapy eligibility. Patients would then be followed up<br>jointly between respiratory and rheumatology for example. In some cases, patients are referred from Respiratory<br>teams to Rheumatology if their clinical picture evolves from that of severe asthma to EGPA vasculitis. Then<br>management would also be shared between specialities. However, this inevitably can lead to delays in initiating<br>appropriate treatment.<br>We know that access to specialist vasculitis MDT care is associated with better outcomes (e.g<br>https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38782514/) but we appreciate that services are not well developed in all<br>regions. In some cases patients can be  followed up in individual specialities without referral to an MDT which is<br>not ideal. The upcoming 2025 BSR management guidelines for ANCA vasculitis will highlight the importance of<br>access to specialist multidisciplinary MDTs, as they have been shown to improve patient outcomes including<br>reducing the number of serious infections and emergency admissions to hospital (VOICES study- Hollick Lancet<br>Rheum 2024).|

**22. In up to 5 bullet** • EGPA is a rare disease, and patients face significant unmet needs, including diagnostic delays, cumulative **points, please summarise** burden of glucocorticoids (with significant adverse effects and impact on health related quality of life ) and a **the key messages of your** lack of other proven or licensed therapies, making effective alternatives like benralizumab highly desirable. **submission.** • Approval of Benralizumab would align with best practice in the management of EGPA and is supported by recent guidance from EULAR, ACR and the upcoming BSR management guidelines. 

• Approval of Benralizumab for EGPA will improve equity of access for this treatment, via inclusion of a broader range of disease manifestations of EGPA (neuro, derm, cardiac, renal, haematological involvement) beyond severe asthma alone, and inclusion of a greater range of specialist MDTs (rheumatology, renal and vasculitis) to support their use. 

   - Benralizumab is targeted therapy for use in EGPA, it is well tolerated with minimal side effects and no blood monitoring requirements, comparing favourably with the current alternatives of non-specific DMARDS and cyclophosphamide. 

   - • Benralizumab requires subcutaneous administration supporting use at home by patients, thereby reducing impact on infusion day units. Effective treatment of EGPA should also reduce impact on acute emergency services including A+E, inpatient and acute outpatient services currently required to treat active disease and glucocorticoid adverse effects.

## **1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY** 

This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the Evidence Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues identified by the EAG. Section 1.2 presents the model outcomes. Section 1.3 summarises all key issues identified by the EAG relating to clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. Section 1.4 summarises the EAG’s preferred assumptions and ICERs. 

Further detail regarding key and non-key issues are described in the main EAG Report (Sections 2 to 6). 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

## _**1.2 Overview of key model outcomes**_ 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

12 



<!-- page 315 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Response rate: Increase the proportion of patients who achieve remission. This affects QALYs in three ways: (1) through the higher utility associated with the remission state, (2) the lower OCS dose, which results in lower disutility associated with OCSassociated acute and chronic adverse events, and (3) through a lower SMR than the stable disease or relapse health states. 

- Annualised Relapse rate: Decrease the proportion of patients in the relapse state. This affects QALYs in two ways: (1) through the lower utility associated with the relapse state, (2) the higher OCS dose associated with the relapse state, which affects the disutility associated with OCS-associated acute and chronic adverse events. 

- Reduce the proportion of patients in the refractory state within the stable state: the refractory state has the lowest estimated utility value because the patient experienced severe depression, anxiety and other symptoms that significantly affected the quality of life of patients. 

- Reduce the percentage of patients receiving OCS. This affects the disutility associated with OCS-associated acute and chronic adverse events by reducing the cumulative OCS dose overall. 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Proportion of patients on benralizumab: With PAS price applied to benralizumab and not for the standard of care, benralizumab is still the treatment with highest acquisition cost among EGPA treatments. 

- Response rate: Increase the proportion of patients who achieve remission. This affects costs in two ways: (1) through the lower costs associated with the remission state, (2) the lower OCS dose, which results in lower cost associated with OCS-associated acute and chronic adverse events. 

- Annualised Relapse rate: Decrease the proportion of patients in the relapse state. This affects costs in two ways: (1) through the higher cost associated with the relapse state, (2) the higher OCS dose associated with the relapse state, which affects the cost associated with OCS-associated acute and chronic adverse events. 

- Reduce the percentage of patients receiving OCS. This affects the cost associated with OCS-associated acute and chronic adverse events by reducing the cumulative OCS dose overall. 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- The no treatment waning assumption has the greatest effect. The drivers of the model are the effect of benrulizumab on the numbers of patients in remission and in the nonrefractory state. 

- The implicit related modelling assumptions that patients who discontinue OCS and those who do not are equally likely to discontinue benrulizumab, and if patients discontinue OCS then they do not restart OCS if they discontinue benrulizumab. 

- Related to the previous, the assumption that the effectiveness of SoC with OCS treatment is the same as SoC without OCS treatment. 

- The benralizumab discontinuation rate remains constant for the duration of the model.

## _**1.3 Description of the EAG’s key clinical and economic issues**_ 

## **Table 1.2: Key issue 1: Company’s trial results may not be generalisable to all EGPA patients (i.e. those with severe EGPA)** 

|**Report section**|3.1, 3.2, 3.4|

|Description of issue and<br>why the EAG has<br>identified it as important|The clinical effectiveness evidence for benralizumab as an<br>add-on treatment for patients with refractory or relapsing<br>EGPA is derived from the MANDARA and MIRRA trials.1,2<br>Both trials use similar study designs, patient characteristics,<br>and outcomes which, along with the inclusion of a common<br>comparator, permit an ITC to compare additional<br>benralizumab treatment to oral corticosteroids (OCS) with or<br>without immunosuppressants (IS). However, both studies<br>excluded patients presenting with organ- or life-threatening<br>EGPA at the time of screening.<br>Clinical advice to the EAG confirms benralizumab would be a<br>relevant treatment option for this subpopulation of patients<br>presenting with severe disease, who are more likely to<br>receive treatment with agents including cyclophosphamide or<br>rituximab. Cyclophosphamide and rituximab were also listed<br>as prohibited medications in the MANDARA and MIRRA<br>trials.1,2There is therefore a lack of evidence on the efficacy<br>and safety of benralizumab in patients with severe EGPA,<br>who may also be receiving cyclophosphamide or rituximab.<br>This means that there is also uncertainty about cost<br>effectiveness modelingas it relates to thisgroup.|
|What alternative approach<br>has the EAG suggested?|The EAG has no suggested alternatives.|

Additionally, if<br>benralizumab receives a NICE recommendation, real-world<br>evidence could be collected in UK clinical practice to help<br>provide conclusions on the effectiveness and cost-<br>effectiveness inpatients with severe EGPA.|

## _**1.4 Summary of the EAG’s preferred assumptions and ICER**_ 

Two changes were made from the company’s base-case to the EAG base-case. 

First, the EAG made utility adjustments in the health state utility values used to inform the model.  The company obtained the utility values from the Adelphi DSP study[3] while considering disutility values related to OCS use from the Gibson et al. (2024) study.[7] The EAG made adjustments to avoid double counting the negative effects of OCS use, as the population in the Adelphi DSP study already suffered from adverse events which could overlap with OCS comorbidities.[3] 

Second, the EAG modelled a linear decline in the OCS discontinuation rate from **% to 0% from 1 year to 5 years. The CS model assumed an annual rate of **% for the duration of benralizumab treatment. 

The probabilistic results from the company and EAG base-case are shown in Table 1.8. Selected results from the company and EAG’s deterministic scenario analysis are shown in Table 1.9.

## _**2.1 Population**_ 

The population defined in the NICE scope is adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA, receiving OCS with or without stable IS therapy.[14] The population outlined in the CS is said to be ‘in line with final scope’. However, the MANDARA and MIRRA trials exclude patients with organ or life-threatening EGPA (hereafter referred to as severe EGPA) < 3 months prior to screening (see Table 13, Appendix D).[15] With regard to the MANDARA’s trial inclusion criteria, the company report that MANDARA was designed to be a head-to-head, non-inferiority study to mepolizumab, which was anticipated to be the standard of care when benralizumab would be entering clinical practice (question A9).[16] The restriction to less severe patients is linked to the company’s statement that cyclophosphamide and rituximab are inappropriate comparators in the decision problem scope as they are predominantly restricted to the treatment of patients with severe EGPA (see Section 2.2).[5] During the Factual Accuracy Check (FAC),[17] the Company reiterated the positioning of benralizumab for patients with non-severe (defined as not organ- of life-threatening) EGPA (Figure 2.1).[17]

Source: Factual accuracy check and confidential information check[17] Abbreviations: IS = immunosuppressant; OCS = oral corticosteroid. 

The management of EGPA takes a severity-based approach, whereby EGPA severe disease is usually defined as life-threatening manifestations and/or organ impairment associated with long-term poor prognosis.[18] EGPA is a rare type of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAVs) that causes inflammation of small and medium-sized blood vessels. AAV severity is assessed with two main tools: BVAS and the Five-Factor Score (FFS).[19,20] FFS (1994) comprises clinical manifestations at the time of diagnosis, renal insufficiency (serum creatinine >1.58 mg/dl), proteinuria >1 g per day, cardiomyopathy, gastrointestinal involvement and central nervous system (CNS) involvement.[21] The subsequent revised FFS (2009) included age >65 years as a poor prognostic factor and removed CNS involvement.[20] Recent evidence-based guidance, developed by a panel of European experts, for the diagnosis and management of EGPA, also highlights that peripheral neuropathy and other rare manifestations (for example alveolar haemorrhage) should be considered when choosing remission-induction strategies.[22] 

CPRD data from AstraZeneca in the CS highlight that ***** of patients with EGPA had an FFS (1996) of 0, which is used in the budget impact model as a proxy for the proportion of non- 

32 



<!-- page 335 -->

severe patients.[8] Potentially therefore, restricting the population to non-severe patients excludes approximately a ******* of patients with EGPA. Clinical advice to the EAG indicated that benralizumab would also benefit the population with severe disease who are more likely than the wider EGPA population to be receiving treatment with cyclophosphamide and, to a lesser extent, rituximab. The EAG are not aware of any data from MANDARA or the CRPD that looks at fluctuations in patient-level data over the duration of the trial in relation to severity. There is however evidence from a post-hoc analysis of pooled treatment groups from MANDARA, which based on the severity of patients’ prior EGPA-associated cumulative manifestations (>3 months prior to study enrolment), highlighted adjusted rates of remission were similar regardless of disease severity history.[23] 

At baseline in MANDARA, 45 patients in the benralizumab arm (64.3%) had relapsing disease (66% for the overall trial population).[5] Based on clinical advice to the EAG, it is  possible that relapses (either during the trial or after follow up) might be severe enough to instigate organ or life threatening disease manifestations, and therefore there is a possibility that the proportion of patients who would be eligible for benralizumab using the MIRRA/MANDARA criteria would increase over time. Clinical advice to the EAG suggests patients with severe disease would likely benefit from treatment with benralizumab based on experience with those eligible due to their concomitant severe eosinophilic asthma and experience with other IL-5 antagonists. Whether the treatment benefit with benralizumab in these patients is comparable to that in patients receiving treatment for milder disease was harder to quantify but it was noted that patients with severe disease may have very limited effective conventional treatment options. 

Evidence from subgroup analysis in the MANDARA trial and the CALIMA trial (which assessed benralizumab as add-on treatment for patients with severe, uncontrolled, eosinophilic asthma) suggests a non-significant trend towards greater improvement in patients with more severe disease (see Table 2.2 below and Table 3 in Appendix E of the CS).[24] Specifically from the CALIMA trial, patients who had experienced more than three exacerbations in the previous year (i.e., greater asthma severity at baseline) had a trend towards greater effects of benralizumab treatment.[25] This analysis showed significance, although the difference between subgroups was non-significant. Further post-hoc analysis demonstrated a 26% risk reduction (rate ratio versus placebo 0.74 (0.51 to 1.09)) for patients who had two prior exacerbations (for benralizumab 30 mg Q4W versus placebo) compared to a 45% risk reduction for patients with three or more exacerbations (rate ratio versus placebo 0.55 (0.37 to 0.81)).[25] The MIRRA trial also showed a subgroup effect in a priori analyses which indicated larger effects of mepolizumab in patients with more severe disease, which may imply a similar effect in other IL-5 antagonists (see Section 3.2.2 for further discussion).

Whilst the NICE scope details adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA, receiving OCS with or without stable IS therapy,[14] the MANDARA/MIRRA trials included only patients without lifethreatening or organ-threatening disease (hereinafter referred to as non-severe EGPA)(see Table 14, CS Appendix D[15] ). Since there is no trial evidence available for the most severe patients in this indication and at the indicated dose for EGPA, the EAG is unable to comment on the risk/benefit ratio for patients with recent severe disease. There is however evidence that the use of benralizumab in patients with more severe, eosinophilic asthma at baseline had the greatest effect of treatment.[25] The eligibility criteria in MANDARA are likely to have excluded approximately a ******* of patients in the UK; those with current/recent organ or lifethreatening relapsed disease at baseline.[8] Those patients with severe disease are also unlikely to be a stable cohort over time, rather those meeting this criterion will change as patients fluctuate between disease stages (including severe relapse). If the MANDARA trial inclusion criteria were adopted in real-world clinical practice, the proportion of EGPA patients eligible for benralizumab will likely increase as patients previously severe become eligible as their disease stabilises, and patients whose disease has relapsed with organ-or lifethreatening manifestations may not meet the proposed stopping criteria to withdraw treatment. Future trials (or real-world evidence) should disaggregate data for both severe and non-severe populations to illuminate efficacy by disease severity. 

## _**2.2 Comparators**_ 

The comparators reported in the NICE scope included OCS, cyclophosphamide, IS and rituximab (none of which have marketing authorisation for this condition).[14] There are currently no licensed treatments for EGPA in the UK. Mepolizumab, the comparator in the benralizumab trial, has a marketing authorisation for EGPA amongst other conditions, but has no NICE guidance for this indication.[26] No recent UK guidelines are available for EGPA, although there are evidence-based 2023 European guidelines for EGPA[22] and 2014 guidelines available from the British Society of Rheumatology for the management of AAVs, which is the group of autoimmune diseases which EGPA falls into.[27] Patients with a worse prognosis (e.g., FFS ≥ 1) are typically treated with a combination of IS and OCS therapy, while those with milder disease (FFS = 0) may be managed using OCS monotherapy.[28] OCS/IS combination therapy is also recommended as a first-line treatment for patients experiencing organ- or lifethreatening manifestations, such as eosinophilic alveolitis, alveolar haemorrhage, or severe peripheral neuropathy.[29] 

As highlighted in the CS, for the non-severe patients eligible for and recruited to the MANDARA trial, who do not have organ or life-threatening EGPA <3 months prior to screening, cyclophosphamide and rituximab are unlikely to be prescribed. The CS highlights the CRPD dataset which reports only **** patients (1.0%) had rituximab and ** patients (2.7%) had cyclophosphamide.[5,8] Clinical advice to the EAG supports these figures, suggesting that neither cyclophosphamide nor rituximab is widely used in patients without severe disease and also that cyclophosphamide is used more than rituximab in EGPA disease with major organ involvement as there is limited trial evidence for EGPA specifically (as trials have combined 

34 



<!-- page 337 -->

patient populations with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) diseases as a whole). However in severe disease with major organ involvement, cyclophosphamide is recommended for remission-induction in life-threatening disease and/or those with poor prognosis (FFS ≥ 1),[30] as it has been shown to be associated with adverse events related to infections, neutropenia and long-term cancer risk.[31] Rituximab has been shown to be an effective alternative treatment, especially in situations where cyclophosphamide use may be problematic (relapse after cyclophosphamide, women of childbearing age, risk of malignancy),[32] but there are strict criteria governing its use as detailed in the NHS England Clinical Commissioning Policy.[5,12] 

Mepolizumab, a humanised anti-interleukin-5 (anti-IL-5) monoclonal antibody is the comparator in the MANDARA trial and is a NICE recommended add-on treatment for severe refractory eosinophilic asthma.[6,33] Whilst mepolizumab has a UK marketing authorisation as an add-on treatment for patients aged 6 years and older with relapsing-remitting or refractory EGPA, there is no NICE recommendation as GlaxoSmithKline did not provide an evidence submission.[34] CPRD prescription rates provided by AstraZeneca highlight ***************** with EGPA received mepolizumab.[8] 

Whilst EGPA patients may be treated by IS (including cyclophosphamide), OS and biologics (rituximab and mepolizumab), for those patients with non-severe disease, IS and OCS are appropriate comparators to benralizumab in the CS. The MANDARA trial prohibited cyclophosphamide and rituximab in the weeks/months before screening/baseline (see Section D.1.6).[15] ******************************************************************************[**] Assuming the focus is on patients with non-severe EGPA disease, the EAG are satisfied that only OCS and IS are appropriate comparators. However, for the population of patients with EGPA more widely, cyclophosphamide and rituximab may be appropriate additions or alternatives to IS as part of comparator treatment in some instances for the patients with severe disease (see Section 3.3.1.1 for further discussion). 

## _**2.3 Outcomes**_ 

The NICE scope encompasses a wide variety of outcomes including mortality, remission (remission rates, total accrued duration of remission), relapse (total accrued duration of remission, time to first relapse, number of relapses), treatment changes (reduction/cessation in systemic steroid use, use of IS), physiological measures (vasculitis activity scores and pulmonary function), adverse events and HRQoL. Whilst the company states that the outcomes reported in the CS are in line with this scope, it is important to highlight that this reporting refers only to the MANDARA trial. As the submission uses an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) to assess effectiveness, nine outcomes were presented for the Bucher ITC related to remission, relapse and OCS dosage. 

Two outcomes were modelled for the matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) (see Table 2.3 for a comparison of the outcomes reported for MANDARA, MIRRA and the ITC/MAIC). Two of the seven Bucher ITC outcomes were used in the cost-effectiveness modelling (the same two outcomes were validated in the MAIC); namely the proportion of patients in remission at weeks 36 and 48 together with the annualised relapse rate that are reported in both the Bucher ITC and MAIC.

The NICE scope encompassed a much broader range of outcomes than that presented in the Bucher ITC, which listed nine outcomes, two of which were incorporated into the costeffectiveness analysis (sensitivity analysis in the cost-effectiveness modelling used the results of a MAIC in addition). The outcomes utilised in the ITC (remission, relapse and OCS dosage) incorporate definitions that use vasculitis activity scores, pulmonary function, and use of IS, which are also listed in the NICE scope. However, this comes with the caveat that the clinical effectiveness of benralizumab related to these outcomes must be derived from other outputs. Furthermore, in the CS Section B.3.4 the company reported on the limitations of SF-36 used in MANDARA to assess HRQoL including its inability to fully capture the symptom burden of EGPA and the loss of validity when mapped to EQ-5D.[5] To inform the HRQoL data, two studies were conducted to generate more robust and accurate data to inform the cost-effectiveness analysis (the Adelphi DSP study and UK-specific vignette study)[5,38] For further discussion see Section 4.2.6. 

The EAG acknowledges that the two key outcomes presented (proportion of patients in remission (main remission definition) at both week 36 and week 48 and the annualised relapse rate) are the most insightful for the model. The Bucher ITC results for the average daily OCS dose during the last 4 weeks of the study are also informative and are included in the NICE scope. 

## _**2.4 Special considerations including issues related to equality**_ 

The use of benralizumab in the CS was shown to reduce OCS dose relative to standard of care (Bucher ITC average daily OCS during the last 4 weeks of the study was OR (95% CI): ****************[*1] ).[15] Tapering of OCS to the minimum effective dosage reduces long-termtoxicity, and the reduction of IS is preferable to limit the risk of complications, especially infections.[22] This is particularly important to older people (aged >65 years), given their increased vulnerability to infectious diseases and increased burden of comorbidities. If OCS dose were reduced, this could be particularly beneficial to older people. 

However, the restriction to non-severe patients included in the MANDARA and MIRRA trials might inadvertently restrict treatment with benralizumab to slightly younger patients. Clinical advice to the EAG suggests patients with severe disease are likely to be older. As such, this has the potential to increase inequalities. 

The CPRD data highlights that only ***% and ****% of patients with EGPA are under 35 or between 35 and 49 years respectively.[8] There also appear to be ******* ***************** ******* ************ ******* in both the CPRD data and the MANDARA trial (question A11, Points for Clarification (PfC)).[8,16] The known adverse effects OCS exposure during pregnancy can have on the mother and newborn,[39] suggests the proportion of younger female patients of child-

bearing age with EGPA may be at particular risk. Therefore, a treatment which reduces the use of OCS may be particularly beneficial for these younger, female patients. 

Clinical advice to the EAG suggests that the inequalities associated with age and sex may not interact: although older patients are more likely to have severe disease, female and male patients are equally likely to present with severe disease although >50% of the patient population as a whole is female.

## **3.1.1 Search methods for the clinical effectiveness SLR** 

The company conducted separate searches for clinical effectiveness studies (presented in the CS Appendix D),[15] and cost effectiveness, HRQoL and cost and resource use studies (CS Appendices G, H and I respectively).[43-45] The EAG used the PRESS checklist to appraise the search strategies.[46] In this section, we present the critique of the search methods for clinical effectiveness studies. The critique of searches for cost effectiveness studies, HRQoL studies and cost and resource use is presented in Section 4.1.1. As some of the issues were the same for all the searches there are cross references to the relevant section to avoid repetition.  The searches were first run in June 2023 and were updated in August 2024 and so are considered up to date. 

## **3.1.2 Search strategies** 

The searches were based on a set of terms related to the condition with the application of a study design (or research type) search filter(s) in some of the electronic bibliographic databases. Terms for the intervention were not included in the search strategies. The set of 

43 



<!-- page 346 -->

condition-related search terms needed to be as sensitive as possible in order to avoid potentially missing relevant studies. The sensitivity of the search could have been increased by allowing for plurals such as ‘granulomatoses’, ‘(poly)angiitides’ or ‘vasculitides’. Only one instance of proximity searching was used meaning that for the remaining phrases the terms had to appear in the order given with no words allowed in between. It may have been worth considering adding the slightly broader controlled vocabulary terms/subject headings to increase the sensitivity e.g. the MeSH term ‘Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody-Associated Vasculitis’, additional to the very specific subject headings used, to allow for less precise application of subject headings within an electronic database. No specific searches for adverse effects of the intervention were conducted. These considerations led to some concerns as to whether potentially relevant studies may have been missed by the searches. However, these concerns were mitigated by the range of other sources searched including grey literature and reference lists of relevant systematic reviews. 

## **3.1.3 Eligibility criteria** 

The SLR predefined eligibility criteria are presented in Table 3.2 (section D.1.2, Table 10)[15] and overall were in line with that specified by the NICE scope.[14] The EAG are satisfied with the predefined eligibility framework for the population/intervention/comparator/outcomes, however, there are some concerns with the study design and company’s prioritisation strategy for inclusion. 

The company initially kept the inclusion criteria broad and adopted an evidence prioritisation strategy which determined that only RCTs and interventional non-RCTs should be prioritised and included in the review for extraction, whilst observational (non-interventional) studies should be deprioritised. The company justified their reasons for prioritisation in section D.1.2,[15] ensuring only the highest quality and relevant evidence was identified and considered for inclusion in the indirect treatment comparison (ITC). Although subject to a higher risk of bias, observational studies may provide supplemental data and real-world evidence such as on the natural history of the condition and treatment patterns, to help contextualise RCT results. It may therefore have been beneficial to have included these studies to check for overall generalisability and robustness of the evidence presented. As part of this submission the company provided additional data including the Adelphi Real World DSP[3] and qualitative insights from patients[47] and clinical experts.[9] 

Furthermore, according to the CS Section D.1.3 which includes the PRISMA diagram,[15] there were in total 37 publications in the SLR update and 29 publications in the original SLR with a non-interventional study design, and therefore excluded as part of the company’s prioritisation strategy. However, as reported in the data extraction workbook, provided by the company (embedded in Appendix D, section D.1.4),[15] a further 31 observational study congress abstracts were also deprioritised in the original SLR but this step was not included in the PRISMA diagram nor stated in the CS section D.1.3.[15] The EAG note these excluded scientific abstracts comprised study abstracts linked to full text records also screened by the company, and abstracts without linked full text publications, which may have provided further supportive evidence as discussed above regarding the inclusion of observational studies. 

In the CS section D.1.2 (Table 10),[15] publication types included peer-reviewed publications and conference abstracts (published in or after 2013). Clinical trial registries were also included but were only used as a supplement for data from published literature. Post-hoc analyses were formally included but were not data extracted, as part of the company’s 

44 



<!-- page 347 -->

prioritisation strategy (section D.1.2).[15] There were three post-hoc analyses of the MIRRA trial; these provided support for clinical benefit from mepolizumab treatment relative to SoC in patients with EGPA, irrespective of baseline clinical characteristics (refractory disease status, IS use, EGPA duration, number of relapses, and OCS dose),[48] and whether patients presented with or without a predominantly vasculitic phenotype.[49,50] Additionally there was one post-hoc analysis of the MANDARA trial, indicating clinical benefits from either benralizumab or mepolizumab treatment for patients with EGPA, irrespective of ANCA status.[51] Post-hoc analyses warrant caution in their interpretation as they can be data-driven, lack statistical power, and subject to multiplicity concerns. The EAG agree the four included post-hoc analyses provide supportive evidence but also agree with the company’s approach to deprioritise the data generated from these in their submission. 

Systematic reviews were excluded, although the bibliographies of systematic reviews and meta-analyses were searched for relevant primary studies that were not found through database searches; in total four systematic reviews were searched. The EAG agree this approach to the selection of publication types ensures the most reliable and high-quality data are included and therefore deem the approach to be appropriate. 

Lasty, the company stipulated studies were limited to English language only at full text and limited to years 2003 onwards (Table 10, Section D.1.2).[15] Whilst language and time restrictions are more subject to bias, the EAG agree that, considering no non-English language records were reported to be excluded at full-text, the rarity of the disease and the treatments available, removing these restrictions would likely not have provided any further relevant evidence.

## _**3.2 Critique of trials of the technology of interest, their analysis and interpretation (and any standard meta-analyses of these)**_ 

Two trials were included in the CS, MANDARA[1] and MIRRA,[2] which are summarised below. Both are international, randomised, double-blind, parallel group, Phase III trials included in the SLR as part of the CS (Section B.2.9.2, Table 19).[5] The MANDARA trial was the only RCT identified investigating the efficacy and safety of benralizumab compared to any comparator (mepolizumab) in patients with refractory and relapsing EGPA, applicable to the NICE scope. 

Because mepolizumab treatment is not a relevant comparator to the decision problem, nor a reimbursed treatment option in the UK, the company performed a feasibility assessment of all RCTs (n=8) identified in the SLR, to enable an anchored ITC.  The company determined SoC in the UK to comprise OCS with or without IS, and concluded MIRRA was the only trial investigating the common comparator, mepolizumab, that would allow an indirect comparison of benralizumab with SoC (OCS with or without IS). 

The company concluded that a Bucher ITC was appropriate owing to the similarity in trial design, patient populations, and outcome measurements between MANDARA and MIRRA. However, as anchored ITCs are subject to systematic bias, population adjustment methods were additionally adopted in a MAIC to validate the results from the ITC. In the CS quality assessments of the MANDARA and MIRRA trials were provided; these indicated robust trial methodologies which the EAG are overall satisfied represent rigorous assessments of the comparisons. However, the EAG recognise that the eligibility criteria for both trials exclude patients with severe EGPA, and those receiving treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, indicating a lack of evidence and certainty in the clinical effectiveness and safety of benralizumab in this patient population which is within remit of the NICE scope, this is further discussed in Key Issue 1. 

## **3.2.1 MANDARA** 

The pivotal trial providing clinical evidence for the effectiveness of benralizumab in patients with EGPA is the MANDARA trial (AstraZeneca) (NCT04157348).[36] The MANDARA trial (AstraZeneca) is an international, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled, non-inferiority study to compare the efficacy and safety of benralizumab versus mepolizumab, in 140 randomised adult patients with relapsing or refractory EGPA on OCS with or without stable IS therapy. In the benralizumab arm patients received one 30 mg benralizumab injection and three placebo to mepolizumab injections, while patients in the mepolizumab arm received three 100 mg mepolizumab injections plus one placebo to benralizumab injection.[1] Injections were administered subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. The trial is being conducted in 50 sites in nine countries (USA, Canada, UK, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Israel, Japan), and currently has an ongoing OLE period.[52] A summary of the EAG’s critique of the design, conduct and analysis of MANDARA trial is presented in 

.

## _3.2.1.1 Eligibility criteria_ 

The eligibility criteria of the MANDARA trial included adult patients aged ≥18 years old who had a documented EGPA diagnosis, at least 6 months prior to screening; a stable OCS dose ≥7.5 mg/day prednisolone/prednisone (but not >50 mg/day) for at least four weeks; and a history of relapsing or refractory disease. The EAG agrees this aligns with the population in the NICE scope,[14] which specifies adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA receiving OCS with or without stable IS therapy. However, patients with severe EGPA were excluded from the trial. As discussed in Section 2.1, clinical advice to the EAG confirmed benralizumab would be a relevant treatment for this subgroup of patients with severe disease, who are also more likely to receive treatment with cyclophosphamide and rituximab in UK clinical practice. The EAG note that prohibited medications in the MANDARA trial included cyclophosphamide and rituximab, which are also listed in the NICE scope. A key concern therefore arises over the representation of patients with severe EGPA, who may be receiving treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab. The Company reiterated the positioning of benralizumab for patients with non-severe EGPA during the FAC.[17] Furthermore, the enrollment of patients with ANCA positive status was capped at 10% in the MANDARA trial.[1] Such patients were verified by clinical expert advice to the EAG, to present with more vasculitis manifestations, whilst patients with a more atopic phenotype that comprised the majority of the MANDARA study population would be less likely to receive treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab in UK practice. This is further discussed in Section 3.3.1.2.In response to the PfC (Question A9),[16] the company provided further rationale for excluding patients with severe disease in the trial in addition to positioning of benralizumab in the treatment pathway. At the time of planning, MANDARA was designed to be a head-to-head, non-inferiority study to mepolizumab which was anticipated to be the SoC for when benralizumab would be entering clinical practice and evaluated by HTA bodies. Consequently, the study population of MANDARA was aligned as closely as possible to MIRRA, which also excluded patients with severe disease (further discussed in Section 3.2.2). The EAG agrees that the alignment of eligibility criteria between trials to be an appropriate approach at the time of designing the trial and this supports transitivity in the ITC included in the submission. Whilst post-hoc analysis from MANDARA which pooled data from both treatment groups, indicated adjusted rates of remission were 

54 



<!-- page 357 -->

similar regardless of history of severe disease.[23] , this still provides a key issue surrounding the uncertainty of clinical effectiveness and safety of benralizumab in patients with severe EGPA.

## _3.2.1.2 Baseline characteristics_ 

In the MANDARA trial ~13% (n=18) of 140 randomised patients were from four sites across the UK; ****** patients were randomised to the benralizumab treatment arm, and the remaining ** patients to mepolizumab.[57] The demographic and disease characteristics were balanced between treatment arms, however, the data reported were not stratified by country. Clinical advice to the EAG confirmed the heterogeneity of the disease to vary greatly, and consultation with UK clinical experts by the company also indicated management of EGPA to vary depending on geographic location.[9] Considering the relatively low proportion of patients from the UK enrolled in the MANDARA trial, the EAG had concerns around how well the patient population and SoC provided in the MANDARA trial reflected the UK patient population and clinical practice. The company in response to the PfC (Questions A4 and A5)[16] provided OCS and IS usage by country and UK study site (Table 3.4 and Figure ). The IS usage, and average OCS dose at baseline for the UK study population, were shown to comparable to the total study population. Furthermore, the progressive decline of OCS dosage throughout the 52week double-blind period was also similar across countries. While differing prescribing practices across treatment sites may account for some of the observed variation, the EAG agree the small sample sizes across sites (London: n=*; Cambridge: n=*; Leicestershire: n=*; Portsmouth: n=*) prevent any inferences from being made.[16]

Baseline characteristics of patients and treatment in the MANDARA trial, were confirmed in clinical expert interviews conducted by the company to be generalizable to patients and realworld practice in the UK.[9] Clinical advice to the EAG verified baseline characteristics reflected patients with non-severe EPGA seen in UK clinical practice, but did not represent patients with severe disease. As discussed in Section 3.2.1.1, clinical advice to the EAG confirmed patients with severe EGPA were more likely to also be receiving treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab. Additionally, patients with severe EGPA in UK clinical practice, were typically older than the trial population; only ************* patients included in the MANDARA trial were >65 years of age.[5] This reinstates the key issue over the efficacy of benralizumab in patients with severe disease in the UK, who also typically tend to be older. 

## **3.2.2 MIRRA trial** 

Data on mepolizumab (from the MIRRA trial) were used by the company to form a connected network with benralizumab (from the MANDARA trial, NCT02020889)[37] to conduct Bucher ITCs and anchored MAICs (see Section 3.3 for further details). 

56 



<!-- page 359 -->

The MIRRA trial (GlaxoSmithKline) is an international, multicentre phase III, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to investigate the efficacy and safety of mepolizumab for EGPA in subjects receiving standard of care therapy (defined as OCS with or without IS). Mepolizumab was administered as multiple subcutaneous injections (comprising three doses of 100 mg) every four weeks (13 administrations).[2] The trial was conducted in 31 academic centres and hospitals across nine countries including Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Spain, USA and the UK. A summary of the EAG’s critique of the design, conduct and analysis of MIRRA is presented in Table 3.5.

## _3.2.2.1 Eligibility criteria_ 

The MANDARA trial was conducted in 50 centres across nine countries.[64] Due to the rarity of the condition, it is conceivable that some of the patients who enrolled in MANDARA were previously included in the placebo arm of the MIRRA trial as there was an overlap in trial sites as well as countries. 

Adult patients with a history of relapsing of refractory disease, taking a stable dose of OCS with or without a stable IS dose (excluding cyclophosphamide) were eligible for inclusion. Patients with life-threatening EGPA within three months prior to screening and through randomisation were excluded, as were patients with organ-threatening EGPA.[5,62] Full reporting of the inclusion criteria of MIRRA, alongside MANDARA are described in Section D.1.6 in the CS.[5] The inclusion criteria across the trials are very comparable. As detailed in the response to clarification question A9,[16] MANDARA was designed to be a head-to-head, non-inferiority study to mepolizumab (which was anticipated to be the standard of care for when benralizumab was being evaluated by regulatory authorities). 

As with the MANDARA trial, the population was restricted to cases of non-severe EGPA. The EAG notes that this is not in line with the original NICE scope for this appraisal[14] and therefore the EAG considers this a key issue (see Table 1.2). The populations in both trials exclude patients with severe EGPA, and clinical advice to the EAG has confirmed that benralizumab is likely to be efficacious to patients with severe disease. Indeed, in MIRRA which assessed the efficacy of an mepolizumab, which like benralizumab is an anti-IL5 monoclonal antibody, there was tentative evidence of a stronger effect relative to placebo in non-severe patients with indicators of greater disease severity (baseline blood eosinophil count ≥150 cells/μL and baseline VDI score ≥5 (Table 3.6).[1] There was a significant difference (p<0.05) for patients with a baseline blood eosinophil count ≥150 cells/μL (OR 95% CI: 26.10 (7.02 to 97.02)) compared to those with counts <150 cells/μL (OR 95% CI: 0.95 (0.28, 3.24)) for mepolizumab/placebo. This pattern is replicated in the baseline VDI scores, although the difference is not statistically significant. Whilst the small sample sizes increase uncertainty, mepolizumab may show greater efficacy in the patients with more severe symptoms amongst patients with non-severe disease. As benralizumab was shown to be non-inferior to mepolizumab in the MANDARA trial, a similar pattern might be replicated for benralizumab. Indeed, in the CALIMA trial which looked at benralizumab as an add-on treatment for patients with severe, uncontrolled, eosinophilic asthma, the study authors found that patients who had experienced three or more exacerbations in the previous year (i.e., greater asthma severity at baseline) had the greatest effects of benralizumab treatment.[25]

## _3.2.2.2 Baseline characteristics_ 

The average age of patients in MIRRA was 49 and 48 with males comprising 38.2% and 44.1% of patients in the mepolizumab and placebo arms respectively. Prednisolone or prednisone dose was 12.0 and 11.0 mg/day for mepolizumab/placebo and IS use at baseline was 60.3% and 45.6% for the intervention/comparator arm.[5] The trial ran between February 2014 and September 2016.[37] Over the past 10 years, EGPA treatment has evolved, and clinical advice to the EAG has highlighted higher doses of OCS would have been used previously relative to current practice.[b] 

Patients for MIRRA were drawn from nine countries; 13 were from the UK.[2] In response to clarification question A4,[16] there was little difference between standard of care across MANDARA trial sites (see Section 3.2.1.2 for further details). It is plausible to consider that this would be replicated in MIRRA. Clinical advice to the EAG has confirmed that the 

> b Whilst there are differences in baseline characteristics across trial arms, particularly with IS use at baseline, the resulting publication does not report whether these differences are significant and as detailed above, approaches to treatment are now more consistent and clinically driven. 

66 



<!-- page 369 -->

demographic and baseline disease characteristics of MANDARA were broadly representative of that seen in UK clinical practice. Since there is comparability in summary data between MANDARA and MIRRA it is likely that this is also the case for MIRRA. As such, the baseline characteristics of MIRRA by association are broadly representative of that seen in UK clinical practice. 

As discussed above (Section 3.2.2.1), MIRRA excluded patients with severe EGPA in the trial. Consequently, the EGPA population in the UK is likely to include severe disease which is not presented by patients in MIRRA at baseline (see Key Issue 1). 

## _**3.3 Critique of trials identified and included in the indirect comparison and/or multiple treatment comparison**_ 

The final scope issued by NICE,[14] defined the relevant comparator as established clinical management without benralizumab, including OCS, CYC, other IS agents, and RTX. In the CS Section B.1.1 (Table 1),[5] the company after consulting clinical guidelines, clinical expert opinion, and UK prescription data determined that OCS with or without IS formed SoC in the UK. The MANDARA trial, the only trial providing relevant clinical data on the intervention in line with the decision problem, compared the efficacy and safety of benralizumab versus mepolizumab in patients with EGPA. As mepolizumab treatment is not a relevant comparator, nor a NICE recommended treatment option in the UK, the company performed an ITC to generate efficacy estimates of benralizumab versus OCS with or without IS, in participants with EGPA. Additionally, the company performed an anchored MAIC to validate the results of the ITC. The EAG’s critique regarding the methodology of the ITC and MAIC are presented in the Sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2. 

## **3.3.1 Bucher ITC** 

The company first carried out a feasibility assessment to identify relevant clinical studies that would permit an anchored ITC with the MANDARA trial (detailed in CS Section B.2.9).[5] With mepolizumab as the common comparator, MIRRA and MANDARA were concluded to permit the generation of comparative efficacy estimates of benralizumab versus SoC. Differences in trial design, population and outcome measurements were reasoned to not be clinically meaningful, and a Bucher ITC was deemed appropriate. Table 3.7 presents a summary of the EAG’s comments regarding the methodology of the Bucher ITC with key points expanded upon in the following sections.

## _3.3.1.1 Included and excluded studies_ 

In the CS Section B.2.9.1, the company conducted a feasibility assessment which evaluated data availability, heterogeneity between trials and network connectivity, for generating an ITC between benralizumab and SoC for EGPA.[5] MANDARA excluded patients with severe disease, or patients that had recently received previous cyclophosphamide or rituximab treatment,[1] subsequently the company reasoned cyclophosphamide and rituximab not to be appropriate comparators for this submission (see Section 2.2 for further discussion). The EAG agree OCS with or without IS matches SoC in the UK for patients presenting with non-severe EGPA, however, cyclophosphamide and rituximab form part of the treatment pathway for patients with severe disease. Uncertainty therefore remains in the clinical effectiveness of benralizumab in patients with EGPA compared to SoC for patients with severe disease, which can include treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab in the UK. 

During the feasibility assessment for an ITC the company also concluded that although these trials included the evaluation of treatments with OCS with or without IS, only the MIRRA trial allowed for an anchored ITC with the MANDARA trial.[5] The EAG note key differences in the study designs, baseline characteristics and outcomes of the other six RCTs in comparison to the MANDARA trial, which would preclude generation of a robust anchored ITC. With further consideration of the limited available evidence and rarity of EGPA, the EAG therefore agree the approach taken by the company to allow an anchored ITC based on patients with relapsing or refractory, non-severe EGPA to be performed appropriate. 

## _3.3.1.2 Included study characteristics and demographics_ 

Clinical advice to the EAG confirms EGPA presents as a heterogenous disease, which can affect multiple organs, and therefore requires a multidisciplinary approach to management of the disease. Furthermore, consultation with UK clinical experts by the company also highlighted management of EGPA to vary by geographic location.[9] Both the MANDARA and MIRRA trials were conducted globally including study sites within the UK. However, only ~10% 

69 



<!-- page 372 -->

(13/136) of the total study population in the MIRRA trial were based in the UK, while ~48% (65/136) patients were based in North America, and the remaining ~42% were based in Belgium (n=3), France (n=13), Germany (n=19), Italy (n=13), Spain (n=4) and Japan (n=6).[2] Similarly in the MANDARA trial ~13% (18/140) of patients were based in UK across a total of four sites.[1,55,57] The remaining MANDARA study population were based in North America (32/140), Belgium (n=4), France (n=33), Germany (n=17), Italy (n=18), Israel (n=10), and Japan (n=8).[1] The relatively low proportion of UK based patients in both trials raised some concerns to the EAG as to the translatability of the two trials to the patient population, and clinical practice in the UK. 

As discussed in Section 3.2.1.2 the OCS dosage and IS usage broken down by country and UK study site in the MANDARA trial were provided by the company in response to the PfC (Question A4 and A5).[16] The company only have access to published summary-level data from the MIRRA trial, therefore country specific data from the MIRRA trial were not provided. The OCS dosage and IS therapy in the UK were comparable to the total study population. Across UK study sites, OCS dose and IS therapy varied, but the company reasoned no firm conclusions can be made owing to differing prescribing practices and small samples sizes.[16] Patient baseline characteristics in MANDARA, and baseline treatment usage were confirmed in clinical expert interviews conducted by the company to be generalisable to patients and real-world practice in the UK.[9] This has also been verified independently through clinical expert advice to the EAG. The EAG therefore consider the OCS dosage and IS usage presented in the MANDARA trial to be translatable to the UK patient population. However, there are concerns due to exclusion of patients with severe EGPA in both the MANDARA and MIRRA trials. Clinical expert advice to EAG confirmed patients in the MANDARA trials presented with non-severe EGPA and indicated benralizumab would also be a relevant treatment in clinical practice for patients with severe disease. Furthermore, clinical advice to the EAG is that patients with severe disease tend to be older; while only ************* patients included in the MANDARA trial were >65 years of age.[5] The EAG believe that this raises a key issue of uncertainty of the efficacy of benralizumab in patients with severe disease in the UK, who typically tend to be the older.

## _3.3.1.3 Transitivity assumption_ 

A key assumption of Bucher ITCs is an absence of important differences between trials in the distribution of effect-modifying variables.[65] . While the EAG agree there are considerable similarities between the MANDARA and MIRRA trials to enable an ITC to be conducted, there are some differences which may have a confounding impact on effect estimates; these are expanded on in the following section. 

In the CS, the company stated the two trial designs were comparable with some minimal differences (CS Section D.1.6, Table 12).[15] Firstly MIRRA used a placebo-controlled design, while MANDARA had an active-comparator non-inferiority design. Both trials were phase III, included the common comparator mepolizumab, and enrolled a similar number of patients. Furthermore, as described in Section 3.3.1.2, study locations were overall similar; both trials included a comparable number of patients from the UK (~10-***).[1,2,5] Of note, MIRRA also 

70 



<!-- page 373 -->

enrolled patients in Spain, and MANDARA also enrolled patients in Israel and there was a markedly higher proportion of patients from North America in MIRRA than the MANDARA trial (~48% vs ~***).[1,2] 

Both trials exclusively enrolled patients diagnosed with relapsing or refractory EGPA and were matched according to the eligibility criteria. Only minimal differences in patient eligibility criteria are notable, which were highlighted by the company (CS Section D.1.6, Table 13)[15] : allergy, intolerance, contradictions, other concurrent medical conditions, prohibited medications, parasitic infection and hepatitis status. Furthermore, comparison of the seven pre-determined efficacy outcomes and their definitions from MANDARA and MIRRA (CS Section D.1.6, Table 15)[15] , identified only one outcome definition to present minor differences: the average daily OCS dose during the last 4 weeks of the study (Week 48–Week 52). The EAG agree the definition for MANDARA trial to be more conservative; however, they do not believe that the difference in definitions, nor the eligibility criteria or trial designs to constitute a substantive difference between the trials. Similarity between MANDARA and MIRRA patient baseline characteristics was also reported on in the CS (CS Section D.1.6, Table 14).[15] The EAG note that the three UK clinical experts interviewed by the company all agreed that the study designs and eligibility criteria of the two trials were comparable.[9] However, compared to MANDARA, two of the clinical experts highlighted the trial population of MIRRA at baseline presented with higher BVAS, indicative of higher disease severity, and all three noted treatment with OCS/IS in MIRRA was greater. Fewer treatment options at the time of the MIRRA trial, 5 years prior to MANDARA, was provided as justification for the observable differences; the level of disease severity may have been addressed with mepolizumab during or after the MIRRA trial thus reducing the levels of IS/OCS treatment. Furthermore, more clinical experience in eosinophil targeted treatment and recent guidelines aiming towards tapering of OCS, may have encouraged a downward trend in OCS treatment by physicians.[1] 

The difference in the timing of the two trials is also relevant; MIRRA took place prior to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (February 2014–September 2016),[37] while MANDARA took place before/during the pandemic (October 2019–August 2023). In the latter trial, COVID-19 was the most common adverse event, experienced by 21% (15/70) and 27% (19/70) of patients in the benralizumab and mepolizumab groups respectively.[1] The MANDARA CSR states that ****** ********** ******************* *********************** ******* ***** **** *** ********** ********************* ***************************** ****************************************[**] **************************************************************** ********************************************************************************************************* 

*****[**] The effect of social distancing measures during the pandemic was suggested in the main study publication as another potential reason for the lower percentage of patients who had a relapse in MANDARA compared to those in MIRRA.[1] 

In the CS Section D.1.10, the company presented a list of potential treatment effect modifiers including eligibility criteria and baseline characteristics from the MANDARA and MIRRA trials to four clinicians.[15] Differences in the ranked, potential effect modifiers were noted between study populations by the clinicians, however these differences were not considered to be meaningful, and confirmed similarity in the trial design, population, and outcomes measurements between the two trials.[5] The company also conducted an anchored MAIC which was adjusted based on a pooled clinical expert-ranked-ordered list of potential, treatment-effect modifiers (see Section 3.3.2 for further discussion).[15] Overall, the EAG consider this approach provides support for the unadjusted Bucher ITC, however as discussed 

71 



<!-- page 374 -->

later in Section 3.3.1.4, not all outcomes in the ITC were validated in the MAIC leaving some uncertainty. 

## _3.3.1.4 Results_ 

The company presented the comparative efficacy of benralizumab versus SoC for nine outcomes in the Bucher ITC, related to remission, relapse and OCS dosage. As discussed in Section 2.3, the definitions of these three outcomes incorporate additional outcomes included in the NICE scope, such as IS usage. Therefore, the clinical effectiveness cannot be independently derived for all outcomes in the ITC. Furthermore, limitations of SF-36 used to measure HRQoL in MANDARA were highlighted by the company which led to the undertaking of two studies to generate more robust evidence to accurately represent QoL in an EGPAspecific population for implementation in the cost-effectiveness analysis (for further discussion see Section 4.2.6). 

The following two outcomes from the ITC: proportion of participants in remission and annualised relapse rate were applied in the company’s economic analysis and are presented in Table 3.8. Compared to SoC, the odds of patients being in remission (main remission definition) at both Week 36 and Week 48 was estimated to be ***** times higher for those receiving benralizumab.[5] Additionally, treatment with benralizumab was estimated to have a *** lower risk of relapse over the course of the year compared to SoC.[5] The company’s consultation with UK clinical experts found that the ITC results were viewed as reasonable.[9] To further validate the results, the company conducted an anchored MAIC for the two outcomes which inform the model, which was adjusted based on the pooled clinical expert rank-ordered list of potential treatment-effect modifiers (discussed in Section 3.3.2.13.3.1.3). The company in response to the PfC (Question A14)[16] confirmed the inputs for the ITC and MAIC to the EAG.[5] The EAG agree the MAIC results for the two outcomes corroborated those generated from the ITC, providing credibility to the Bucher ITC (Table 3.9). However, after adjustment in the MAIC, the effective sample size of the MANDARA trial reduced from 140 to 55,[15] raising some concern; this is further discussed in Section 3.3.2.13.3.2. The EAG further note that Bucher ITCs were conducted for the remaining seven outcomes (CS Section D.1.9, Table 16),[15] however, MAICs were not, leaving some uncertainty relating to these seven outcomes. Considering these additional outcomes did not inform the model, the EAG do not believe this approach to be a major concern.

## _3.3.2.1 Covariates included in the MAIC_ 

In the CS Section D.1.10, the company presented a list of potential treatment effect modifiers including eligibility criteria and baseline characteristics from the MANDARA and MIRRA trials and drawn from consulting the literature.[15] Four clinical experts were individually consulted to identify “crucial” factors, and to rank the remaining “not important” factors in order of importance based on the likelihood the covariate to modify treatment effect (Table 3.10). In response to the PfC (Question A6)[16] the company confirmed these clinical experts to be global specialists in the management and research of EGPA; one UK-based expert in vasculitis, lupus and rare renal disease; two US-based experts specializing in asthma, vasculitis, eosinophilic lung disease and EGPA; and one Canadian-based expert with a special interest in vasculitis. 

A resulting pooled rank-ordered list of potential treatment effect modifiers was used to adjust the MANDARA trial population to match outcome definitions and the distribution of potential treatment effect modifiers in the MIRRA trial. The top 11 factors considered most important and adjusted for in the MAIC; in descending order were: prednisolone or prednisone dose, refractory disease, absolute eosinophil count per mm[3 ] at baseline, immunosuppressive therapy [at baseline], relapsing disease, sinonasal abnormality, immunosuppressive therapy [historical], body mass index, duration since diagnosis of EGPA, BVAS>0 at baseline, and ANCA-positive status [historical].[15] After reweighting the remaining participants, the means, and standard deviations of covariates from the MANDARA trial were almost equal to those of the published MIRRA trial, which is used as the reference (CS Section D.1.10).[15] After adjustment the effective sample size was reduced to 55 (from 140 in the full analysis set) for the MANDARA trial population.[15] As the company only have access to the published summarylevel data from the MIRRA trial which the estimates were based on, the EAG have some concern over the reduced power and accuracy of the analyses. However, the EAG note that while the 95% confidence interval for the OR of remission widened, the confidence interval for the RR of the ARR, remained closely matched to that from the Bucher ITC (Table 3.8 **Error!
